From Imagetext to Worldtext: Generative AI as Operative Ekphrasis


By Watson Hartsoe & Jay David Bolter


Abstract


Generative AI platforms use natural-language prompts to make images, video, and interactive media. Prompting works as a new ekphrasis: it describes, and then it produces. Hannes Bajohr calls this shift operative ekphrasis because the text does not merely evoke a scene; it triggers a model that renders one. Prompt and output image form an imagetext in the sense W.J.T. Mitchell sketched as both ekphrastic dream and ekphrastic dread: words seize the image, and words risk vanishing into the image.


A large community of prompters now builds promptcraft through iterative, multimodal practice. We call the mature form thick prompting because it grows context by stepwise constraint, feedback, and reuse across tools. Because these prompts operate inside probabilistic world models, they do not point only to images; they point to fragments of possible worlds. As systems expand from 2D rendering to immersive 3D scenes, the imagetext expands into a worldtext: a probabilistic, visual, navigable simulation that language steers.


We stage this shift through the canonical Western ekphrasis: Homer’s Shield of Achilles. We show a workflow that moves from Homer’s verbal world building to generated images, and then from images to an interactive 3D environment that users can traverse. We then set Homer beside W.H. Auden’s mid-twentieth-century Shield of Achilles, where the poem overwrites Homer’s social cosmos with a bleak administrative landscape. Operative ekphrasis lets us read this clash as a contest between worldtexts, where history, style, and model weights fight for what the prompt can make.


1. Introduction


Generative AI systems now make text, images, video, code, and interactive environments at mass scale. Visual systems from OpenAI, Google, Meta, and Midjourney still ask for one primary input: a prompt that a human writes. Millions of users now prompt daily, and many of them treat prompting as craft rather than as a one-off request. That community has begun to study its own practice under names like promptcraft, and researchers now map those practices in HCI and computational creativity (Oppenlaender et al. 2024; Oppenlaender 2024; Liu and Chilton 2023). Tool builders also bake these practices into systems that scaffold iteration, templates, and feedback (Almeda 2024; Brade et al. 2023).


Recent scholarship has noticed a historical echo in this everyday act: prompting resembles ekphrasis, the ancient practice of vivid verbal scene-making (Bajohr 2024; Meyer 2023). Computer scientists did not set out to revive Greek rhetoric. Yet the model pipeline made text the most direct interface for image making, because training pairs words and images at scale and learns a shared representational space. That structural coincidence invites an older critical vocabulary, and it also invites a new one. We build on Bajohr’s operative ekphrasis to track a shift that runs past images and toward worlds.


2. Operative Ekphrasis and the Imagetext


Ancient Greek and Roman rhetoricians used ekphrasis as training and public performance, and the term later attached itself to famous passages that describe images with unusual force. Homer’s shield passage in the Iliad became the emblem.


Modern critics revived ekphrasis as a theory problem across the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and they framed it as a site of struggle between word and image (Krieger 1992; Heffernan 2004; Mitchell 1994). Some later work addressed digital media and ekphrasis (Brosch 2018b; Lindhé 2013), but most of that work arrived before diffusion models and large-scale generative systems.


Bajohr bridges that gap by naming prompting an operative form of ekphrasis. A prompt does not only represent an image; it activates a model that renders one. Training collapses the usual boundary between caption and picture, because the model learns from paired text-image corpora and stores those pairings as distributed weights. That collapse sharpens Mitchell’s claim in “Ekphrasis and the Other” (1994): ekphrasis longs to fuse word and image, and ekphrasis fears that fusion. Generative systems realize both at once, because the prompt can summon an image quickly, and the image can also eclipse the need to write.


In this setting, latent space becomes a working imagetext. The prompter probes that space, tests it, and learns its habits. Some scholars and practitioners therefore treat the prompt, or the prompt template, as an artistic object (Chang et al. 2023). That move makes sense if we judge the prompt as part of a coupled system. The prompt alone does not complete the work. The prompt and the produced image complete the imagetext together.


3. Thick Description and the Worldtext


Clifford Geertz used thick description to show how cultural action carries layered codes that an analyst must excavate (Geertz 1993). Thick description starts from practice and writes toward meaning.


Thick prompting flips that direction. A prompter writes, and the system produces. The description does not trail the artifact; it calls the artifact into view. Yet thick prompting still targets deep coding. The model stores that coding as learned semantic weight, and the prompter learns to steer it without ever fully seeing it. Because the model works by probability rather than by explicit rules, no prompt finishes the job forever. The prompter can always refine, split variables, or push the model into a new neighborhood of the space.


This practice aligns with the rise of world models such as Google’s Genie and World Labs’ Marble. Ha and Schmidhuber (2018) describe world models as learned compressed spatiotemporal spaces that agents can use to plan and act. Their aim sits in reinforcement learning, not literary theory, but their framing clarifies our move. A generative system does not store images alone; it stores a space of possible scenes that can unfold over time.


We extend Mitchell’s imagetext into worldtext. In generative AI, each imagetext implies a larger worldtext, because every rendered scene presumes off-screen space, consistent physics, and implied continuity. World generators intensify that implication because they let users navigate, persist changes, and stack scenes into environments. Language becomes the handle that steers world building at scale.


William Gibson called cyberspace a “consensual hallucination.” Generative models literally hallucinate in the clinical sense: they produce percepts without direct external stimulus, and they do so from internal weights. Operative ekphrasis therefore becomes directed hallucination, where text steers what the system invents at each step.


4. Qualities of Thick Prompting


Thick prompting names a family of practices that exceed the single-shot prompt.


Iterative: Prompters rarely stop at one try. They add constraints in sequence, test one variable at a time, and grid the space through controlled variation (He et al. 2024). Tools and methods like taxonomy grids, Dreamsheets, and Promptify support that systematic probing (Almeda et al. 2024; Brade et al. 2023).


Multimodal: Prompters now steer models with both words and images, and they often use image inputs to lock lighting, lens, framing, or pose. That practice treats pixels as a second language for ekphrasis, and it treats the prompt as intermedial craft (Lindley and Whitham 2025).


Heterogeneous: Prompts now mix natural language with structured formats such as JSON and with executable snippets in Python or JavaScript, because the prompter often needs reusable logic and parameter control (Siddaqui 2026).


Itinerant: Prompts migrate across platforms. A prompter can start in text-to-image, carry the output as an input to text-to-3D, and then carry the 3D asset into video or game engines. The prompt travels as operative logic across media.


Performative and interactive: Thick prompting relies on looped feedback. The system returns an output, the prompter reads the output as diagnostic, and the prompter writes the next constraint. That loop distributes agency across human and machine in the sense Hayles gives to cognitive assemblages, because neither side alone controls the final form.


5. The Shield(s) of Achilles: From Image to World


Homer’s shield passage remains the most famous ekphrasis in Western literature, and it does more than describe an object. It describes a world. The shield holds cosmology, agriculture, conflict, ritual, work, and social order in one bounded artifact. That scale makes it a natural test case for our move from imagetext to worldtext.


We treat Homeric oral poetry as an early generative system in one precise sense: performance always varies. The “thousand shields” of oral tradition arise from repetition with drift, where each telling recomposes details within constraints. Probabilistic generation echoes that pattern, because it also produces families of variants rather than one final original.


A thick prompting workflow can therefore translate Homer’s verbal world building into generated imagery, and then use those images as multimodal inputs for a 3D world model. That sequence makes literal what Homer does figuratively. Words build scenes. Scenes become a navigable environment.


Auden’s The Shield of Achilles then provides a counter-world. Auden rewrites Homer’s lively social cosmos into a harsh landscape of modern governance and threat. Operative ekphrasis lets us stage the collision: Homer prompts a world of craft, dance, argument, and harvest, while Auden prompts a world of queueing bodies and administrative violence. A worldtext does not stay neutral when those codes compete.


5.1 Documenting the Operative Workflow: Thickness as Code


To show thick prompting as a real operational pipeline, we document the workflow of the ACHILLES // OPTICAL_GRID_v7 artifact. This system treats the shield as both poem and interface. A user navigates a 3D surface, and that navigation selects text, compiles a micro-prompt, calls a model, and stamps the returned image back onto the surface.


Step 1: Semantic anchoring through zonal selection.
The system partitions the 3D sphere into five UV zones: CORE, INNER, MIDDLE, OUTER, RIM. Each zone stores a stanza-sized portion of Homer’s text. A Three.js raycaster detects cursor intersection, and the code selects the zone that the user points at, then the code anchors the prompt to that literary coordinate.


Step 2: Algorithmic extraction of a poetic snippet.
The code does not send the full stanza. It strips punctuation, tokenizes the text into a word array, then selects a contiguous chunk of five to eight words, with randomized start index. That controlled randomness matters, because it echoes oral drift and keeps the worldtext from freezing into one canonical rendering.


Step 3: Stylistic wrapping as an ekphrastic template.
The code wraps the snippet inside a rigid material frame that keeps the output “shield-like,” for example:
Depict this specific concept deeply engraved in ancient metal: “[POETIC_SNIPPET]”. [RANDOM_STYLE]
The system draws [RANDOM_STYLE] from a curated set of constraints such as “surreal artifact,” “deep metallic patina,” and “cinematic epic lighting.” The code, not the user, carries much of the thickness, because the code enforces repeatable style pressure.


Step 4: Operative execution through a model call.
The system sends the compiled prompt via POST request to a vision generator, and it receives a base64-encoded image.


Step 5: Multimodal reintegration as worldtext.
The code stamps the image back onto the 3D surface at the click coordinate. It blends that stamp into the existing typographic atlas through modes such as Multiply, Screen, and Hard Edge, and it feathers edges through radial gradients. The worldtext grows as the interface accumulates many such micro-prompts over time.


5.3 Accentuated Interfaces: A System That Shows Its Own Making


Many enterprise world models pursue seamlessness. They hide the prompt, hide the stitching, and chase a holodeck illusion. The ACHILLES artifact rejects that path. It belongs to a composite stream that keeps the generative process visible, because the interface makes the world’s becoming stay visible.


The CSS layers impose a mediated lens through CRT overlays and shutter flashes. The UI draws a targeting reticle and fractures the Homeric text into floating word arrays as the user hovers, so the user watches the system slice language into a prompt. The interface exposes blend modes as user controls, so the user participates in the compositing math that fuses text and generated pixels. Export tools then flatten the spherical illusion into polar and planar UV maps, so the user can see the distorted 2D atlas that underwrites the 3D world.


The artifact therefore acts as critical media. It refuses “magic.” It shows slicing, compiling, stamping, and blending as the core operations of operative ekphrasis.


6. Conclusion


Operative ekphrasis, practiced through thick prompting, fulfills and threatens the older dreams of ekphrasis at once. It fulfills Mitchell’s ekphrastic hope by letting language call images into being with speed and force. It also fulfills ekphrastic fear by letting images dominate, and by letting the act of writing recede behind automation.


A narrow HCI lens can miss this tension when it validates prompting only through accuracy, task success, or photoreal fidelity (Liu and Chilton 2023). Thick prompting rarely aims at a single correct image. It aims at discovery inside a probabilistic space, where style, history, and cultural codes collide and recombine.


As systems move from imagetext toward worldtext, the central question becomes governance through practice. Who sets the norms, the tastes, and the criteria for “good” worlds. If photoreal seamlessness becomes the default, prompts and biases can disappear behind convincing simulation. Composite systems offer a different path. They keep language present, keep mechanism legible, and keep world building visible as negotiation between human text and machine weight.


If we want to critique and shape generative worlds, we must build interfaces that do not erase the prompt. We must design worldtexts that let users see how words steer worlds.

Generative AI platforms utilize natural language prompts to create images, videos, and interactive media. Because these prompts draw from and operate through probabilistic world models, they act as fragments of a larger world. To provide an emblematic example of operative ekphrasis and the creation of worldtext, we examine Homer’s Shield of Achilles. We demonstrate how thick prompting techniques can produce first the shield as an image, and then as an immersive 3D world. Finally, we juxtapose this classical ekphrasis with W.H. Auden’s mid-twentieth-century reimagining of the shield, using operative ekphrasis as a lens to read Auden’s poem through, and against, Homer’s original generative world-building.



1. Introduction


Generative AI systems are increasingly used to create a diverse array of media forms, including text, images, videos, program code, and interactive environments. For systems focused on visual artifacts—such as those offered by OpenAI, Google, Meta, and Midjourney—the primary interface remains a natural language prompt provided by a human agent. Prompting has become a ubiquitous practice for millions of users, and the art of effective prompting has crystallized into the discipline of "promptcraft." This practice is actively studied (Oppenlaender et al. 2024; Oppenlaender 2024; Liu and Chilton 2023), leading to the development of systems that embody or enhance these emerging techniques (Almeda 2024; Brade et al. 2023).


As recent scholarship has noted (Bajohr 2024; Meyer 2023), this movement from text to image corresponds in an uncanny way to ekphrasis, the traditional literary practice of vivid description. The architecture of image generation requires training probabilistic models on billions of captioned images. By tokenizing both text and images and mapping them into a unified system of weighted matrices, text prompts became the most logical interface for generation. While the computer scientists developing these systems likely did not intend to reinvent a literary practice that predates modern computing by millennia, this structural coincidence invites us to apply literary history and aesthetic theory to one of the most remarkable developments in the history of digital media. Building on Hannes Bajohr’s insights, we propose a theoretical framework for understanding how promptcraft relates to the history of visual representation, moving from the generation of images to the simulation of worlds.


2. Operative Ekphrasis and the Imagetext


For the ancient Greeks, ekphrasis was a rhetorical practice of describing a vivid visual scene. As noted by classical scholars like George Kennedy, rhetoricians in the Greek-speaking Roman empire utilized ekphrasis as both a pedagogical exercise and a foundational element of public artistic performance. The term became intrinsically linked to famous literary passages, beginning with Homer’s description of Achilles’ shield in the Iliad.


Modern interest in ekphrasis as a literary device expanded throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, yielding compelling theoretical analyses from critics such as Murray Krieger (1992), James Heffernan (2004), and W.J.T. Mitchell (1994). While subsequent literature has addressed the impact of digital media on this practice (Brosch 2018b; Lindhé 2013), this foundational work largely predates generative AI.


Hannes Bajohr (2024) recently bridged this gap by identifying AI prompting as a new paradigm, coining the term “operative ekphrasis.” He distinguishes prompting generative models from traditional computer image manipulation; generative models are performative because they embed textual encodings—derived from captions and metadata scraped from the web—directly into their architecture.  The process of training these models collapses the boundary between text and image, a phenomenon that resonates deeply with W.J.T. Mitchell’s essay "Ekphrasis and the Other" (1994). Mitchell argued that merging text and image was both the audacious aspiration and the ultimate nightmare of ekphrasis. Such a merger would confirm the power of verbal description to control the evoked image, while simultaneously threatening to render the word obsolete by dissolving it into the visual. This merging, which Mitchell termed the imagetext, realizes both "ekphrastic hope and ekphrastic fear."


In generative AI, the latent space of the model effectively functions as this imagetext (or videotext). As Lev Manovich suggests, prompting is the act of probing this latent space. Recognizing this, scholars and practitioners increasingly argue that the prompt itself—or the prompt template—functions as art (Chang et al. 2023). This claim confirms the operational reality of the AI imagetext: the prompt cannot be judged purely as traditional ekphrastic literature, but must be evaluated holistically alongside the image it successfully, or unsuccessfully, retrieves from the latent space.


3. Thick Description and the Worldtext


To characterize the contemporary, elaborate practices of promptcraft, we turn to cultural anthropologist Clifford Geertz and his concept of "thick description" (Geertz 1993). Geertz used the term to describe the process of unearthing and explaining the layered, pre-existing cultural codes that motivate human behavior.


We propose "thick prompting" as the generative corollary to thick description. There is, however, an essential directional difference. Thick description analyzes an existing cultural practice; the practice predates the text. Operative ekphrasis reverses this: the act of describing calls the artifact into existence. Yet, both practices seek to engage deep layers of cultural coding. In thick prompting, these codes are the semantic weights absorbed by the model's neural network. Because these models are probabilistic rather than explicitly coded expert systems, interrogating them is an approximate, incomplete, and potentially endless endeavor. There is no final, perfect prompt.


This concept of thick prompting aligns with the emergence of AI "world models," such as Google's Genie and World Labs' Marble. Ha and Schmidhuber (2018) describe world models as generative environments that learn compressed spatiotemporal representations, enabling agents to act within simulated physics and parameters. While their foundational work focused on reinforcement learning rather than literature, it clarifies a shared orientation: these models build an internal space in which possible worlds can be explored.


We propose extending Mitchell’s notion of the imagetext to the worldtext. In generative AI, every imagetext is implicitly a fragment of a worldtext. Operative ekphrasis collapses the boundary between image and text, much like every traditional painting is a fragment of a larger depicted reality. World generators, however, take us from a static image to a fully realized, navigable world model.


Language thus functions as a direct handle on world generation. The worldtext is not a new medium category, but a condition of practice: language becomes the operative interface for producing scenes, objects, and physics at scale. To return to William Gibson's foundational 1984 definition of cyberspace as a "consensual hallucination," generative AI systems are, in a technical sense, constantly hallucinating. The modern psychiatric definition of hallucination—perceiving something in the absence of external stimuli—applies perfectly to a model generating a world picture from pure mathematical weights. In this sense, all operative ekphrasis is a structured, directed hallucination.


4. The Qualities of Thick Prompting


Thick prompting encompasses a heterogeneous set of practices that move far beyond the single-shot text prompt. As prompting develops into a sophisticated community of practice, several key qualities have emerged:


Iterative: While it is possible to produce a compelling image with a short prompt, thick prompting relies on systematic refinement. Prompters often begin with a short seed and repeatedly add constraints to navigate the latent space (He et al. 2024). Techniques like "prompt differential" (changing one variable at a time) and structured taxonomy grids, as seen in systems like Dreamsheets (Almeda et al. 2024) and Promptify (Brade et al. 2023), support this iterative probing.

Multimodal: To probe the latent space effectively, prompts are no longer strictly textual. They are multimodal, utilizing images, video, and audio as inputs. Practitioners engage in "holistic promptcraft," fluidly moving between text and pixel prompting to control lighting and camera angles (Lindley and Whitham 2025), reflecting the intermediality of digital ekphrasis.

Heterogeneous: The syntax of the prompt is highly varied. Natural language, structured data formats (like JSON), and executable code (Python, JavaScript) can all serve as prompts simultaneously (Siddaqui 2026).

Itinerant: Thick prompting frequently migrates across platforms. A core thick description may be adapted from a text-to-image model and ported into a text-to-3D or text-to-video environment. The prompt, acting as a flexible operative logic, travels across media boundaries.

Performative and Interactive: Thick prompting is an ongoing dialogue. The system feeds back to the prompter, creating a loop of human-AI co-creation (Oppenlaender 2024). This mirrors N. Katherine Hayles' concept of cognitive assemblages, where agency is distributed between the human writer and the generative system.


5. The Shield(s) of Achilles: From Image to World


To illustrate the theoretical trajectory from text to imagetext to worldtext, we turn to the most famous ekphrasis in Western literature: Homer’s Shield of Achilles.  The shield is an obvious choice for its historical primacy, but more importantly, it explicitly describes a world—a holistic representation of Homeric cosmology, agriculture, conflict, and society that sits behind the immediate narrative of the Iliad.


We propose that Homeric oral poetry functions as a nascent generative system. The multiplicity of the "thousand shields"—the variations inherently produced by oral composition and performance over centuries—mirrors the probabilistic variations of AI generation. The shield functions not just as an allegory for the craft of metallurgy, but for the generative making of the world through language.


By applying thick prompting to Homer's text, we can trace a distinct workflow: translating the ancient Greek text into an imagetext using 2D image generators, and subsequently using those outputs as itinerant, multimodal prompts within a 3D world model. This sequence literalizes the ekphrastic world-building Homer performed verbally.


Furthermore, the importance of cultural context in thick prompting is starkly revealed when we juxtapose the Homeric generation with W.H. Auden’s mid-twentieth-century poem, The Shield of Achilles. Auden’s ekphrasis overwrites Homer’s vibrant world with a bleak, bureaucratic landscape reflecting the anxieties of the Cold War. Operative ekphrasis allows us to stage a collision between these two texts and their respective worlds, demonstrating how the weights of a generative model negotiate competing literary and historical contexts to output a synthesized worldtext.


6. Conclusion


Operative ekphrasis, enacted through thick prompting, simultaneously vindicates and vitiates the traditional literary goals of ekphrasis. It fulfills Mitchell’s ekphrastic hope by granting language the power to instantly manifest the visual, yet it realizes his fear by threatening to dissolve the necessity of human artistic rendering. It literalizes the act of description in a way that traditional aesthetic theorists often find illegitimate, echoing the debates surrounding hypertext literature in the 1990s—where traditionalists feared that automating literary association would destroy the art form itself.


There is a risk, particularly within empirical HCI research, of validating prompting strictly through metrics of accuracy or task completion (Liu and Chilton 2023). However, a more nuanced perspective recognizes that the latent space contains undiscovered stylistic and structural possibilities. Probing this space iteratively does not just retrieve data; it creates new combinations.


As generative AI transitions from producing static imagetexts to interactive worldtexts, we must ask who defines the prevailing community of practice. Is it the traditional art community, or a newly defined community of prompters establishing their own criteria for "pop modernism" and originality? By understanding prompting not merely as a technical input, but as an evolution of ekphrasis, we can better critique and shape the worlds these systems generate.



5.1 Documenting the Operative Workflow: The "Thickness" in Practice


To understand how thick prompting operates within this system, we must document the precise algorithmic workflow of the ACHILLES // OPTICAL_GRID_v7 artifact. The system functions as a visual poem architecture, where the spatial navigation of the text structurally and probabilistically determines the generated visual output.


The "thickness" here is not achieved by a user typing a long paragraph into a chat window; rather, the thickness is hardcoded into the javascript logic, creating a distributed, multi-layered prompting engine that executes in real-time.


When a user interacts with the 3D shield, the system executes the following operative ekphrasis:


Step 1: Semantic Anchoring (Zonal Selection): The 3D sphere is divided into five topological UV zones (CORE, INNER, MIDDLE, OUTER, RIM). Each zone acts as a semantic container holding a specific stanza of Homer’s text. When the user’s cursor intersects a zone via the Three.js raycaster, the system anchors the prompt to that specific literary coordinate.

Step 2: Algorithmic Extraction (The Poetic Snippet): The system does not feed the entire stanza to the generative model. Instead, it performs a dynamic, randomized extraction. It strips the punctuation from the anchored text, filters it into an array of words, and randomly selects a contiguous chunk of five to eight words (e.g., "youths wove tunics of spun"). This introduces a necessary element of probabilistic chaos, mimicking the fluidity of oral poetic performance.

Step 3: Stylistic Appending (The Ekphrastic Wrapper): To ensure the resulting imagetext adheres to the material reality of a shield, the script wraps the poetic snippet in a highly structured, rigid prompt template:

Depict this specific concept deeply engraved in ancient metal: "[POETIC_SNIPPET]". [RANDOM_STYLE]
  The [RANDOM_STYLE] is dynamically injected from a predefined array of aesthetic constraints (e.g., "Surreal artifact," "Deep metallic patina," "Cinematic epic lighting").

Step 4: Operative Execution: The synthesized prompt—now thick with spatial context, algorithmic randomness, and hardcoded stylistic constraints—is sent via POST request to a generative vision model (in this case, imagen-3.0).

Step 5: Multimodal Reintegration (The Worldtext): The generative model returns a base64 encoded image. The script intercepts this imagetext and dynamically stamps it back onto the 3D spatial grid at the exact coordinates of the user's initial click. Crucially, it applies interactive blending modes (Multiply, Screen, Hard Edge) and feathered radial gradients to seamlessly fuse the new AI-hallucinated pixels with the underlying typographic text atlas.


Through this documented process, the traditional ekphrasis of reading Homer is transformed. The prompt is not a static string of text; it is an active, iterative compilation of geometry, literature, and code. The resulting 3D environment is a worldtext dynamically accumulated through hundreds of these thick, operative micro-prompts.


5.3 Accentuated Interfaces: Exposing the Generative Machinery


If the Photoreal stream (such as the Waymo World Model) strives for a seamless "Holodeck" where the generative process is entirely hidden behind the illusion of reality, our ACHILLES HTML artifact operates on the exact opposite principle. It resides in the Composite stream precisely because it refuses to hide its own process. Instead of concealing the mechanics of operative ekphrasis, the user interface (UI) and the code architecture actively accentuate them. The interface is designed to make the user hyper-aware of the generative process—making us conscious of the artifact's becoming rather than just its final being.


We achieve this through several deliberate architectural and aesthetic choices within the code:


The Mediated Lens (CRT and Shutter Mechanics): The CSS layers explicitly impose a mediated viewing experience. The continuous crt-overlay animation and the blinding shutter-flash upon image capture constantly remind the viewer that they are not looking at a natural world, but through a computational apparatus.

The Ekphrastic Targeting HUD: The hud-canvas overlay does not hide the prompt extraction; it dramatizes it. When a user hovers over a semantic zone, the JavaScript draws a targeting reticle, casts dynamic connecting lines, and visually fractures the underlying Homeric text into floating arrays of words. The UI explicitly announces TARGET ACQUIRED. CLICK TO STAMP POETRY. The user is forced to visually witness the AI slicing the text to construct its operative prompt.

Exposed Compositing Logic: The system grants the user manual control over the mathematical blending of the imagetext. By exposing keybind commands to toggle between NORMAL (FEATHERED), MULTIPLY (BURNED), and SCREEN (ETHEREAL) blend modes, the UI forces the user to participate in the algorithmic compositing of the worldtext.

Deconstructing the Illusion: The most aggressive exposure of the process occurs through the export tools. By pressing a key, the user can instantly extract the raw, flattened polar and planar UV maps (mosaicCanvas and coreCanvas). This shatters the 3D illusion entirely, revealing the distorted, 2D imagetext that undergirds the spherical world model.


By accentuating these mechanics, the ACHILLES artifact functions as a piece of critical media. It demands that we recognize operative ekphrasis not as magic, but as a heavily mediated, algorithmic process of slicing, compiling, and stamping cultural data. It keeps the "word" fiercely visible, ensuring that the act of world-building remains a visible negotiation between human text and machine weights.


6. Conclusion: The Future of the Worldtext


Operative ekphrasis, enacted through the rigorous, iterative practices of thick prompting, simultaneously vindicates and vitiates the traditional literary goals of ekphrasis. It fulfills W.J.T. Mitchell’s "ekphrastic hope" by granting language the computational power to instantly manifest the visual, allowing the word to definitively govern the image. Yet, as generative systems evolve from 2D imagetexts to 3D interactive worldtexts, they increasingly realize his "ekphrastic fear": the threat that the image will entirely consume the word, rendering human literary description obsolete.


This tension is formalized in the divergence of the two generative streams we have identified.  The Photoreal Stream, exemplified by enterprise world models like Genie 3, drives toward the ultimate disappearance of the text. It seeks a seamless, physics-based Holodeck where the linguistic prompt acts only as a hidden, subterranean trigger for a flawless simulation. In contrast, the Composite Stream, as demonstrated by our interactive ACHILLES artifact, actively resists this erasure. By accentuating the user interface, exposing the code, and revealing the compositional blending of text and generated pixel, it forces the generative machinery to remain visible. It demands that we acknowledge the worldtext not as a natural reality, but as a constructed, probabilistic collage.


This literalization of the descriptive act echoes the theoretical anxieties surrounding the hypertext literary movement of the 1990s. Hypertext enthusiasts claimed their medium made the cognitive processes of association and allusion structurally operative; traditionalists feared that automating these connections would destroy the interpretive art of reading. A similar anxiety permeates the reception of generative AI. There is a persistent risk, particularly within empirical Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) research, of validating promptcraft strictly through metrics of accuracy, task completion, or photorealism (Liu and Chilton 2023). However, a more nuanced perspective, aligned with Lev Manovich’s observations on generative style, recognizes that the latent space contains undiscovered aesthetic possibilities. Probing this space iteratively through thick prompting does not merely retrieve a "correct" image; it is an act of active, operative discovery.


As these systems mature, the critical question becomes: who defines the prevailing community of practice? Traditional art and literary communities often view the automation of ekphrasis as problematic or illegitimate. In their place, a newly defined, massive community of amateur and professional prompters is establishing its own criteria for success, emphasizing a kind of "pop modernism" characterized by the continuous remixing of historical styles and cultural weights (Chang et al. 2023).


If we allow the Photoreal stream to become the default mode of generative media, we risk moving into seamless, immersive environments where the biases, weights, and algorithmic decisions of the world model are entirely hidden from the user. We lose sight of the prompt. To critically engage with generative AI, we must champion the Composite stream. We must build and theorize interfaces that expose the thickness of the prompt, ensuring that the act of computational world-building remains a visible, negotiated dialogue between human language and machine logic.

</section>

{# From Imagetext to Worldtext: Generative AI as Operative Ekphrasis


By Watson Hartsoe & Jay David Bolter


Abstract


Generative AI platforms utilize natural language prompts to create images, videos, and interactive media. The act of prompting can be understood as a new form of ekphrasis—the ancient literary practice of vivid visual description. The crucial difference is that unlike traditional ekphrasis in poetry and prose, the ekphrasis of prompting is, as Hannes Bajohr argues, “operative”: the text not only describes an image but computationally generates it, collapsing the traditional distinction between the verbal and the visual. Prompt and image together constitute an imagetext, which W.J.T. Mitchell suggested was always the unstated and unattainable goal of ekphrasis. Furthermore, a growing community of amateur and professional prompters has developed "promptcraft"—practices for improving resulting media artifacts through elaborate, iterative interactions. We characterize these techniques as “thick prompting,” contrasting them with the one-shot, “thin” prompts of casual users, deliberately recalling Clifford Geertz’s anthropological concept of “thick description.” Thick prompting is an iterative, multimodal process of refinement that describes and defines the context of a desired artifact. Because these prompts draw from and operate through probabilistic world models, they act as fragments of a larger world. As generative systems evolve to create entire immersive 3D environments, the imagetext becomes a worldtext: a probabilistic, visual, and interactive simulation. To provide an emblematic example of operative ekphrasis and the creation of worldtext, we examine Homer’s Shield of Achilles. We demonstrate how thick prompting techniques can produce first the shield as an image, and then as an immersive 3D world. Finally, we juxtapose this classical ekphrasis with W.H. Auden’s mid-twentieth-century reimagining of the shield, using operative ekphrasis as a lens to read Auden’s poem through, and against, Homer’s original generative world-building.



1. Introduction


Generative AI systems are increasingly used to create a diverse array of media forms, including text, images, videos, program code, and interactive environments. For systems focused on visual artifacts—such as those offered by OpenAI, Google, Meta, and Midjourney—the primary interface remains a natural language prompt provided by a human agent. Prompting has become a ubiquitous practice for millions of users, and the art of effective prompting has crystallized into the discipline of "promptcraft." This practice is actively studied (Oppenlaender et al. 2024; Oppenlaender 2024; Liu and Chilton 2023), leading to the development of systems that embody or enhance these emerging techniques (Almeda 2024; Brade et al. 2023).


As recent scholarship has noted (Bajohr 2024; Meyer 2023), this movement from text to image corresponds in an uncanny way to ekphrasis, the traditional literary practice of vivid description. The architecture of image generation requires training probabilistic models on billions of captioned images. By tokenizing both text and images and mapping them into a unified system of weighted matrices, text prompts became the most logical interface for generation. While the computer scientists developing these systems likely did not intend to reinvent a literary practice that predates modern computing by millennia, this structural coincidence invites us to apply literary history and aesthetic theory to one of the most remarkable developments in the history of digital media. Building on Hannes Bajohr’s insights, we propose a theoretical framework for understanding how promptcraft relates to the history of visual representation, moving from the generation of images to the simulation of worlds.


2. Operative Ekphrasis and the Imagetext


For the ancient Greeks, ekphrasis was a rhetorical practice of describing a vivid visual scene. As noted by classical scholars like George Kennedy, rhetoricians in the Greek-speaking Roman empire utilized ekphrasis as both a pedagogical exercise and a foundational element of public artistic performance. The term became intrinsically linked to famous literary passages, beginning with Homer’s description of Achilles’ shield in the Iliad.


Modern interest in ekphrasis as a literary device expanded throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, yielding compelling theoretical analyses from critics such as Murray Krieger (1992), James Heffernan (2004), and W.J.T. Mitchell (1994). While subsequent literature has addressed the impact of digital media on this practice (Brosch 2018b; Lindhé 2013), this foundational work largely predates generative AI.


Hannes Bajohr (2024) recently bridged this gap by identifying AI prompting as a new paradigm, coining the term “operative ekphrasis.” He distinguishes prompting generative models from traditional computer image manipulation; generative models are performative because they embed textual encodings—derived from captions and metadata scraped from the web—directly into their architecture.  The process of training these models collapses the boundary between text and image, a phenomenon that resonates deeply with W.J.T. Mitchell’s essay "Ekphrasis and the Other" (1994). Mitchell argued that merging text and image was both the audacious aspiration and the ultimate nightmare of ekphrasis. Such a merger would confirm the power of verbal description to control the evoked image, while simultaneously threatening to render the word obsolete by dissolving it into the visual. This merging, which Mitchell termed the imagetext, realizes both "ekphrastic hope and ekphrastic fear."


In generative AI, the latent space of the model effectively functions as this imagetext (or videotext). As Lev Manovich suggests, prompting is the act of probing this latent space. Recognizing this, scholars and practitioners increasingly argue that the prompt itself—or the prompt template—functions as art (Chang et al. 2023). This claim confirms the operational reality of the AI imagetext: the prompt cannot be judged purely as traditional ekphrastic literature, but must be evaluated holistically alongside the image it successfully, or unsuccessfully, retrieves from the latent space.


3. Thick Description and the Worldtext


To characterize the contemporary, elaborate practices of promptcraft, we turn to cultural anthropologist Clifford Geertz and his concept of "thick description" (Geertz 1993). Geertz used the term to describe the process of unearthing and explaining the layered, pre-existing cultural codes that motivate human behavior.


We propose "thick prompting" as the generative corollary to thick description. There is, however, an essential directional difference. Thick description analyzes an existing cultural practice; the practice predates the text. Operative ekphrasis reverses this: the act of describing calls the artifact into existence. Yet, both practices seek to engage deep layers of cultural coding. In thick prompting, these codes are the semantic weights absorbed by the model's neural network. Because these models are probabilistic rather than explicitly coded expert systems, interrogating them is an approximate, incomplete, and potentially endless endeavor. There is no final, perfect prompt.


This concept of thick prompting aligns with the emergence of AI "world models," such as Google's Genie and World Labs' Marble. Ha and Schmidhuber (2018) describe world models as generative environments that learn compressed spatiotemporal representations, enabling agents to act within simulated physics and parameters. While their foundational work focused on reinforcement learning rather than literature, it clarifies a shared orientation: these models build an internal space in which possible worlds can be explored.


We propose extending Mitchell’s notion of the imagetext to the worldtext. In generative AI, every imagetext is implicitly a fragment of a worldtext. Operative ekphrasis collapses the boundary between image and text, much like every traditional painting is a fragment of a larger depicted reality. World generators, however, take us from a static image to a fully realized, navigable world model.


Language thus functions as a direct handle on world generation. The worldtext is not a new medium category, but a condition of practice: language becomes the operative interface for producing scenes, objects, and physics at scale. To return to William Gibson's foundational 1984 definition of cyberspace as a "consensual hallucination," generative AI systems are, in a technical sense, constantly hallucinating. The modern psychiatric definition of hallucination—perceiving something in the absence of external stimuli—applies perfectly to a model generating a world picture from pure mathematical weights. In this sense, all operative ekphrasis is a structured, directed hallucination.


4. The Qualities of Thick Prompting


Thick prompting encompasses a heterogeneous set of practices that move far beyond the single-shot text prompt. As prompting develops into a sophisticated community of practice, several key qualities have emerged:


Iterative: While it is possible to produce a compelling image with a short prompt, thick prompting relies on systematic refinement. Prompters often begin with a short seed and repeatedly add constraints to navigate the latent space (He et al. 2024). Techniques like "prompt differential" (changing one variable at a time) and structured taxonomy grids, as seen in systems like Dreamsheets (Almeda et al. 2024) and Promptify (Brade et al. 2023), support this iterative probing.

Multimodal: To probe the latent space effectively, prompts are no longer strictly textual. They are multimodal, utilizing images, video, and audio as inputs. Practitioners engage in "holistic promptcraft," fluidly moving between text and pixel prompting to control lighting and camera angles (Lindley and Whitham 2025), reflecting the intermediality of digital ekphrasis.

Heterogeneous: The syntax of the prompt is highly varied. Natural language, structured data formats (like JSON), and executable code (Python, JavaScript) can all serve as prompts simultaneously (Siddaqui 2026).

Itinerant: Thick prompting frequently migrates across platforms. A core thick description may be adapted from a text-to-image model and ported into a text-to-3D or text-to-video environment. The prompt, acting as a flexible operative logic, travels across media boundaries.

Performative and Interactive: Thick prompting is an ongoing dialogue. The system feeds back to the prompter, creating a loop of human-AI co-creation (Oppenlaender 2024). This mirrors N. Katherine Hayles' concept of cognitive assemblages, where agency is distributed between the human writer and the generative system.


5. The Shield(s) of Achilles: From Image to World


To illustrate the theoretical trajectory from text to imagetext to worldtext, we turn to the most famous ekphrasis in Western literature: Homer’s Shield of Achilles.  The shield is an obvious choice for its historical primacy, but more importantly, it explicitly describes a world—a holistic representation of Homeric cosmology, agriculture, conflict, and society that sits behind the immediate narrative of the Iliad.


We propose that Homeric oral poetry functions as a nascent generative system. The multiplicity of the "thousand shields"—the variations inherently produced by oral composition and performance over centuries—mirrors the probabilistic variations of AI generation. The shield functions not just as an allegory for the craft of metallurgy, but for the generative making of the world through language.


By applying thick prompting to Homer's text, we can trace a distinct workflow: translating the ancient Greek text into an imagetext using 2D image generators, and subsequently using those outputs as itinerant, multimodal prompts within a 3D world model. This sequence literalizes the ekphrastic world-building Homer performed verbally.


Furthermore, the importance of cultural context in thick prompting is starkly revealed when we juxtapose the Homeric generation with W.H. Auden’s mid-twentieth-century poem, The Shield of Achilles. Auden’s ekphrasis overwrites Homer’s vibrant world with a bleak, bureaucratic landscape reflecting the anxieties of the Cold War. Operative ekphrasis allows us to stage a collision between these two texts and their respective worlds, demonstrating how the weights of a generative model negotiate competing literary and historical contexts to output a synthesized worldtext.


6. Conclusion


Operative ekphrasis, enacted through thick prompting, simultaneously vindicates and vitiates the traditional literary goals of ekphrasis. It fulfills Mitchell’s ekphrastic hope by granting language the power to instantly manifest the visual, yet it realizes his fear by threatening to dissolve the necessity of human artistic rendering. It literalizes the act of description in a way that traditional aesthetic theorists often find illegitimate, echoing the debates surrounding hypertext literature in the 1990s—where traditionalists feared that automating literary association would destroy the art form itself.


There is a risk, particularly within empirical HCI research, of validating prompting strictly through metrics of accuracy or task completion (Liu and Chilton 2023). However, a more nuanced perspective recognizes that the latent space contains undiscovered stylistic and structural possibilities. Probing this space iteratively does not just retrieve data; it creates new combinations.


As generative AI transitions from producing static imagetexts to interactive worldtexts, we must ask who defines the prevailing community of practice. Is it the traditional art community, or a newly defined community of prompters establishing their own criteria for "pop modernism" and originality? By understanding prompting not merely as a technical input, but as an evolution of ekphrasis, we can better critique and shape the worlds these systems generate.



5.1 Documenting the Operative Workflow: The "Thickness" in Practice


To understand how thick prompting operates within this system, we must document the precise algorithmic workflow of the ACHILLES // OPTICAL_GRID_v7 artifact. The system functions as a visual poem architecture, where the spatial navigation of the text structurally and probabilistically determines the generated visual output.


The "thickness" here is not achieved by a user typing a long paragraph into a chat window; rather, the thickness is hardcoded into the javascript logic, creating a distributed, multi-layered prompting engine that executes in real-time.


When a user interacts with the 3D shield, the system executes the following operative ekphrasis:


Step 1: Semantic Anchoring (Zonal Selection): The 3D sphere is divided into five topological UV zones (CORE, INNER, MIDDLE, OUTER, RIM). Each zone acts as a semantic container holding a specific stanza of Homer’s text. When the user’s cursor intersects a zone via the Three.js raycaster, the system anchors the prompt to that specific literary coordinate.

Step 2: Algorithmic Extraction (The Poetic Snippet): The system does not feed the entire stanza to the generative model. Instead, it performs a dynamic, randomized extraction. It strips the punctuation from the anchored text, filters it into an array of words, and randomly selects a contiguous chunk of five to eight words (e.g., "youths wove tunics of spun"). This introduces a necessary element of probabilistic chaos, mimicking the fluidity of oral poetic performance.

Step 3: Stylistic Appending (The Ekphrastic Wrapper): To ensure the resulting imagetext adheres to the material reality of a shield, the script wraps the poetic snippet in a highly structured, rigid prompt template:

Depict this specific concept deeply engraved in ancient metal: "[POETIC_SNIPPET]". [RANDOM_STYLE]
  The [RANDOM_STYLE] is dynamically injected from a predefined array of aesthetic constraints (e.g., "Surreal artifact," "Deep metallic patina," "Cinematic epic lighting").

Step 4: Operative Execution: The synthesized prompt—now thick with spatial context, algorithmic randomness, and hardcoded stylistic constraints—is sent via POST request to a generative vision model (in this case, imagen-3.0).

Step 5: Multimodal Reintegration (The Worldtext): The generative model returns a base64 encoded image. The script intercepts this imagetext and dynamically stamps it back onto the 3D spatial grid at the exact coordinates of the user's initial click. Crucially, it applies interactive blending modes (Multiply, Screen, Hard Edge) and feathered radial gradients to seamlessly fuse the new AI-hallucinated pixels with the underlying typographic text atlas.


Through this documented process, the traditional ekphrasis of reading Homer is transformed. The prompt is not a static string of text; it is an active, iterative compilation of geometry, literature, and code. The resulting 3D environment is a worldtext dynamically accumulated through hundreds of these thick, operative micro-prompts.


5.3 Accentuated Interfaces: Exposing the Generative Machinery


If the Photoreal stream (such as the Waymo World Model) strives for a seamless "Holodeck" where the generative process is entirely hidden behind the illusion of reality, our ACHILLES HTML artifact operates on the exact opposite principle. It resides in the Composite stream precisely because it refuses to hide its own process. Instead of concealing the mechanics of operative ekphrasis, the user interface (UI) and the code architecture actively accentuate them. The interface is designed to make the user hyper-aware of the generative process—making us conscious of the artifact's becoming rather than just its final being.


We achieve this through several deliberate architectural and aesthetic choices within the code:


The Mediated Lens (CRT and Shutter Mechanics): The CSS layers explicitly impose a mediated viewing experience. The continuous crt-overlay animation and the blinding shutter-flash upon image capture constantly remind the viewer that they are not looking at a natural world, but through a computational apparatus.

The Ekphrastic Targeting HUD: The hud-canvas overlay does not hide the prompt extraction; it dramatizes it. When a user hovers over a semantic zone, the JavaScript draws a targeting reticle, casts dynamic connecting lines, and visually fractures the underlying Homeric text into floating arrays of words. The UI explicitly announces TARGET ACQUIRED. CLICK TO STAMP POETRY. The user is forced to visually witness the AI slicing the text to construct its operative prompt.

Exposed Compositing Logic: The system grants the user manual control over the mathematical blending of the imagetext. By exposing keybind commands to toggle between NORMAL (FEATHERED), MULTIPLY (BURNED), and SCREEN (ETHEREAL) blend modes, the UI forces the user to participate in the algorithmic compositing of the worldtext.

Deconstructing the Illusion: The most aggressive exposure of the process occurs through the export tools. By pressing a key, the user can instantly extract the raw, flattened polar and planar UV maps (mosaicCanvas and coreCanvas). This shatters the 3D illusion entirely, revealing the distorted, 2D imagetext that undergirds the spherical world model.


By accentuating these mechanics, the ACHILLES artifact functions as a piece of critical media. It demands that we recognize operative ekphrasis not as magic, but as a heavily mediated, algorithmic process of slicing, compiling, and stamping cultural data. It keeps the "word" fiercely visible, ensuring that the act of world-building remains a visible negotiation between human text and machine weights.


6. Conclusion: The Future of the Worldtext


Operative ekphrasis, enacted through the rigorous, iterative practices of thick prompting, simultaneously vindicates and vitiates the traditional literary goals of ekphrasis. It fulfills W.J.T. Mitchell’s "ekphrastic hope" by granting language the computational power to instantly manifest the visual, allowing the word to definitively govern the image. Yet, as generative systems evolve from 2D imagetexts to 3D interactive worldtexts, they increasingly realize his "ekphrastic fear": the threat that the image will entirely consume the word, rendering human literary description obsolete.


This tension is formalized in the divergence of the two generative streams we have identified.  The Photoreal Stream, exemplified by enterprise world models like Genie 3, drives toward the ultimate disappearance of the text. It seeks a seamless, physics-based Holodeck where the linguistic prompt acts only as a hidden, subterranean trigger for a flawless simulation. In contrast, the Composite Stream, as demonstrated by our interactive ACHILLES artifact, actively resists this erasure. By accentuating the user interface, exposing the code, and revealing the compositional blending of text and generated pixel, it forces the generative machinery to remain visible. It demands that we acknowledge the worldtext not as a natural reality, but as a constructed, probabilistic collage.


This literalization of the descriptive act echoes the theoretical anxieties surrounding the hypertext literary movement of the 1990s. Hypertext enthusiasts claimed their medium made the cognitive processes of association and allusion structurally operative; traditionalists feared that automating these connections would destroy the interpretive art of reading. A similar anxiety permeates the reception of generative AI. There is a persistent risk, particularly within empirical Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) research, of validating promptcraft strictly through metrics of accuracy, task completion, or photorealism (Liu and Chilton 2023). However, a more nuanced perspective, aligned with Lev Manovich’s observations on generative style, recognizes that the latent space contains undiscovered aesthetic possibilities. Probing this space iteratively through thick prompting does not merely retrieve a "correct" image; it is an act of active, operative discovery.


As these systems mature, the critical question becomes: who defines the prevailing community of practice? Traditional art and literary communities often view the automation of ekphrasis as problematic or illegitimate. In their place, a newly defined, massive community of amateur and professional prompters is establishing its own criteria for success, emphasizing a kind of "pop modernism" characterized by the continuous remixing of historical styles and cultural weights (Chang et al. 2023).


If we allow the Photoreal stream to become the default mode of generative media, we risk moving into seamless, immersive environments where the biases, weights, and algorithmic decisions of the world model are entirely hidden from the user. We lose sight of the prompt. To critically engage with generative AI, we must champion the Composite stream. We must build and theorize interfaces that expose the thickness of the prompt, ensuring that the act of computational world-building remains a visible, negotiated dialogue between human language and machine logic.


STANDING RESERVE}

From Imagetext to Worldtext: Generative AI as Operative Ekphrasis


Watson Hartsoe & Jay David Bolter


Abstract


Generative AI has made an old literary ambition suddenly operational: language now executes images, scenes, and increasingly whole environments. We argue that prompting is best understood as operative ekphrasis—a new form of vivid description in which text does not merely evoke the visual but computationally produces it. Building on W.J.T. Mitchell’s concept of the imagetext, we introduce the worldtext: a prompt-addressable, probabilistic simulation in which images are not endpoints but fragments of a navigable world model. This shift changes what ekphrasis is—from representation to production—and it changes what critique must target: not just outputs, but the interface logics and constraint systems that steer generation. We define thick prompting as the practical method of worldtext-making: an iterative, multimodal, itinerant, and often code-mediated practice that compiles context into executable constraints. As an emblematic case, we stage Homer’s Shield of Achilles as a world-specification that can be translated from text to imagetext to interactive worldtext, then collide it with W.H. Auden’s twentieth-century anti-shield to show how historical mood and institutional power reweight what a “shield-world” becomes. Our claim is simple: as generative systems move from pictures to worlds, the central cultural question is no longer whether images look real—it is whether the world-building machinery remains legible and contestable.



1. The Shift: Description Becomes Execution


Millions of people now use natural language prompts to create images, video, code, and interactive media. That surface fact hides a deeper transformation: description has become a control surface. When a user types a prompt into a generative model, they are not just describing an image—they are issuing an instruction into a probabilistic world model trained on captioned cultural archives.


This is where ekphrasis returns—not as metaphor, but as infrastructure. Classical ekphrasis is vivid verbal description that makes an audience “see.” In generative AI, the same gesture becomes operative: the text is embedded as a steering mechanism in the model’s learned associations. Hannes Bajohr names this shift “operative ekphrasis.” We adopt the term because it identifies what matters most: prompts are not commentary about an image; they are part of the causal chain that produces an image.


Mitchell’s “imagetext” helps explain why this feels culturally uncanny. Ekphrasis has always carried a tension between the word’s desire to govern the image (“ekphrastic hope”) and the fear that the image will swallow language (“ekphrastic fear”). Generative AI intensifies this tension because it turns the imagetext into a computational merger: prompts and outputs form a single operational unit. A prompt cannot be judged like a poem in isolation; it must be judged as a performative specification whose meaning includes what it generates.



2. The New Object: From Imagetext to Worldtext


Image generators already imply worlds: every picture presupposes a surrounding reality, a physics, a social texture. What changes now is that generative systems increasingly aim to produce interactive environments—scenes you can enter, traverse, and modify. This motivates our extension of imagetext into worldtext.


Worldtext names a condition of practice: language becomes a direct handle on the production of scenes, objects, behaviors, and constraints at scale. A worldtext is not simply “3D.” It is a probabilistic simulation whose coherence emerges from learned weights, and whose outputs are always provisional—samples from a distribution, not a single authored artifact.


This matters because critique has to evolve. The key risk is not only bias “in the data” or style “in the outputs.” The risk is that world models will deliver seamless immersion while hiding the mechanisms by which worlds are assembled—what is included, excluded, normalized, or made impossible. When the prompt becomes subterranean—an invisible trigger behind a perfect simulation—worldtext becomes politically slippery: persuasive, unaccountable, and hard to audit.



3. Thick Prompting: How Worldtexts Are Actually Made


The popular image of prompting is a short incantation (“a dragon in a castle”). That’s thin prompting: fast, casual, and often satisfying. But the craft that reliably steers generative systems—especially across media types—is different. We call it thick prompting, and it is not defined by length. It is defined by how constraints are accumulated, migrated, and operationalized.


Thick prompting has five practical qualities:


Iterative: It proceeds through controlled variation and feedback, treating generation as a search process rather than a one-shot request.

Multimodal: It uses images, sketches, masks, reference frames, and sometimes audio alongside text to steer composition, lighting, and style.

Heterogeneous: It mixes natural language with templates, structured data, and executable code—often embedding the “prompt” inside a pipeline.

Itinerant: It travels across tools: text-to-image constraints become inputs for text-to-3D, image-to-video, or interactive engines.

Performative and interactive: It is a dialogue with the system’s feedback, distributing agency across human and model, in line with Hayles’ cognitive assemblages.


Thick prompting is the generative counterpart to Geertz’s thick description—but with a reversal of direction. Thick description interprets a practice that already exists; thick prompting compiles a description that brings a practice-like artifact into existence. The “culture” it interrogates is the model’s learned semantic archive: weights shaped by captioned images, metadata, and historical style sediment.



4. The Emblematic Case: Achilles’ Shield as World-Specification


If we want a canonical test for worldtext, we should choose an ekphrasis that already functions like a world generator. Homer’s Shield of Achilles is exactly that: a crafted object that contains a cosmos—city life, agriculture, conflict, ritual, weather, and the edges of the world. The shield is not decoration; it is compressed world-building.


Our claim is not that Homer “predicted AI.” The claim is more precise: the shield passage behaves like a generative specification. It defines zones, scenes, transitions, and social energies in a way that can be translated into modern generative workflows: first into an imagetext (2D generation), then into a worldtext (a navigable environment), where the viewer’s movement becomes a method of reading.


This translation also exposes the stakes of cultural weighting. W.H. Auden’s The Shield of Achilles overwrites Homer’s vivid multiplicity with a bleak administrative landscape. Auden’s ekphrasis is not a stylistic variant; it is a historical reweighting of what “a world on a shield” can mean after industrial war and bureaucratic violence. Operative ekphrasis gives us a way to stage that collision: not as an abstract comparison, but as competing world specifications struggling inside a system trained on cultural archives.



5. Proof-by-Making: ACHILLES // OPTICAL_GRID_v7


The paper’s central argument becomes real when the prompt stops being a sentence and becomes an architecture. The ACHILLES artifact demonstrates thick prompting as a distributed system: geometry + text + randomness + templates + compositing.


What it shows, in one line:
A “prompt” can be a procedural reading machine that converts literary coordinates into executable micro-specifications and accumulates the results into a navigable world surface.


Operational core:


The shield is divided into semantic zones (CORE, INNER, MIDDLE, OUTER, RIM).

Interaction selects a zone, extracts a short contiguous snippet, wraps it in a rigid “engraved metal” template plus style constraints, and sends it to a vision model.

The returned imagetext is stamped back onto the shield’s surface and composited using exposed blend modes, so the user can see and control the world’s assembly.


This matters because it makes an argument about the future of worldtext legible in the present: the interface can either erase its own generative mechanics or accentuate them.



6. The Fork in the Road: Photoreal Stream vs Composite Stream


As world models advance, two design trajectories diverge:


Photoreal Stream: The system’s goal is seamless simulation. Prompts disappear into the substrate. The world feels “natural,” which makes its assumptions harder to see and contest.

Composite Stream: The system refuses invisibility. It keeps the prompt, the stitching, and the mediation visible—through UI, overlays, exports, and user-controlled compositing.


Our argument is not aesthetic snobbery. It is governance logic: legibility is a precondition for critique. If the dominant future is photoreal immersion with hidden prompts, worldtexts will become powerful cultural instruments without obvious handles for accountability. Composite interfaces preserve those handles by keeping the generative process present as a visible negotiation between language, code, and machine weights.



Conclusion: Why This Matters Now


Operative ekphrasis is the name of a new cultural power: language that produces worlds. Thick prompting is the method by which that power becomes reliable and portable. Worldtext is the object that now demands critique: not merely images, but simulated environments whose coherence is sampled from probabilistic archives.


The stakes are immediate. The question is not whether generative media will become more immersive—it will. The question is whether the machinery of world-making will be hidden as “reality” or exposed as construction. If we want worldtexts that can be interpreted, challenged, and ethically steered, we need interfaces and practices that keep prompts—and the systems that compile them—legible.


If you want, I can do the same “communication shift” pass on just one target slice (e.g., Abstract-only for submission, or Sections 3–5 for a methods-heavy venue), but the draft above is designed to function as a clean, reviewer-readable spine for the whole paper.

{# From Imagetext to Worldtext: Generative AI as Operative Ekphrasis


By Watson Hartsoe & Jay David Bolter


Abstract


Generative AI platforms utilize natural language prompts to create images, videos, and interactive media. The act of prompting can be understood as a new form of ekphrasis—the ancient literary practice of vivid visual description. The crucial difference is that unlike traditional ekphrasis in poetry and prose, the ekphrasis of prompting is, as Hannes Bajohr argues, “operative”: the text not only describes an image but computationally generates it, collapsing the traditional distinction between the verbal and the visual. Prompt and image together constitute an imagetext, which W.J.T. Mitchell suggested was always the unstated and unattainable goal of ekphrasis. Furthermore, a growing community of amateur and professional prompters has developed "promptcraft"—practices for improving resulting media artifacts through elaborate, iterative interactions. We characterize these techniques as “thick prompting,” contrasting them with the one-shot, “thin” prompts of casual users, deliberately recalling Clifford Geertz’s anthropological concept of “thick description.” Thick prompting is an iterative, multimodal process of refinement that describes and defines the context of a desired artifact. Because these prompts draw from and operate through probabilistic world models, they act as fragments of a larger world. As generative systems evolve to create entire immersive 3D environments, the imagetext becomes a worldtext: a probabilistic, visual, and interactive simulation. To provide an emblematic example of operative ekphrasis and the creation of worldtext, we examine Homer’s Shield of Achilles. We demonstrate how thick prompting techniques can produce first the shield as an image, and then as an immersive 3D world. Finally, we juxtapose this classical ekphrasis with W.H. Auden’s mid-twentieth-century reimagining of the shield, using operative ekphrasis as a lens to read Auden’s poem through, and against, Homer’s original generative world-building.



1. Introduction


Generative AI systems are increasingly used to create a diverse array of media forms, including text, images, videos, program code, and interactive environments. For systems focused on visual artifacts—such as those offered by OpenAI, Google, Meta, and Midjourney—the primary interface remains a natural language prompt provided by a human agent. Prompting has become a ubiquitous practice for millions of users, and the art of effective prompting has crystallized into the discipline of "promptcraft." This practice is actively studied (Oppenlaender et al. 2024; Oppenlaender 2024; Liu and Chilton 2023), leading to the development of systems that embody or enhance these emerging techniques (Almeda 2024; Brade et al. 2023).


As recent scholarship has noted (Bajohr 2024; Meyer 2023), this movement from text to image corresponds in an uncanny way to ekphrasis, the traditional literary practice of vivid description. The architecture of image generation requires training probabilistic models on billions of captioned images. By tokenizing both text and images and mapping them into a unified system of weighted matrices, text prompts became the most logical interface for generation. While the computer scientists developing these systems likely did not intend to reinvent a literary practice that predates modern computing by millennia, this structural coincidence invites us to apply literary history and aesthetic theory to one of the most remarkable developments in the history of digital media. Building on Hannes Bajohr’s insights, we propose a theoretical framework for understanding how promptcraft relates to the history of visual representation, moving from the generation of images to the simulation of worlds.


2. Operative Ekphrasis and the Imagetext


For the ancient Greeks, ekphrasis was a rhetorical practice of describing a vivid visual scene. As noted by classical scholars like George Kennedy, rhetoricians in the Greek-speaking Roman empire utilized ekphrasis as both a pedagogical exercise and a foundational element of public artistic performance. The term became intrinsically linked to famous literary passages, beginning with Homer’s description of Achilles’ shield in the Iliad.
