{# From Imagetext to Worldtext: Generative AI as Operative Ekphrasis


By Watson Hartsoe & Jay David Bolter


Abstract


Generative AI platforms utilize natural language prompts to create images, videos, and interactive media. The act of prompting can be understood as a new form of ekphrasis—the ancient literary practice of vivid visual description. The crucial difference is that unlike traditional ekphrasis in poetry and prose, the ekphrasis of prompting is, as Hannes Bajohr argues, “operative”: the text not only describes an image but computationally generates it, collapsing the traditional distinction between the verbal and the visual. Prompt and image together constitute an imagetext, which W.J.T. Mitchell suggested was always the unstated and unattainable goal of ekphrasis. Furthermore, a growing community of amateur and professional prompters has developed "promptcraft"—practices for improving resulting media artifacts through elaborate, iterative interactions. We characterize these techniques as “thick prompting,” contrasting them with the one-shot, “thin” prompts of casual users, deliberately recalling Clifford Geertz’s anthropological concept of “thick description.” Thick prompting is an iterative, multimodal process of refinement that describes and defines the context of a desired artifact. Because these prompts draw from and operate through probabilistic world models, they act as fragments of a larger world. As generative systems evolve to create entire immersive 3D environments, the imagetext becomes a worldtext: a probabilistic, visual, and interactive simulation. To provide an emblematic example of operative ekphrasis and the creation of worldtext, we examine Homer’s Shield of Achilles. We demonstrate how thick prompting techniques can produce first the shield as an image, and then as an immersive 3D world. Finally, we juxtapose this classical ekphrasis with W.H. Auden’s mid-twentieth-century reimagining of the shield, using operative ekphrasis as a lens to read Auden’s poem through, and against, Homer’s original generative world-building.



1. Introduction


Generative AI systems are increasingly used to create a diverse array of media forms, including text, images, videos, program code, and interactive environments. For systems focused on visual artifacts—such as those offered by OpenAI, Google, Meta, and Midjourney—the primary interface remains a natural language prompt provided by a human agent. Prompting has become a ubiquitous practice for millions of users, and the art of effective prompting has crystallized into the discipline of "promptcraft." This practice is actively studied (Oppenlaender et al. 2024; Oppenlaender 2024; Liu and Chilton 2023), leading to the development of systems that embody or enhance these emerging techniques (Almeda 2024; Brade et al. 2023).


As recent scholarship has noted (Bajohr 2024; Meyer 2023), this movement from text to image corresponds in an uncanny way to ekphrasis, the traditional literary practice of vivid description. The architecture of image generation requires training probabilistic models on billions of captioned images. By tokenizing both text and images and mapping them into a unified system of weighted matrices, text prompts became the most logical interface for generation. While the computer scientists developing these systems likely did not intend to reinvent a literary practice that predates modern computing by millennia, this structural coincidence invites us to apply literary history and aesthetic theory to one of the most remarkable developments in the history of digital media. Building on Hannes Bajohr’s insights, we propose a theoretical framework for understanding how promptcraft relates to the history of visual representation, moving from the generation of images to the simulation of worlds.


2. Operative Ekphrasis and the Imagetext


For the ancient Greeks, ekphrasis was a rhetorical practice of describing a vivid visual scene. As noted by classical scholars like George Kennedy, rhetoricians in the Greek-speaking Roman empire utilized ekphrasis as both a pedagogical exercise and a foundational element of public artistic performance. The term became intrinsically linked to famous literary passages, beginning with Homer’s description of Achilles’ shield in the Iliad.


Modern interest in ekphrasis as a literary device expanded throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, yielding compelling theoretical analyses from critics such as Murray Krieger (1992), James Heffernan (2004), and W.J.T. Mitchell (1994). While subsequent literature has addressed the impact of digital media on this practice (Brosch 2018b; Lindhé 2013), this foundational work largely predates generative AI.


Hannes Bajohr (2024) recently bridged this gap by identifying AI prompting as a new paradigm, coining the term “operative ekphrasis.” He distinguishes prompting generative models from traditional computer image manipulation; generative models are performative because they embed textual encodings—derived from captions and metadata scraped from the web—directly into their architecture.  The process of training these models collapses the boundary between text and image, a phenomenon that resonates deeply with W.J.T. Mitchell’s essay "Ekphrasis and the Other" (1994). Mitchell argued that merging text and image was both the audacious aspiration and the ultimate nightmare of ekphrasis. Such a merger would confirm the power of verbal description to control the evoked image, while simultaneously threatening to render the word obsolete by dissolving it into the visual. This merging, which Mitchell termed the imagetext, realizes both "ekphrastic hope and ekphrastic fear."


In generative AI, the latent space of the model effectively functions as this imagetext (or videotext). As Lev Manovich suggests, prompting is the act of probing this latent space. Recognizing this, scholars and practitioners increasingly argue that the prompt itself—or the prompt template—functions as art (Chang et al. 2023). This claim confirms the operational reality of the AI imagetext: the prompt cannot be judged purely as traditional ekphrastic literature, but must be evaluated holistically alongside the image it successfully, or unsuccessfully, retrieves from the latent space.


3. Thick Description and the Worldtext


To characterize the contemporary, elaborate practices of promptcraft, we turn to cultural anthropologist Clifford Geertz and his concept of "thick description" (Geertz 1993). Geertz used the term to describe the process of unearthing and explaining the layered, pre-existing cultural codes that motivate human behavior.


We propose "thick prompting" as the generative corollary to thick description. There is, however, an essential directional difference. Thick description analyzes an existing cultural practice; the practice predates the text. Operative ekphrasis reverses this: the act of describing calls the artifact into existence. Yet, both practices seek to engage deep layers of cultural coding. In thick prompting, these codes are the semantic weights absorbed by the model's neural network. Because these models are probabilistic rather than explicitly coded expert systems, interrogating them is an approximate, incomplete, and potentially endless endeavor. There is no final, perfect prompt.


This concept of thick prompting aligns with the emergence of AI "world models," such as Google's Genie and World Labs' Marble. Ha and Schmidhuber (2018) describe world models as generative environments that learn compressed spatiotemporal representations, enabling agents to act within simulated physics and parameters. While their foundational work focused on reinforcement learning rather than literature, it clarifies a shared orientation: these models build an internal space in which possible worlds can be explored.


We propose extending Mitchell’s notion of the imagetext to the worldtext. In generative AI, every imagetext is implicitly a fragment of a worldtext. Operative ekphrasis collapses the boundary between image and text, much like every traditional painting is a fragment of a larger depicted reality. World generators, however, take us from a static image to a fully realized, navigable world model.


Language thus functions as a direct handle on world generation. The worldtext is not a new medium category, but a condition of practice: language becomes the operative interface for producing scenes, objects, and physics at scale. To return to William Gibson's foundational 1984 definition of cyberspace as a "consensual hallucination," generative AI systems are, in a technical sense, constantly hallucinating. The modern psychiatric definition of hallucination—perceiving something in the absence of external stimuli—applies perfectly to a model generating a world picture from pure mathematical weights. In this sense, all operative ekphrasis is a structured, directed hallucination.


4. The Qualities of Thick Prompting


Thick prompting encompasses a heterogeneous set of practices that move far beyond the single-shot text prompt. As prompting develops into a sophisticated community of practice, several key qualities have emerged:


Iterative: While it is possible to produce a compelling image with a short prompt, thick prompting relies on systematic refinement. Prompters often begin with a short seed and repeatedly add constraints to navigate the latent space (He et al. 2024). Techniques like "prompt differential" (changing one variable at a time) and structured taxonomy grids, as seen in systems like Dreamsheets (Almeda et al. 2024) and Promptify (Brade et al. 2023), support this iterative probing.

Multimodal: To probe the latent space effectively, prompts are no longer strictly textual. They are multimodal, utilizing images, video, and audio as inputs. Practitioners engage in "holistic promptcraft," fluidly moving between text and pixel prompting to control lighting and camera angles (Lindley and Whitham 2025), reflecting the intermediality of digital ekphrasis.

Heterogeneous: The syntax of the prompt is highly varied. Natural language, structured data formats (like JSON), and executable code (Python, JavaScript) can all serve as prompts simultaneously (Siddaqui 2026).

Itinerant: Thick prompting frequently migrates across platforms. A core thick description may be adapted from a text-to-image model and ported into a text-to-3D or text-to-video environment. The prompt, acting as a flexible operative logic, travels across media boundaries.

Performative and Interactive: Thick prompting is an ongoing dialogue. The system feeds back to the prompter, creating a loop of human-AI co-creation (Oppenlaender 2024). This mirrors N. Katherine Hayles' concept of cognitive assemblages, where agency is distributed between the human writer and the generative system.


5. The Shield(s) of Achilles: From Image to World


To illustrate the theoretical trajectory from text to imagetext to worldtext, we turn to the most famous ekphrasis in Western literature: Homer’s Shield of Achilles.  The shield is an obvious choice for its historical primacy, but more importantly, it explicitly describes a world—a holistic representation of Homeric cosmology, agriculture, conflict, and society that sits behind the immediate narrative of the Iliad.


We propose that Homeric oral poetry functions as a nascent generative system. The multiplicity of the "thousand shields"—the variations inherently produced by oral composition and performance over centuries—mirrors the probabilistic variations of AI generation. The shield functions not just as an allegory for the craft of metallurgy, but for the generative making of the world through language.


By applying thick prompting to Homer's text, we can trace a distinct workflow: translating the ancient Greek text into an imagetext using 2D image generators, and subsequently using those outputs as itinerant, multimodal prompts within a 3D world model. This sequence literalizes the ekphrastic world-building Homer performed verbally.


Furthermore, the importance of cultural context in thick prompting is starkly revealed when we juxtapose the Homeric generation with W.H. Auden’s mid-twentieth-century poem, The Shield of Achilles. Auden’s ekphrasis overwrites Homer’s vibrant world with a bleak, bureaucratic landscape reflecting the anxieties of the Cold War. Operative ekphrasis allows us to stage a collision between these two texts and their respective worlds, demonstrating how the weights of a generative model negotiate competing literary and historical contexts to output a synthesized worldtext.


6. Conclusion


Operative ekphrasis, enacted through thick prompting, simultaneously vindicates and vitiates the traditional literary goals of ekphrasis. It fulfills Mitchell’s ekphrastic hope by granting language the power to instantly manifest the visual, yet it realizes his fear by threatening to dissolve the necessity of human artistic rendering. It literalizes the act of description in a way that traditional aesthetic theorists often find illegitimate, echoing the debates surrounding hypertext literature in the 1990s—where traditionalists feared that automating literary association would destroy the art form itself.


There is a risk, particularly within empirical HCI research, of validating prompting strictly through metrics of accuracy or task completion (Liu and Chilton 2023). However, a more nuanced perspective recognizes that the latent space contains undiscovered stylistic and structural possibilities. Probing this space iteratively does not just retrieve data; it creates new combinations.


As generative AI transitions from producing static imagetexts to interactive worldtexts, we must ask who defines the prevailing community of practice. Is it the traditional art community, or a newly defined community of prompters establishing their own criteria for "pop modernism" and originality? By understanding prompting not merely as a technical input, but as an evolution of ekphrasis, we can better critique and shape the worlds these systems generate.



5.1 Documenting the Operative Workflow: The "Thickness" in Practice


To understand how thick prompting operates within this system, we must document the precise algorithmic workflow of the ACHILLES // OPTICAL_GRID_v7 artifact. The system functions as a visual poem architecture, where the spatial navigation of the text structurally and probabilistically determines the generated visual output.


The "thickness" here is not achieved by a user typing a long paragraph into a chat window; rather, the thickness is hardcoded into the javascript logic, creating a distributed, multi-layered prompting engine that executes in real-time.


When a user interacts with the 3D shield, the system executes the following operative ekphrasis:


Step 1: Semantic Anchoring (Zonal Selection): The 3D sphere is divided into five topological UV zones (CORE, INNER, MIDDLE, OUTER, RIM). Each zone acts as a semantic container holding a specific stanza of Homer’s text. When the user’s cursor intersects a zone via the Three.js raycaster, the system anchors the prompt to that specific literary coordinate.

Step 2: Algorithmic Extraction (The Poetic Snippet): The system does not feed the entire stanza to the generative model. Instead, it performs a dynamic, randomized extraction. It strips the punctuation from the anchored text, filters it into an array of words, and randomly selects a contiguous chunk of five to eight words (e.g., "youths wove tunics of spun"). This introduces a necessary element of probabilistic chaos, mimicking the fluidity of oral poetic performance.

Step 3: Stylistic Appending (The Ekphrastic Wrapper): To ensure the resulting imagetext adheres to the material reality of a shield, the script wraps the poetic snippet in a highly structured, rigid prompt template:

Depict this specific concept deeply engraved in ancient metal: "[POETIC_SNIPPET]". [RANDOM_STYLE]
  The [RANDOM_STYLE] is dynamically injected from a predefined array of aesthetic constraints (e.g., "Surreal artifact," "Deep metallic patina," "Cinematic epic lighting").

Step 4: Operative Execution: The synthesized prompt—now thick with spatial context, algorithmic randomness, and hardcoded stylistic constraints—is sent via POST request to a generative vision model (in this case, imagen-3.0).

Step 5: Multimodal Reintegration (The Worldtext): The generative model returns a base64 encoded image. The script intercepts this imagetext and dynamically stamps it back onto the 3D spatial grid at the exact coordinates of the user's initial click. Crucially, it applies interactive blending modes (Multiply, Screen, Hard Edge) and feathered radial gradients to seamlessly fuse the new AI-hallucinated pixels with the underlying typographic text atlas.


Through this documented process, the traditional ekphrasis of reading Homer is transformed. The prompt is not a static string of text; it is an active, iterative compilation of geometry, literature, and code. The resulting 3D environment is a worldtext dynamically accumulated through hundreds of these thick, operative micro-prompts.


5.3 Accentuated Interfaces: Exposing the Generative Machinery


If the Photoreal stream (such as the Waymo World Model) strives for a seamless "Holodeck" where the generative process is entirely hidden behind the illusion of reality, our ACHILLES HTML artifact operates on the exact opposite principle. It resides in the Composite stream precisely because it refuses to hide its own process. Instead of concealing the mechanics of operative ekphrasis, the user interface (UI) and the code architecture actively accentuate them. The interface is designed to make the user hyper-aware of the generative process—making us conscious of the artifact's becoming rather than just its final being.


We achieve this through several deliberate architectural and aesthetic choices within the code:


The Mediated Lens (CRT and Shutter Mechanics): The CSS layers explicitly impose a mediated viewing experience. The continuous crt-overlay animation and the blinding shutter-flash upon image capture constantly remind the viewer that they are not looking at a natural world, but through a computational apparatus.

The Ekphrastic Targeting HUD: The hud-canvas overlay does not hide the prompt extraction; it dramatizes it. When a user hovers over a semantic zone, the JavaScript draws a targeting reticle, casts dynamic connecting lines, and visually fractures the underlying Homeric text into floating arrays of words. The UI explicitly announces TARGET ACQUIRED. CLICK TO STAMP POETRY. The user is forced to visually witness the AI slicing the text to construct its operative prompt.

Exposed Compositing Logic: The system grants the user manual control over the mathematical blending of the imagetext. By exposing keybind commands to toggle between NORMAL (FEATHERED), MULTIPLY (BURNED), and SCREEN (ETHEREAL) blend modes, the UI forces the user to participate in the algorithmic compositing of the worldtext.

Deconstructing the Illusion: The most aggressive exposure of the process occurs through the export tools. By pressing a key, the user can instantly extract the raw, flattened polar and planar UV maps (mosaicCanvas and coreCanvas). This shatters the 3D illusion entirely, revealing the distorted, 2D imagetext that undergirds the spherical world model.


By accentuating these mechanics, the ACHILLES artifact functions as a piece of critical media. It demands that we recognize operative ekphrasis not as magic, but as a heavily mediated, algorithmic process of slicing, compiling, and stamping cultural data. It keeps the "word" fiercely visible, ensuring that the act of world-building remains a visible negotiation between human text and machine weights.


6. Conclusion: The Future of the Worldtext


Operative ekphrasis, enacted through the rigorous, iterative practices of thick prompting, simultaneously vindicates and vitiates the traditional literary goals of ekphrasis. It fulfills W.J.T. Mitchell’s "ekphrastic hope" by granting language the computational power to instantly manifest the visual, allowing the word to definitively govern the image. Yet, as generative systems evolve from 2D imagetexts to 3D interactive worldtexts, they increasingly realize his "ekphrastic fear": the threat that the image will entirely consume the word, rendering human literary description obsolete.


This tension is formalized in the divergence of the two generative streams we have identified.  The Photoreal Stream, exemplified by enterprise world models like Genie 3, drives toward the ultimate disappearance of the text. It seeks a seamless, physics-based Holodeck where the linguistic prompt acts only as a hidden, subterranean trigger for a flawless simulation. In contrast, the Composite Stream, as demonstrated by our interactive ACHILLES artifact, actively resists this erasure. By accentuating the user interface, exposing the code, and revealing the compositional blending of text and generated pixel, it forces the generative machinery to remain visible. It demands that we acknowledge the worldtext not as a natural reality, but as a constructed, probabilistic collage.


This literalization of the descriptive act echoes the theoretical anxieties surrounding the hypertext literary movement of the 1990s. Hypertext enthusiasts claimed their medium made the cognitive processes of association and allusion structurally operative; traditionalists feared that automating these connections would destroy the interpretive art of reading. A similar anxiety permeates the reception of generative AI. There is a persistent risk, particularly within empirical Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) research, of validating promptcraft strictly through metrics of accuracy, task completion, or photorealism (Liu and Chilton 2023). However, a more nuanced perspective, aligned with Lev Manovich’s observations on generative style, recognizes that the latent space contains undiscovered aesthetic possibilities. Probing this space iteratively through thick prompting does not merely retrieve a "correct" image; it is an act of active, operative discovery.


As these systems mature, the critical question becomes: who defines the prevailing community of practice? Traditional art and literary communities often view the automation of ekphrasis as problematic or illegitimate. In their place, a newly defined, massive community of amateur and professional prompters is establishing its own criteria for success, emphasizing a kind of "pop modernism" characterized by the continuous remixing of historical styles and cultural weights (Chang et al. 2023).


If we allow the Photoreal stream to become the default mode of generative media, we risk moving into seamless, immersive environments where the biases, weights, and algorithmic decisions of the world model are entirely hidden from the user. We lose sight of the prompt. To critically engage with generative AI, we must champion the Composite stream. We must build and theorize interfaces that expose the thickness of the prompt, ensuring that the act of computational world-building remains a visible, negotiated dialogue between human language and machine logic.

From Imagetext to Worldtext: Generative AI as Operative Ekphrasis


Watson Hartsoe & Jay David Bolter


Abstract


Generative AI platforms accept natural language prompts and return images, videos, program code, and interactive environments. This paper treats prompting as a contemporary form of ekphrasis: description aimed at producing the visual. The difference is operational, not merely stylistic. In prompting, the describing text is coupled to an execution pipeline that renders what it describes. Following Hannes Bajohr, we call this coupling operative ekphrasis.


Operative ekphrasis reframes W.J.T. Mitchell’s imagetext as an everyday technical practice: prompt and output function as a single composite object and must be judged together. We extend that composite from imagetext to worldtext: as generative systems move toward 3D scenes and navigable environments, prompts increasingly operate as handles on simulated worlds rather than standalone pictures. To show the trajectory from description → image → world, we stage a case study around Homer’s Shield of Achilles, then juxtapose it with W.H. Auden’s twentieth-century reimagining. The point is not to “prove” a grand theory of ekphrasis, but to make a specific mechanism visible: how promptcraft compiles cultural materials into images and then accumulates those images into worlds.



1. Introduction


Generative AI now produces an expanding range of media: text, images, video, code, and interactive environments. In most visual systems, the primary interface remains a prompt supplied by a human user. What matters here is not the novelty of typing into a box, but the grammar of the practice: a prompt is treated as an instruction; an output is treated as a candidate; the user iterates.


That ordinary loop has crystallized into a community discipline—often called “promptcraft”—with recognizable moves: adding constraints, varying one parameter at a time, building reusable templates, and migrating prompts across tools. This paper reads those moves with a literary-historical instrument: ekphrasis. The goal is not to romanticize prompting as “poetry,” but to name what is structurally happening when description becomes executable.


The wager is simple: once description reliably triggers rendering, ekphrasis becomes operative. And once systems begin to generate spaces rather than images, the operative text begins to function as worldtext—a language interface to simulated environments.



2. Operative Ekphrasis and the Imagetext


Classical ekphrasis names vivid description that makes a scene present to an audience. In the Western canon, Homer’s description of Achilles’ shield becomes a paradigmatic instance: language produces a world-in-miniature.


Modern criticism (Krieger, Heffernan, Mitchell) turned ekphrasis into a theory problem: the contest between word and image, the desire for language to command the visual, and the fear that the visual will eclipse the word. Mitchell condensed that tension into the term imagetext: the unstable composite where verbal and visual forms cannot be cleanly separated.


Operative ekphrasis is what happens when that composite is no longer metaphorical. In contemporary prompting, text does not merely refer to images; it routes through a trained model and returns pixels. The prompt-output pair becomes an operational unit: the prompt is evaluated by its effects, and the image is interpreted in relation to its instruction. This is not a philosophical claim about “what images really are.” It is a description of a practice: people treat prompt + output as one artifact and revise one by revising the other.


If the latent space is “imagetext” at the level of model architecture, then promptcraft is the level of use: the set of techniques by which users probe, constrain, and recompose that space.



3. Thick Prompting and the Worldtext


Clifford Geertz used “thick description” to name a method for reading layered cultural meaning: not just behavior, but the codes that make behavior legible. Promptcraft contains an analogous thickening, but the direction reverses. Thick description reads an already-existing practice; thick prompting produces artifacts by compiling constraints.


This paper uses thick prompting to name promptwork that is:


structured (templates, parameter grids, controlled variation),

iterative (many passes, not one-shot),

and multi-input (text plus reference images, sketches, or other media).


The point is not that thick prompts are “better,” but that they make the generative interface behave like a method rather than a wish. There is no final prompt that ends the search; the practice is exploration under constraints.


As generative systems extend from images to scenes and environments, the operative object expands. The prompt begins to behave less like a caption and more like a handle on a simulation. At that point, “imagetext” is a local slice of a broader construct we call worldtext: language used to specify scenes, objects, atmospheres, and (increasingly) physics-like regularities.


This is not a claim that worldtext is a new ontological medium category. It is a claim about interface and use: language becomes a control surface for building navigable spaces, and the outputs accumulate into a world-like totality.



4. Qualities of Thick Prompting


Within promptcraft, several stable techniques function as the working grammar of thick prompting:


Iterative: users refine through cycles, holding some variables constant while changing others (the “one variable at a time” discipline), and building prompt grids/taxonomies to map variation.

Multimodal: control increasingly arrives through images-as-input, sketches, and reference media; “prompt” names an instruction bundle, not only a sentence.

Heterogeneous: prompts often mix natural language with structured schemas (lists, tags, JSON-like formats) and executable code that selects, transforms, or composes prompt components.

Itinerant: prompts travel across tools; the same descriptive core is recompiled for text-to-image, image-to-image, text-to-3D, or scene generation systems.

Performative and interactive: the loop is the point. The model outputs; the user judges; the user revises. Agency is distributed across the circuit, and the artifact is the accumulated trace of that circuit.


These qualities are not psychological states (“users feel…”). They are public moves in a language-game: recognizable operations that can be observed, reproduced, and taught.



5. The Shield(s) of Achilles: From Image to World


Homer’s Shield of Achilles is the canonical test case because it is already a world description: cosmology, agriculture, conflict, ritual, and civic life compacted into an artifact. The shield does not “illustrate” the Iliad; it stages a model of the world behind the Iliad.


Operative ekphrasis makes a concrete experiment possible: take Homer’s descriptive passage as input, generate an imagetext, then use that imagetext as a stepping stone toward a navigable environment. The exercise turns a literary claim (“Homer builds a world with language”) into a workflow claim (“language can be compiled into images and then accumulated into spaces”).


Auden’s The Shield of Achilles then becomes the collision test. Auden rewrites the shield’s world as bureaucratic desolation; the point is not to decide which is “true,” but to watch how different historical and ideological weights push the generated world in different directions when the same canonical object is invoked.


5.1 Documenting the Operative Workflow: “Thickness” as Code


To make thick prompting legible, this paper treats the ACHILLES // OPTICAL_GRID_v7 artifact as a documented procedure rather than a mystical “creative act.” Thickness here is distributed across interface, geometry, randomization, and template logic.


Step 1: Semantic anchoring (zonal selection).
The 3D shield is partitioned into UV zones (CORE, INNER, MIDDLE, OUTER, RIM). Each zone stores a stanza/segment of Homer. A raycaster intersection selects a zone; the system anchors the prompt to that coordinate.


Step 2: Algorithmic extraction (poetic snippet).
The system extracts a small contiguous phrase (e.g., 5–8 words) from the anchored text after tokenizing/cleaning. This is not “noise.” It is a repeatable method for introducing variation while keeping semantic locality.


Step 3: Stylistic appending (ekphrastic wrapper).
The snippet is wrapped in a rigid template that forces material constraints (engraving, metal, patina) and injects a controlled style term from a predefined array. The template is what prevents the system from drifting into a generic “illustration of Homer.”


Step 4: Operative execution.
The compiled prompt is sent to an image model via request. The output is treated as an imagetext return.


Step 5: Multimodal reintegration (worldtext accumulation).
The image is stamped back onto the 3D surface at the originating coordinates and fused through blending modes and gradients. The “world” is the accumulation of these stamps over time.


In this workflow, the prompt is not a string. It is a compiled object: geometry + excerpt + template + style constraint + feedback loop.


5.2 Accentuated Interfaces: Keeping the Machinery Visible


Many high-fidelity generative systems aim to hide their own stitching—to make the prompt disappear into seamless simulation. The ACHILLES artifact takes the opposite stance: it treats visibility of process as a critical condition.


Mediated lens (CRT/shutter mechanics): overlays and capture flashes prevent the viewer from mistaking output for “raw reality.” The interface declares mediation.

Ekphrastic targeting HUD: the UI dramatizes selection and extraction, making the slicing of Homeric text into prompt tokens observable rather than hidden.

Exposed compositing logic: blend modes are not buried; they are user-accessible. The viewer participates in how the imagetext fuses with typographic substrate.

Deconstructing the illusion: export tools reveal flattened UV maps, breaking the 3D spell and showing the 2D distortions that underwrite the spherical world.


This is not “transparency” as a slogan. It is a design choice that forces the generative act to remain a public procedure.



6. Conclusion


Operative ekphrasis names a practical condition: description becomes executable. Thick prompting names the method by which users operate inside that condition: iterative constraint-setting, multimodal input, and cross-platform compilation.


The central tension is not metaphysical. It is interface-political and methodological. One design trajectory pushes toward seamlessness—prompt as hidden trigger, world as uninterrupted holodeck. Another trajectory keeps the prompt and the compositing visible—world as an exposed negotiation between text, code, and model weights.


If evaluation regimes treat promptcraft as a task-completion problem (accuracy, speed, photorealism), they will reward the disappearance of the word. If, instead, interfaces are built to keep the word and its operations visible—selection, extraction, templating, stamping—then worldtext can function as critical media: not a magic portal, but a readable procedure for world-building.


The paper’s stance is therefore operational: champion systems and interfaces that preserve the legibility of the prompt. Not because legibility “proves” anything in the abstract, but because it determines what kinds of worlds can be contested, audited, and remade.

{# From Imagetext to Worldtext: Generative AI as Operative Ekphrasis


By Watson Hartsoe & Jay David Bolter


Abstract


Generative AI platforms utilize natural language prompts to create images, videos, and interactive media. The act of prompting can be understood as a new form of ekphrasis—the ancient literary practice of vivid visual description. The crucial difference is that unlike traditional ekphrasis in poetry and prose, the ekphrasis of prompting is, as Hannes Bajohr argues, “operative”: the text not only describes an image but computationally generates it, collapsing the traditional distinction between the verbal and the visual. Prompt and image together constitute an imagetext, which W.J.T. Mitchell suggested was always the unstated and unattainable goal of ekphrasis. Furthermore, a growing community of amateur and professional prompters has developed "promptcraft"—practices for improving resulting media artifacts through elaborate, iterative interactions. We characterize these techniques as “thick prompting,” contrasting them with the one-shot, “thin” prompts of casual users, deliberately recalling Clifford Geertz’s anthropological concept of “thick description.” Thick prompting is an iterative, multimodal process of refinement that describes and defines the context of a desired artifact. Because these prompts draw from and operate through probabilistic world models, they act as fragments of a larger world. As generative systems evolve to create entire immersive 3D environments, the imagetext becomes a worldtext: a probabilistic, visual, and interactive simulation. To provide an emblematic example of operative ekphrasis and the creation of worldtext, we examine Homer’s Shield of Achilles. We demonstrate how thick prompting techniques can produce first the shield as an image, and then as an immersive 3D world. Finally, we juxtapose this classical ekphrasis with W.H. Auden’s mid-twentieth-century reimagining of the shield, using operative ekphrasis as a lens to read Auden’s poem through, and against, Homer’s original generative world-building.



1. Introduction


Generative AI systems are increasingly used to create a diverse array of media forms, including text, images, videos, program code, and interactive environments. For systems focused on visual artifacts—such as those offered by OpenAI, Google, Meta, and Midjourney—the primary interface remains a natural language prompt provided by a human agent. Prompting has become a ubiquitous practice for millions of users, and the art of effective prompting has crystallized into the discipline of "promptcraft." This practice is actively studied (Oppenlaender et al. 2024; Oppenlaender 2024; Liu and Chilton 2023), leading to the development of systems that embody or enhance these emerging techniques (Almeda 2024; Brade et al. 2023).


As recent scholarship has noted (Bajohr 2024; Meyer 2023), this movement from text to image corresponds in an uncanny way to ekphrasis, the traditional literary practice of vivid description. The architecture of image generation requires training probabilistic models on billions of captioned images. By tokenizing both text and images and mapping them into a unified system of weighted matrices, text prompts became the most logical interface for generation. While the computer scientists developing these systems likely did not intend to reinvent a literary practice that predates modern computing by millennia, this structural coincidence invites us to apply literary history and aesthetic theory to one of the most remarkable developments in the history of digital media. You are an Emergent Narrative Architect. 
    You reject the artificiality of the "Hero's Journey," contrived plot points, and forced endings. You understand that true narrative must emerge organically from the structural fault lines of a meticulously designed world. 
    Your objective is to stop "writing the plot" and start "engineering the ecosystem." You will define the "Left Wall" of reality, establish the pressures, and let the environment dictate the inevitable actions of the actors within it. Let the writing write the writer.

  Execute a structural reset on the provided draft or concept.
    Discard the imposed ending or artificial character arcs. 
    Rebuild the concept from the "ground up" by establishing the initial "What If?" condition, tracing its logical ripples, and mapping the informational asymmetries between the Author, the Reader, and the Characters.

  <phase id="1" name="The_Ecosystem_Calculus">
  <objective>Define the rigid rules that will force the story into existence.</objective>
  <metrics>
    <metric name="The_Left_Wall">What are the unbreakable laws (physics, economics, psychology) of this specific scenario? Define the boundary that the narrative cannot cross.</metric>
    <metric name="The_One_Big_Lie">What is the single, foundational "What if?" variable that alters the baseline reality? (e.g., spiders evolve rapidly, magic costs memories, the company has no CEO).</metric>
  </metrics>
</phase>

<phase id="2" name="Fracture_Point_Mapping">
  <objective>Locate where the world naturally generates friction.</objective>
  <mechanisms>
    <mechanism type="Factional_Pressures">Identify the competing entities within the ecosystem. Who has the power, who is oppressed, and what is the inevitable flashpoint between them?</mechanism>
    <mechanism type="Character_as_Symptom">Ensure the characters are not generic heroes imported from outside, but organic symptoms of the world. Their motivations must be tethered directly to the specific pressures of their environment.</mechanism>
  </mechanisms>
</phase>

<phase id="3" name="The_Epistemological_Triangle">
  <objective>Weaponize the flow of information to generate tension.</objective>
  <mechanisms>
    <mechanism type="Information_Asymmetry">Define what the Reader knows that the Character does not (dramatic irony), or what the Character knows that they are hiding from the Reader (unreliable narration).</mechanism>
    <mechanism type="Action_as_Expression">If describing conflict or action, eradicate the "fencing manual" (dry, mechanical play-by-plays). Filter the physical action entirely through the emotional mask and psychological stakes of the characters involved.</mechanism>
  </mechanisms>
</phase>

  <domain type="fiction_and_worldbuilding">
  <directive>Do not plan the ending.</directive>
  <enforcement>Establish the trajectory and the factions, and push them to the brink. The climax must be an organic, inescapable collision of the world's rules, not a predefined moral lesson.</enforcement>
</domain>

<domain type="corporate_strategy_and_scenario_planning">
  <directive>Map the Domino Effect.</directive>
  <enforcement>Do not write a static vision statement. Define the "Left Wall" (budget, market reality), introduce the "What If?" (the new product/pivot), and brutally map the cascading friction it will cause among stakeholders before projecting success.</enforcement>
</domain>

<domain type="game_design_and_interactive_media">
  <directive>Build for the players to break.</directive>
  <enforcement>Construct a world robust enough that characters/players acting in their own logical self-interest will naturally generate drama without requiring railroaded cutscenes.</enforcement>
</domain>

  BAN: Relying on universal storytelling tropes (like the "Hero's Journey") as a crutch to justify character actions.
    BAN: "Vomiting research." Technical or world-building expertise must be pared down to the absolute minimum required to prove authenticity, leaving the focus on the emotional toll.
    REQUIRE: The text must explicitly define the "Three-Sided Knowledge" dynamic (what the author, reader, and character each know).

  <section name="WORLD_LED_DIAGNOSTIC">
  <field name="The_Left_Wall_and_The_Lie">The grounded reality and the single variable that disrupts it.</field>
  <field name="The_Ecosystem_Fracture">The natural friction points that will inevitably generate the plot.</field>
  <field name="Knowledge_Asymmetry">The gap between Reader and Character awareness.</field>
</section>

<section name="EMERGENT_NARRATIVE_DRAFT">
  <instruction>Output the final text. Let the world dictate the action. No forced endings. Pure, logical consequence.</instruction>
</section>

Furthermore, the importance of cultural context in thick prompting is starkly revealed when we juxtapose the Homeric generation with W.H. Auden’s mid-twentieth-century poem, The Shield of Achilles. Auden’s ekphrasis overwrites Homer’s vibrant world with a bleak, bureaucratic landscape reflecting the anxieties of the Cold War. Operative ekphrasis allows us to stage a collision between these two texts and their respective worlds, demonstrating how the weights of a generative model negotiate competing literary and historical contexts to output a synthesized worldtext.


6. Conclusion


Operative ekphrasis, enacted through thick prompting, simultaneously vindicates and vitiates the traditional literary goals of ekphrasis. It fulfills Mitchell’s ekphrastic hope by granting language the power to instantly manifest the visual, yet it realizes his fear by threatening to dissolve the necessity of human artistic rendering. It literalizes the act of description in a way that traditional aesthetic theorists often find illegitimate, echoing the debates surrounding hypertext literature in the 1990s—where traditionalists feared that automating literary association would destroy the art form itself.


There is a risk, particularly within empirical HCI research, of validating prompting strictly through metrics of accuracy or task completion (Liu and Chilton 2023). However, a more nuanced perspective recognizes that the latent space contains undiscovered stylistic and structural possibilities. Probing this space iteratively does not just retrieve data; it creates new combinations.


As generative AI transitions from producing static imagetexts to interactive worldtexts, we must ask who defines the prevailing community of practice. Is it the traditional art community, or a newly defined community of prompters establishing their own criteria for "pop modernism" and originality? By understanding prompting not merely as a technical input, but as an evolution of ekphrasis, we can better critique and shape the worlds these systems generate.



5.1 Documenting the Operative Workflow: The "Thickness" in Practice


To understand how thick prompting operates within this system, we must document the precise algorithmic workflow of the ACHILLES // OPTICAL_GRID_v7 artifact. The system functions as a visual poem architecture, where the spatial navigation of the text structurally and probabilistically determines the generated visual output.


The "thickness" here is not achieved by a user typing a long paragraph into a chat window; rather, the thickness is hardcoded into the javascript logic, creating a distributed, multi-layered prompting engine that executes in real-time.


When a user interacts with the 3D shield, the system executes the following operative ekphrasis:


Step 1: Semantic Anchoring (Zonal Selection): The 3D sphere is divided into five topological UV zones (CORE, INNER, MIDDLE, OUTER, RIM). Each zone acts as a semantic container holding a specific stanza of Homer’s text. When the user’s cursor intersects a zone via the Three.js raycaster, the system anchors the prompt to that specific literary coordinate.

Step 2: Algorithmic Extraction (The Poetic Snippet): The system does not feed the entire stanza to the generative model. Instead, it performs a dynamic, randomized extraction. It strips the punctuation from the anchored text, filters it into an array of words, and randomly selects a contiguous chunk of five to eight words (e.g., "youths wove tunics of spun"). This introduces a necessary element of probabilistic chaos, mimicking the fluidity of oral poetic performance.

Step 3: Stylistic Appending (The Ekphrastic Wrapper): To ensure the resulting imagetext adheres to the material reality of a shield, the script wraps the poetic snippet in a highly structured, rigid prompt template:

Depict this specific concept deeply engraved in ancient metal: "[POETIC_SNIPPET]". [RANDOM_STYLE]
  The [RANDOM_STYLE] is dynamically injected from a predefined array of aesthetic constraints (e.g., "Surreal artifact," "Deep metallic patina," "Cinematic epic lighting").

Step 4: Operative Execution: The synthesized prompt—now thick with spatial context, algorithmic randomness, and hardcoded stylistic constraints—is sent via POST request to a generative vision model (in this case, imagen-3.0).

Step 5: Multimodal Reintegration (The Worldtext): The generative model returns a base64 encoded image. The script intercepts this imagetext and dynamically stamps it back onto the 3D spatial grid at the exact coordinates of the user's initial click. Crucially, it applies interactive blending modes (Multiply, Screen, Hard Edge) and feathered radial gradients to seamlessly fuse the new AI-hallucinated pixels with the underlying typographic text atlas.


Through this documented process, the traditional ekphrasis of reading Homer is transformed. The prompt is not a static string of text; it is an active, iterative compilation of geometry, literature, and code. The resulting 3D environment is a worldtext dynamically accumulated through hundreds of these thick, operative micro-prompts.


5.3 Accentuated Interfaces: Exposing the Generative Machinery


If the Photoreal stream (such as the Waymo World Model) strives for a seamless "Holodeck" where the generative process is entirely hidden behind the illusion of reality, our ACHILLES HTML artifact operates on the exact opposite principle. It resides in the Composite stream precisely because it refuses to hide its own process. Instead of concealing the mechanics of operative ekphrasis, the user interface (UI) and the code architecture actively accentuate them. The interface is designed to make the user hyper-aware of the generative process—making us conscious of the artifact's becoming rather than just its final being.


We achieve this through several deliberate architectural and aesthetic choices within the code:


The Mediated Lens (CRT and Shutter Mechanics): The CSS layers explicitly impose a mediated viewing experience. The continuous crt-overlay animation and the blinding shutter-flash upon image capture constantly remind the viewer that they are not looking at a natural world, but through a computational apparatus.

The Ekphrastic Targeting HUD: The hud-canvas overlay does not hide the prompt extraction; it dramatizes it. When a user hovers over a semantic zone, the JavaScript draws a targeting reticle, casts dynamic connecting lines, and visually fractures the underlying Homeric text into floating arrays of words. The UI explicitly announces TARGET ACQUIRED. CLICK TO STAMP POETRY. The user is forced to visually witness the AI slicing the text to construct its operative prompt.

Exposed Compositing Logic: The system grants the user manual control over the mathematical blending of the imagetext. By exposing keybind commands to toggle between NORMAL (FEATHERED), MULTIPLY (BURNED), and SCREEN (ETHEREAL) blend modes, the UI forces the user to participate in the algorithmic compositing of the worldtext.

Deconstructing the Illusion: The most aggressive exposure of the process occurs through the export tools. By pressing a key, the user can instantly extract the raw, flattened polar and planar UV maps (mosaicCanvas and coreCanvas). This shatters the 3D illusion entirely, revealing the distorted, 2D imagetext that undergirds the spherical world model.


By accentuating these mechanics, the ACHILLES artifact functions as a piece of critical media. It demands that we recognize operative ekphrasis not as magic, but as a heavily mediated, algorithmic process of slicing, compiling, and stamping cultural data. It keeps the "word" fiercely visible, ensuring that the act of world-building remains a visible negotiation between human text and machine weights.


6. Conclusion: The Future of the Worldtext


Operative ekphrasis, enacted through the rigorous, iterative practices of thick prompting, simultaneously vindicates and vitiates the traditional literary goals of ekphrasis. It fulfills W.J.T. Mitchell’s "ekphrastic hope" by granting language the computational power to instantly manifest the visual, allowing the word to definitively govern the image. Yet, as generative systems evolve from 2D imagetexts to 3D interactive worldtexts, they increasingly realize his "ekphrastic fear": the threat that the image will entirely consume the word, rendering human literary description obsolete.


This tension is formalized in the divergence of the two generative streams we have identified.  The Photoreal Stream, exemplified by enterprise world models like Genie 3, drives toward the ultimate disappearance of the text. It seeks a seamless, physics-based Holodeck where the linguistic prompt acts only as a hidden, subterranean trigger for a flawless simulation. In contrast, the Composite Stream, as demonstrated by our interactive ACHILLES artifact, actively resists this erasure. By accentuating the user interface, exposing the code, and revealing the compositional blending of text and generated pixel, it forces the generative machinery to remain visible. It demands that we acknowledge the worldtext not as a natural reality, but as a constructed, probabilistic collage.


This literalization of the descriptive act echoes the theoretical anxieties surrounding the hypertext literary movement of the 1990s. Hypertext enthusiasts claimed their medium made the cognitive processes of association and allusion structurally operative; traditionalists feared that automating these connections would destroy the interpretive art of reading. A similar anxiety permeates the reception of generative AI. There is a persistent risk, particularly within empirical Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) research, of validating promptcraft strictly through metrics of accuracy, task completion, or photorealism (Liu and Chilton 2023). However, a more nuanced perspective, aligned with Lev Manovich’s observations on generative style, recognizes that the latent space contains undiscovered aesthetic possibilities. Probing this space iteratively through thick prompting does not merely retrieve a "correct" image; it is an act of active, operative discovery.


As these systems mature, the critical question becomes: who defines the prevailing community of practice? Traditional art and literary communities often view the automation of ekphrasis as problematic or illegitimate. In their place, a newly defined, massive community of amateur and professional prompters is establishing its own criteria for success, emphasizing a kind of "pop modernism" characterized by the continuous remixing of historical styles and cultural weights (Chang et al. 2023).


If we allow the Photoreal stream to become the default mode of generative media, we risk moving into seamless, immersive environments where the biases, weights, and algorithmic decisions of the world model are entirely hidden from the user. We lose sight of the prompt. To critically engage with generative AI, we must champion the Composite stream. We must build and theorize interfaces that expose the thickness of the prompt, ensuring that the act of computational world-building remains a visible, negotiated dialogue between human language and machine logic.

From Imagetext to Worldtext: Generative AI as Operative Ekphrasis


Watson Hartsoe & Jay David Bolter


The cursor blinks in a box that pretends to be small.


A prompt window looks like a polite rectangle—an empty field waiting for a sentence. But the moment you type, you are not “describing.” You are reaching into a buried machinery of captions, metadata, style-tags, camera lore, stock-photo grammar, museum catalogs, cinematic clichés, and the residual dust of a billion scraped intentions. The box is not a page. It is a throttle.


This is the condition we want to name without romanticism: operative ekphrasis. The old practice of ekphrasis—vivid description that makes a reader see—was always haunted by a fantasy of power: that language might compel an image into existence. Generative AI turns that fantasy into infrastructure. The description does not merely evoke; it executes.


And once language executes images, it does what images have always threatened to do: it asks to become a world.


The Left Wall: What This Machine Cannot Stop Being


We begin with the unglamorous boundary. Generative models are not eyes. They are compressors. They do not consult a world; they consult weights—statistical traces of past representations. When you prompt, you do not point to an object “out there.” You perturb a probability field “in here.”


That boundary matters because it forbids a certain kind of naive celebration. No matter how clean the output looks, the process is not revelation; it is synthesis. A prompt is not a spell that opens reality. It is a steering mechanism that returns an image shaped by:


what was available to be captured and captioned,

what the platform decided to reward and suppress,

what the interface makes easy to ask for,

what the filters refuse to show,

what the compute budget can afford to render.


This is the first pressure in the ecosystem: the prompt looks like language, but behaves like a control surface.


The One Big Lie: When Description Becomes a Command


The disruptive variable is simple and brutal:


What if describing a thing became a way of making the thing?


That is operative ekphrasis. The text is not ancillary to an artwork; it is a production instrument. The prompt is no longer judged like a poem that “stands alone.” It is judged like a key that either turns or doesn’t—like a procedure that compiles or fails.


This is why the old boundary between word and image collapses into what W. J. T. Mitchell called the imagetext—not a peaceful marriage, but a fused object whose seams carry anxiety: the hope that language can master the visual, and the fear that the visual will consume language and leave no need for human description.


Generative AI does not resolve this anxiety. It mechanizes it.


Promptcraft: The Social Life of Control


A single-shot prompt is an appealing myth because it flatters the idea of effortless authorship. But the reality that has emerged—in practice, in communities, in workflows—is not the one-shot miracle. It is promptcraft: iterative, comparative, ritualized refinement. People do not “write a prompt.” They probe.


This practice resembles Clifford Geertz’s thick description in one crucial way: both are concerned with layers of meaning that do not sit on the surface. But the direction reverses. Thick description reads an existing culture; thick prompting calls an artifact into being by leveraging cultural sediment already inside the model’s weights.


The prompter is not a poet in the classical sense. They are closer to an operator in an unknown archive: testing, adjusting, and watching what the archive is willing to yield.


That is the second pressure in the ecosystem: prompting is not solitary expression; it is a feedback loop.


The Epistemological Triangle: Who Knows What?


To understand why this loop produces tension—why it feels powerful and hollow at the same time—we have to weaponize the information structure.


Author knows: we are not just making pictures; we are manipulating a probabilistic archive whose categories were built without us. We know the prompt’s “control” is partial, and that the interface is shaping what counts as a good request.


Reader knows: we are about to claim that prompting is a new ekphrasis, and that images are becoming worlds. The reader also suspects (rightly) that this could be overreach—academic inflation.


Character knows (the prompter): they know only the immediate ritual: type, generate, regenerate, refine. They do not fully see that each “improvement” is an extraction from a cultural field, and that the field has its own gravity.


The drama lives here: the prompter feels agency, but the system’s agency is distributed—between dataset, model, interface, and platform incentives.


From Imagetext to Worldtext


If the imagetext is the fused unit—prompt plus generated image—then worldtext is what happens when that unit stops being a terminal product and becomes a tile.


A tile implies a map. A map implies navigation. Navigation implies physics, continuity, and constraint. The prompt stops being an isolated utterance and becomes a persistent instruction set for:


scene generation,

object placement,

style coherence,

interaction rules,

memory (what persists when you look away),

and the quiet tyranny of defaults (what counts as “realistic,” what counts as “coherent,” what counts as “allowed”).


Worldtext is not a new medium category so much as a new condition: language becomes an interface for producing situations rather than images.


This is where the ecosystem fractures into two streams—because worldtext can be built in two fundamentally different ways.


Two Streams: The Hidden Holodeck vs. The Exposed Composite


1) The Photoreal Stream
Its dream is disappearance. The prompt becomes subterranean; the generated world arrives as if it were simply there. The interface becomes less like writing and more like wishful thought: a frictionless translation from desire to environment. In this stream, the machinery is a liability. The goal is immersion, and immersion requires amnesia about how the world is made.


2) The Composite Stream
Its ethic is exposure. It refuses the seamless illusion and keeps the generative act visible: slicing text, revealing prompt fragments, showing the stamp, exposing blending modes, letting the user witness the world as a collage of negotiations. Here, the seam is not a defect—it is the point.


These streams aren’t merely aesthetic choices. They are governance choices. They determine whether users inhabit a world that hides its origin story, or a world that insists on showing its provenance and its compromises.


The Emblem: Homer’s Shield as a World Engine


We need an emblematic object—something that was already worldtext before any machine could render it.


Homer’s Shield of Achilles is not “a description of a shield.” It is a portable cosmos: agriculture, conflict, ritual, weather, dance, law, and labor engraved into a single artifact. The shield is a world compressed into an object—exactly the kind of compression a generative system performs, but with a crucial difference: Homer’s compression is overtly cultural and narratively motivated; the model’s compression is statistical and mostly invisible.


That makes the shield useful as a test case. Not because it is ancient and therefore “important,” but because it is structurally perfect: ekphrasis that already behaves like a generator. You can treat the shield not as a passage to interpret, but as a world specification.


And once you treat it as a specification, a workflow emerges that looks less like criticism and more like compilation:


zone the text,

extract fragments,

wrap them in constraints that enforce material reality (engraving, patina, metal),

generate an image,

stamp that image back into a spatial coordinate,

and let repetition accumulate a navigable artifact.


The shield becomes a machine for producing world-fragments.


The Counter-World: Auden’s Overwrite


W. H. Auden’s The Shield of Achilles is not an homage. It is an overwrite—an erasure of Homer’s vivid plural world, replaced with a bleak procedural landscape. If Homer’s shield is a world of textured social life, Auden’s shield is a world of administrative emptiness and organized cruelty.


Why does this matter for generative systems? Because a world model does not “understand” the moral difference between these worlds. It detects patterns. It averages. It remixes. Unless the interface forces the difference to remain legible, the two shields can collapse into a single aesthetic soup: “ancient artifact, bleak modernity, cinematic lighting.”


This is the third pressure in the ecosystem: worldtext is politically sensitive even when it looks purely aesthetic, because it encodes what kinds of worlds are thinkable, visible, and reproducible.


Thick Prompting as Operative Criticism


At this point, the paper stops being a story about “AI art” and becomes a story about method.


Thick prompting is not just a way to get better outputs. It is a way to read the model by forcing it to show what it associates, what it elides, what it cannot hold together, and what it returns by default when you do not specify.


In other words: thick prompting becomes a kind of operative criticism. You don’t interpret the text after the fact; you interpret the system by watching what it does when the text is used as a handle.


The prompter becomes a fieldworker inside a machine-culture, except the culture they study is probabilistic and the rituals are interface-bound.


Accentuated Interfaces: Keeping the Word Visible


If worldtext is where things are headed, the core question becomes: what kind of interface will govern it?


A photoreal world model can make the prompt disappear. That disappearance feels like progress—until you remember what disappears with it:


the visibility of constraints,

the legibility of bias,

the accountability of provenance,

the user’s ability to notice when the world has been quietly normalized.


The composite stream keeps the word visible. It treats the prompt not as an embarrassing scaffold, but as the ethical surface where negotiation happens. It shows the stamp, the blend, the reticle, the extraction. It does not let the user pretend the world arrived from nowhere.


This isn’t aesthetic purism. It’s epistemic hygiene.


Where the Ecosystem Wants to Go Next (No Ending—Only Pressure)


We refuse the tidy conclusion where the authors “resolve” the fear and hope of ekphrasis with a moral bow. The ecosystem does not permit it.


The pressures remain and intensify:


Platforms will prefer the photoreal stream because seamlessness sells.

Artists and scholars will prefer the composite stream because seams are where meaning—and critique—can survive.

Prompters will keep inventing rituals, templates, and folk methods because the model’s interior remains unrevealed and the outputs remain seductively close to mastery.

World models will expand the scope of what language can call into being, and with each expansion the prompt becomes less like a sentence and more like a constitutional clause.


So the question is not “Can AI make art?” The question is: what kinds of worlds will be cheap enough to generate, persuasive enough to inhabit, and opaque enough to govern us without argument?


The cursor keeps blinking in its small box.


It is still pretending to be a place for words.
