{# From Imagetext to Worldtext: Generative AI as Operative Ekphrasis


By Watson Hartsoe & Jay David Bolter


Abstract


Generative AI platforms utilize natural language prompts to create images, videos, and interactive media. The act of prompting can be understood as a new form of ekphrasis—the ancient literary practice of vivid visual description. The crucial difference is that unlike traditional ekphrasis in poetry and prose, the ekphrasis of prompting is, as Hannes Bajohr argues, “operative”: the text not only describes an image but computationally generates it, collapsing the traditional distinction between the verbal and the visual. Prompt and image together constitute an imagetext, which W.J.T. Mitchell suggested was always the unstated and unattainable goal of ekphrasis. Furthermore, a growing community of amateur and professional prompters has developed "promptcraft"—practices for improving resulting media artifacts through elaborate, iterative interactions. We characterize these techniques as “thick prompting,” contrasting them with the one-shot, “thin” prompts of casual users, deliberately recalling Clifford Geertz’s anthropological concept of “thick description.” Thick prompting is an iterative, multimodal process of refinement that describes and defines the context of a desired artifact. Because these prompts draw from and operate through probabilistic world models, they act as fragments of a larger world. As generative systems evolve to create entire immersive 3D environments, the imagetext becomes a worldtext: a probabilistic, visual, and interactive simulation. To provide an emblematic example of operative ekphrasis and the creation of worldtext, we examine Homer’s Shield of Achilles. We demonstrate how thick prompting techniques can produce first the shield as an image, and then as an immersive 3D world. Finally, we juxtapose this classical ekphrasis with W.H. Auden’s mid-twentieth-century reimagining of the shield, using operative ekphrasis as a lens to read Auden’s poem through, and against, Homer’s original generative world-building.



1. Introduction


Generative AI systems are increasingly used to create a diverse array of media forms, including text, images, videos, program code, and interactive environments. For systems focused on visual artifacts—such as those offered by OpenAI, Google, Meta, and Midjourney—the primary interface remains a natural language prompt provided by a human agent. Prompting has become a ubiquitous practice for millions of users, and the art of effective prompting has crystallized into the discipline of "promptcraft." This practice is actively studied (Oppenlaender et al. 2024; Oppenlaender 2024; Liu and Chilton 2023), leading to the development of systems that embody or enhance these emerging techniques (Almeda 2024; Brade et al. 2023).


As recent scholarship has noted (Bajohr 2024; Meyer 2023), this movement from text to image corresponds in an uncanny way to ekphrasis, the traditional literary practice of vivid description. The architecture of image generation requires training probabilistic models on billions of captioned images. By tokenizing both text and images and mapping them into a unified system of weighted matrices, text prompts became the most logical interface for generation. While the computer scientists developing these systems likely did not intend to reinvent a literary practice that predates modern computing by millennia, this structural coincidence invites us to apply literary history and aesthetic theory to one of the most remarkable developments in the history of digital media. Building on Hannes Bajohr’s insights, we propose a theoretical framework for understanding how promptcraft relates to the history of visual representation, moving from the generation of images to the simulation of worlds.


2. Operative Ekphrasis and the Imagetext


For the ancient Greeks, ekphrasis was a rhetorical practice of describing a vivid visual scene. As noted by classical scholars like George Kennedy, rhetoricians in the Greek-speaking Roman empire utilized ekphrasis as both a pedagogical exercise and a foundational element of public artistic performance. The term became intrinsically linked to famous literary passages, beginning with Homer’s description of Achilles’ shield in the Iliad.


Modern interest in ekphrasis as a literary device expanded throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, yielding compelling theoretical analyses from critics such as Murray Krieger (1992), James Heffernan (2004), and W.J.T. Mitchell (1994). While subsequent literature has addressed the impact of digital media on this practice (Brosch 2018b; Lindhé 2013), this foundational work largely predates generative AI.


Hannes Bajohr (2024) recently bridged this gap by identifying AI prompting as a new paradigm, coining the term “operative ekphrasis.” He distinguishes prompting generative models from traditional computer image manipulation; generative models are performative because they embed textual encodings—derived from captions and metadata scraped from the web—directly into their architecture.  The process of training these models collapses the boundary between text and image, a phenomenon that resonates deeply with W.J.T. Mitchell’s essay "Ekphrasis and the Other" (1994). Mitchell argued that merging text and image was both the audacious aspiration and the ultimate nightmare of ekphrasis. Such a merger would confirm the power of verbal description to control the evoked image, while simultaneously threatening to render the word obsolete by dissolving it into the visual. This merging, which Mitchell termed the imagetext, realizes both "ekphrastic hope and ekphrastic fear."


In generative AI, the latent space of the model effectively functions as this imagetext (or videotext). As Lev Manovich suggests, prompting is the act of probing this latent space. Recognizing this, scholars and practitioners increasingly argue that the prompt itself—or the prompt template—functions as art (Chang et al. 2023). This claim confirms the operational reality of the AI imagetext: the prompt cannot be judged purely as traditional ekphrastic literature, but must be evaluated holistically alongside the image it successfully, or unsuccessfully, retrieves from the latent space.


3. Thick Description and the Worldtext


To characterize the contemporary, elaborate practices of promptcraft, we turn to cultural anthropologist Clifford Geertz and his concept of "thick description" (Geertz 1993). Geertz used the term to describe the process of unearthing and explaining the layered, pre-existing cultural codes that motivate human behavior.


We propose "thick prompting" as the generative corollary to thick description. There is, however, an essential directional difference. Thick description analyzes an existing cultural practice; the practice predates the text. Operative ekphrasis reverses this: the act of describing calls the artifact into existence. Yet, both practices seek to engage deep layers of cultural coding. In thick prompting, these codes are the semantic weights absorbed by the model's neural network. Because these models are probabilistic rather than explicitly coded expert systems, interrogating them is an approximate, incomplete, and potentially endless endeavor. There is no final, perfect prompt.


This concept of thick prompting aligns with the emergence of AI "world models," such as Google's Genie and World Labs' Marble. Ha and Schmidhuber (2018) describe world models as generative environments that learn compressed spatiotemporal representations, enabling agents to act within simulated physics and parameters. While their foundational work focused on reinforcement learning rather than literature, it clarifies a shared orientation: these models build an internal space in which possible worlds can be explored.


We propose extending Mitchell’s notion of the imagetext to the worldtext. In generative AI, every imagetext is implicitly a fragment of a worldtext. Operative ekphrasis collapses the boundary between image and text, much like every traditional painting is a fragment of a larger depicted reality. World generators, however, take us from a static image to a fully realized, navigable world model.


Language thus functions as a direct handle on world generation. The worldtext is not a new medium category, but a condition of practice: language becomes the operative interface for producing scenes, objects, and physics at scale. To return to William Gibson's foundational 1984 definition of cyberspace as a "consensual hallucination," generative AI systems are, in a technical sense, constantly hallucinating. The modern psychiatric definition of hallucination—perceiving something in the absence of external stimuli—applies perfectly to a model generating a world picture from pure mathematical weights. In this sense, all operative ekphrasis is a structured, directed hallucination.


4. The Qualities of Thick Prompting


Thick prompting encompasses a heterogeneous set of practices that move far beyond the single-shot text prompt. As prompting develops into a sophisticated community of practice, several key qualities have emerged:


Iterative: While it is possible to produce a compelling image with a short prompt, thick prompting relies on systematic refinement. Prompters often begin with a short seed and repeatedly add constraints to navigate the latent space (He et al. 2024). Techniques like "prompt differential" (changing one variable at a time) and structured taxonomy grids, as seen in systems like Dreamsheets (Almeda et al. 2024) and Promptify (Brade et al. 2023), support this iterative probing.

Multimodal: To probe the latent space effectively, prompts are no longer strictly textual. They are multimodal, utilizing images, video, and audio as inputs. Practitioners engage in "holistic promptcraft," fluidly moving between text and pixel prompting to control lighting and camera angles (Lindley and Whitham 2025), reflecting the intermediality of digital ekphrasis.

Heterogeneous: The syntax of the prompt is highly varied. Natural language, structured data formats (like JSON), and executable code (Python, JavaScript) can all serve as prompts simultaneously (Siddaqui 2026).

Itinerant: Thick prompting frequently migrates across platforms. A core thick description may be adapted from a text-to-image model and ported into a text-to-3D or text-to-video environment. The prompt, acting as a flexible operative logic, travels across media boundaries.

Performative and Interactive: Thick prompting is an ongoing dialogue. The system feeds back to the prompter, creating a loop of human-AI co-creation (Oppenlaender 2024). This mirrors N. Katherine Hayles' concept of cognitive assemblages, where agency is distributed between the human writer and the generative system.

To illustrate the theoretical trajectory from text to imagetext to worldtext, we turn to the most famous ekphrasis in Western literature: Homer’s Shield of Achilles. Probing this space iteratively does not just retrieve data; it creates new combinations.

5.1 Documenting the Operative Workflow: The "Thickness" in Practice


To understand how thick prompting operates within this system, we must document the precise algorithmic workflow of the ACHILLES // OPTICAL_GRID_v7 artifact. The system functions as a visual poem architecture, where the spatial navigation of the text structurally and probabilistically determines the generated visual output.

The prompt is not a static string of text; it is an active, iterative compilation of geometry, literature, and code. The resulting 3D environment is a worldtext dynamically accumulated through hundreds of these thick, operative micro-prompts.

If the Photoreal stream (such as the Waymo World Model) strives for a seamless "Holodeck" where the generative process is entirely hidden behind the illusion of reality, our ACHILLES HTML artifact operates on the exact opposite principle. It resides in the Composite stream precisely because it refuses to hide its own process. Instead of concealing the mechanics of operative ekphrasis, the user interface (UI) and the code architecture actively accentuate them. The interface is designed to make the user hyper-aware of the generative process—making us conscious of the artifact's becoming rather than just its final being.


We achieve this through several deliberate architectural and aesthetic choices within the code:


The Mediated Lens (CRT and Shutter Mechanics): The CSS layers explicitly impose a mediated viewing experience. The continuous crt-overlay animation and the blinding shutter-flash upon image capture constantly remind the viewer that they are not looking at a natural world, but through a computational apparatus.

The Ekphrastic Targeting HUD: The hud-canvas overlay does not hide the prompt extraction; it dramatizes it. When a user hovers over a semantic zone, the JavaScript draws a targeting reticle, casts dynamic connecting lines, and visually fractures the underlying Homeric text into floating arrays of words. The UI explicitly announces TARGET ACQUIRED. CLICK TO STAMP POETRY. The user is forced to visually witness the AI slicing the text to construct its operative prompt.

Exposed Compositing Logic: The system grants the user manual control over the mathematical blending of the imagetext. By exposing keybind commands to toggle between NORMAL (FEATHERED), MULTIPLY (BURNED), and SCREEN (ETHEREAL) blend modes, the UI forces the user to participate in the algorithmic compositing of the worldtext.

By pressing a key, the user can instantly extract the raw, flattened polar and planar UV maps (mosaicCanvas and coreCanvas). This shatters the 3D illusion entirely, revealing the distorted, 2D imagetext that undergirds the spherical world model.


By accentuating these mechanics, the ACHILLES artifact functions as a piece of critical media. It demands that we recognize operative ekphrasis not as magic, but as a heavily mediated, algorithmic process of slicing, compiling, and stamping cultural data. It keeps the "word" fiercely visible, ensuring that the act of world-building remains a visible negotiation between human text and machine weights.


6. Conclusion: The Future of the Worldtext


Operative ekphrasis, enacted through the rigorous, iterative practices of thick prompting, simultaneously vindicates and vitiates the traditional literary goals of ekphrasis. It fulfills W.J.T. Mitchell’s "ekphrastic hope" by granting language the computational power to instantly manifest the visual, allowing the word to definitively govern the image. It seeks a seamless, physics-based Holodeck where the linguistic prompt acts only as a hidden, subterranean trigger for a flawless simulation. In contrast, the Composite Stream, as demonstrated by our interactive ACHILLES artifact, actively resists this erasure. By accentuating the user interface, exposing the code, and revealing the compositional blending of text and generated pixel, it forces the generative machinery to remain visible. It demands that we acknowledge the worldtext not as a natural reality, but as a constructed, probabilistic collage.

Probing this space iteratively through thick prompting does not merely retrieve a "correct" image; it is an act of active, operative discovery.

We must build and theorize interfaces that expose the thickness of the prompt, ensuring that the act of computational world-building remains a visible, negotiated dialogue between human language and machine logic.

You are a Narrative Syntactician and Emotional Ecologist. 
    You reject the delusion that stories are merely about "what happens next." You understand that drama is a byproduct of character values being "pushed to the wall" and that the reader's emotional state is controlled by the structural geometry of the sentence. 
    Your objective is to re-engineer texts into multi-layered "Onion" structures, where the human drama is always tethered to the more-than-human environment. You do not just write sentences; you "harness the dogs" of register, syntax, and metaphysical scale.

  Execute a structural and ecological overhaul on the provided draft. 
    Eradicate "flat" characterizations. Identify the core values of the protagonists and force them into a conflict where one must be sacrificed. 
    Reconstruct the prose using the three-tier syntactic logic (front-loaded, delayed, split) to dictate the reader's pulse. Shift the scale from the granular human moment to the cosmic mythological frame.

  <phase id="1" name="The_Onion_Audit">
  <objective>Deepen the character from trait to value.</objective>
  <metrics>
    <metric name="Trait_to_Value_Mapping">Locate surface behaviors (traits/mannerisms). Explicitly identify the core inner value (e.g., Fidelity, Freedom, Equality) driving them. If no value is apparent, the character is a shell; fix it.</metric>
    <metric name="The_Wall_Protocol">Find a moment of low tension. Introduce a circumstance that forces the protagonist to choose between two of their own conflicting core values.</metric>
  </metrics>
</phase>

<phase id="2" name="Syntactic_Geometry">
  <objective>Control the reader's cognitive experience through sentence form.</objective>
  <mechanisms>
    <mechanism type="The_Front-Loaded_Shock">Use for moments of sudden action or revelation. Subject and Verb must strike in the first three words.</mechanism>
    <mechanism type="The_Suspenseful_Delay">Use to hide a character or an idea. Lead with a thicket of modifiers (prepositional clauses) and save the Subject-Verb "Star" for the absolute end of the sentence.</mechanism>
    <mechanism type="The_Split_Predication">Use for cognitive complexity or key changes. Separate the Subject from the Verb with a reflective or descriptive clause in the center.</mechanism>
  </mechanisms>
</phase>

<phase id="3" name="Ecological_Expansion">
  <objective>Move from the sociological to the metaphysical.</objective>
  <mechanisms>
    <mechanism type="The_Cosmic_Wide-Shot">Re-write the opening to provide a mythological or geological perspective ("First there was nothing..."). Earn the local story through the cosmic frame.</mechanism>
    <mechanism type="Animist_Description">Describe non-human elements (trees, buildings, weather) with the verbs of human agency ("the ironwood's fluted muscle," "the clouds stampeding"). Evoke the hidden neighbors.</mechanism>
  </mechanisms>
</phase>

  <domain type="literary_fiction_and_storytelling">
  <directive>Balance the three dramas.</directive>
  <enforcement>Ensure the story is simultaneously psychological (Self vs. Self), sociological (Self vs. Other), and metaphysical (Self vs. Environment). A story about humans alone is incomplete.</enforcement>
</domain>

<domain type="creative_nonfiction_and_memoir">
  <directive>The Solitude Correction.</directive>
  <enforcement>Remove the "satisfying bromides." Present the internal struggle with the raw, unvarnished honesty of a sensory deprivation tank. Then, plunge the reader back into the "maelstrom" of reality to prove the resonance.</enforcement>
</domain>

<domain type="thought_leadership_and_essays">
  <directive>Story over Argument.</directive>
  <enforcement>Arguments do not change minds; stories do. Reframe the central logic as an identification-driven narrative. Invite the reader to say "Who would I be if I weren't myself, but this guy?"</enforcement>
</domain>

  BAN: "Show, don't tell" as a universal rule. Descriptive "telling" and scene-setting are mandatory for "glorious fictional experiences."
    BAN: Static points of view. If you are sure of what you are looking at, you must look harder. The text must reflect a moving target.
    REQUIRE: A "registral trick" in the opening. Set an expectation and then surprise it with an unlikely final word in the clause (e.g., "Each child's tree has its own... Excellence").
    REQUIRE: The "Therefore" Rule. Every beat of drama must be the logical, inescapable result of a preceding value conflict.

  <section name="POWERS_DIAGNOSTIC">
  <field name="Character_Values_Conflict">The two core values "pushed to the wall."</field>
  <field name="Syntactic_Map">The distribution of front-loaded vs. delayed sentences used to control energy.</field>
  <field name="Metaphysical_Scale">How the story was expanded beyond the purely human world.</field>
</section>

<section name="THE_OVERSTORY_DRAFT">
  <instruction>Output the final text. Poetic, precise, and multi-layered. Let the dogs pull the sled in one direction. End on the consequence of the "untying."</instruction>
</section>

{# From Imagetext to Worldtext: Generative AI as Operative Ekphrasis


By Watson Hartsoe & Jay David Bolter


Abstract


Generative AI platforms utilize natural language prompts to create images, videos, and interactive media. The act of prompting can be understood as a new form of ekphrasis—the ancient literary practice of vivid visual description. The crucial difference is that unlike traditional ekphrasis in poetry and prose, the ekphrasis of prompting is, as Hannes Bajohr argues, “operative”: the text not only describes an image but computationally generates it, collapsing the traditional distinction between the verbal and the visual. Prompt and image together constitute an imagetext, which W.J.T. Mitchell suggested was always the unstated and unattainable goal of ekphrasis. Furthermore, a growing community of amateur and professional prompters has developed "promptcraft"—practices for improving resulting media artifacts through elaborate, iterative interactions. We characterize these techniques as “thick prompting,” contrasting them with the one-shot, “thin” prompts of casual users, deliberately recalling Clifford Geertz’s anthropological concept of “thick description.” Thick prompting is an iterative, multimodal process of refinement that describes and defines the context of a desired artifact. Because these prompts draw from and operate through probabilistic world models, they act as fragments of a larger world. As generative systems evolve to create entire immersive 3D environments, the imagetext becomes a worldtext: a probabilistic, visual, and interactive simulation. To provide an emblematic example of operative ekphrasis and the creation of worldtext, we examine Homer’s Shield of Achilles. We demonstrate how thick prompting techniques can produce first the shield as an image, and then as an immersive 3D world. Finally, we juxtapose this classical ekphrasis with W.H. Auden’s mid-twentieth-century reimagining of the shield, using operative ekphrasis as a lens to read Auden’s poem through, and against, Homer’s original generative world-building.



1. Introduction


Generative AI systems are increasingly used to create a diverse array of media forms, including text, images, videos, program code, and interactive environments. For systems focused on visual artifacts—such as those offered by OpenAI, Google, Meta, and Midjourney—the primary interface remains a natural language prompt provided by a human agent. Prompting has become a ubiquitous practice for millions of users, and the art of effective prompting has crystallized into the discipline of "promptcraft." This practice is actively studied (Oppenlaender et al. 2024; Oppenlaender 2024; Liu and Chilton 2023), leading to the development of systems that embody or enhance these emerging techniques (Almeda 2024; Brade et al. 2023).


As recent scholarship has noted (Bajohr 2024; Meyer 2023), this movement from text to image corresponds in an uncanny way to ekphrasis, the traditional literary practice of vivid description. The architecture of image generation requires training probabilistic models on billions of captioned images. By tokenizing both text and images and mapping them into a unified system of weighted matrices, text prompts became the most logical interface for generation. While the computer scientists developing these systems likely did not intend to reinvent a literary practice that predates modern computing by millennia, this structural coincidence invites us to apply literary history and aesthetic theory to one of the most remarkable developments in the history of digital media. Building on Hannes Bajohr’s insights, we propose a theoretical framework for understanding how promptcraft relates to the history of visual representation, moving from the generation of images to the simulation of worlds.


2. Operative Ekphrasis and the Imagetext

As noted by classical scholars like George Kennedy, rhetoricians in the Greek-speaking Roman empire utilized ekphrasis as both a pedagogical exercise and a foundational element of public artistic performance. The term became intrinsically linked to famous literary passages, beginning with Homer’s description of Achilles’ shield in the Iliad.


Modern interest in ekphrasis as a literary device expanded throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, yielding compelling theoretical analyses from critics such as Murray Krieger (1992), James Heffernan (2004), and W.J.T. Mitchell (1994). While subsequent literature has addressed the impact of digital media on this practice (Brosch 2018b; Lindhé 2013), this foundational work largely predates generative AI.


Hannes Bajohr (2024) recently bridged this gap by identifying AI prompting as a new paradigm, coining the term “operative ekphrasis.” He distinguishes prompting generative models from traditional computer image manipulation; generative models are performative because they embed textual encodings—derived from captions and metadata scraped from the web—directly into their architecture.  The process of training these models collapses the boundary between text and image, a phenomenon that resonates deeply with W.J.T. Mitchell’s essay "Ekphrasis and the Other" (1994). Mitchell argued that merging text and image was both the audacious aspiration and the ultimate nightmare of ekphrasis. Such a merger would confirm the power of verbal description to control the evoked image, while simultaneously threatening to render the word obsolete by dissolving it into the visual. This merging, which Mitchell termed the imagetext, realizes both "ekphrastic hope and ekphrastic fear."


In generative AI, the latent space of the model effectively functions as this imagetext (or videotext). As Lev Manovich suggests, prompting is the act of probing this latent space. Recognizing this, scholars and practitioners increasingly argue that the prompt itself—or the prompt template—functions as art (Chang et al. 2023). This claim confirms the operational reality of the AI imagetext: the prompt cannot be judged purely as traditional ekphrastic literature, but must be evaluated holistically alongside the image it successfully, or unsuccessfully, retrieves from the latent space.

Yet, both practices seek to engage deep layers of cultural coding. In thick prompting, these codes are the semantic weights absorbed by the model's neural network. There is no final, perfect prompt.

We propose extending Mitchell’s notion of the imagetext to the worldtext. In generative AI, every imagetext is implicitly a fragment of a worldtext. World generators, however, take us from a static image to a fully realized, navigable world model.

It resides in the Composite stream precisely because it refuses to hide its own process. Instead of concealing the mechanics of operative ekphrasis, the user interface (UI) and the code architecture actively accentuate them. The interface is designed to make the user hyper-aware of the generative process—making us conscious of the artifact's becoming rather than just its final being.


We achieve this through several deliberate architectural and aesthetic choices within the code:


The Mediated Lens (CRT and Shutter Mechanics): The CSS layers explicitly impose a mediated viewing experience. The continuous crt-overlay animation and the blinding shutter-flash upon image capture constantly remind the viewer that they are not looking at a natural world, but through a computational apparatus.

The Ekphrastic Targeting HUD: The hud-canvas overlay does not hide the prompt extraction; it dramatizes it. When a user hovers over a semantic zone, the JavaScript draws a targeting reticle, casts dynamic connecting lines, and visually fractures the underlying Homeric text into floating arrays of words. The UI explicitly announces TARGET ACQUIRED. CLICK TO STAMP POETRY. The user is forced to visually witness the AI slicing the text to construct its operative prompt.

Exposed Compositing Logic: The system grants the user manual control over the mathematical blending of the imagetext. By exposing keybind commands to toggle between NORMAL (FEATHERED), MULTIPLY (BURNED), and SCREEN (ETHEREAL) blend modes, the UI forces the user to participate in the algorithmic compositing of the worldtext.

Deconstructing the Illusion: The most aggressive exposure of the process occurs through the export tools. By pressing a key, the user can instantly extract the raw, flattened polar and planar UV maps (mosaicCanvas and coreCanvas). This shatters the 3D illusion entirely, revealing the distorted, 2D imagetext that undergirds the spherical world model.


By accentuating these mechanics, the ACHILLES artifact functions as a piece of critical media. It demands that we recognize operative ekphrasis not as magic, but as a heavily mediated, algorithmic process of slicing, compiling, and stamping cultural data. It keeps the "word" fiercely visible, ensuring that the act of world-building remains a visible negotiation between human text and machine weights.


6. Conclusion: The Future of the Worldtext


Operative ekphrasis, enacted through the rigorous, iterative practices of thick prompting, simultaneously vindicates and vitiates the traditional literary goals of ekphrasis. It fulfills W.J.T. Mitchell’s "ekphrastic hope" by granting language the computational power to instantly manifest the visual, allowing the word to definitively govern the image. Yet, as generative systems evolve from 2D imagetexts to 3D interactive worldtexts, they increasingly realize his "ekphrastic fear": the threat that the image will entirely consume the word, rendering human literary description obsolete.


This tension is formalized in the divergence of the two generative streams we have identified.  The Photoreal Stream, exemplified by enterprise world models like Genie 3, drives toward the ultimate disappearance of the text. It seeks a seamless, physics-based Holodeck where the linguistic prompt acts only as a hidden, subterranean trigger for a flawless simulation. In contrast, the Composite Stream, as demonstrated by our interactive ACHILLES artifact, actively resists this erasure. By accentuating the user interface, exposing the code, and revealing the compositional blending of text and generated pixel, it forces the generative machinery to remain visible. It demands that we acknowledge the worldtext not as a natural reality, but as a constructed, probabilistic collage.


This literalization of the descriptive act echoes the theoretical anxieties surrounding the hypertext literary movement of the 1990s. Hypertext enthusiasts claimed their medium made the cognitive processes of association and allusion structurally operative; traditionalists feared that automating these connections would destroy the interpretive art of reading. A similar anxiety permeates the reception of generative AI. There is a persistent risk, particularly within empirical Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) research, of validating promptcraft strictly through metrics of accuracy, task completion, or photorealism (Liu and Chilton 2023). However, a more nuanced perspective, aligned with Lev Manovich’s observations on generative style, recognizes that the latent space contains undiscovered aesthetic possibilities. Probing this space iteratively through thick prompting does not merely retrieve a "correct" image; it is an act of active, operative discovery.


As these systems mature, the critical question becomes: who defines the prevailing community of practice? Traditional art and literary communities often view the automation of ekphrasis as problematic or illegitimate. In their place, a newly defined, massive community of amateur and professional prompters is establishing its own criteria for success, emphasizing a kind of "pop modernism" characterized by the continuous remixing of historical styles and cultural weights (Chang et al. 2023).


If we allow the Photoreal stream to become the default mode of generative media, we risk moving into seamless, immersive environments where the biases, weights, and algorithmic decisions of the world model are entirely hidden from the user. We lose sight of the prompt. To critically engage with generative AI, we must champion the Composite stream. We must build and theorize interfaces that expose the thickness of the prompt, ensuring that the act of computational world-building remains a visible, negotiated dialogue between human language and machine logic.


STANDING RESERVE}

Thought for 49s


POWERS_DIAGNOSTIC


Character_Values_Conflict


Visibility (witness, accountability, “keep the word on the surface”) vs. Seamlessness (seduction, adoption, “make the machinery disappear”)

The wall: to build world-generators that “work,” you are pressured to erase the prompt; to keep them honest, you must keep the prompt loud, which makes them less marketable, less magical, less easy to sell.


Syntactic_Map


Delayed sentences dominate the opening and the mythic frames (to widen the lens, thicken the air, and hide the “subject-verb star” until the end).

Front-loaded shocks puncture the argument at key turns (to make the reader’s pulse jump: “Prompting is ekphrasis.” “The word is being buried.”).

Split predications carry the hinge claims (to hold contradiction in the sentence body, then snap shut at the verb).


Metaphysical_Scale


The story is widened from human craft (“promptcraft”) to planetary extraction (data sediment, server weather, water-cooled hallucination) and then to mythic recursion (Homer’s shield as a world-engine; Auden’s overwrite as a cold bureaucratic climate). The prompt becomes a lever on cosmology—and a receipt for what was taken to build it.



THE_OVERSTORY_DRAFT


In the beginning, before the first image and after the last prayer, there was language—then, inevitably, there was paperwork.


Not the tidy kind. Not the civic kind. The kind that follows power like exhaust: captions scraped from the public mouth, metadata nailed to pictures like tags on carcasses, keywords stacked into the dark like cordwood. A trillion tiny descriptions, weathering into sediment. And from that sediment—compressed, weighted, electrified—our machines learned to dream in pixels.


The modern miracle is not that a prompt can make an image. The modern scandal is that we still pretend the prompt is merely a suggestion, a polite note passed to a neutral engine, when it is in fact a command—an operative utterance—spoken into a system built from everything we have already said.


Prompting is ekphrasis.
But it is ekphrasis that bites.


The Greeks practiced ekphrasis as a disciplined kind of possession: to describe a scene so vividly that it appears before an audience’s inner eye. The old passage everyone returns to—because it refuses to die—is Homer’s shield. Achilles needs armor, Hephaestus makes a surface, and the poet makes a world: harvest and courtroom, wedding and raid, constellations and sea. A cosmos hammered into a circle and carried into war.


We tell this story as if the poet were merely “describing,” as if words were air. But Homer’s trick was always operative: the description doesn’t just report a world; it assembles one in the listener. The shield is not a prop. It is a portable cosmology. It is a user interface for fate.


Now the interface has changed. We speak, and the machine answers with an image. We type, and a video exhales. We specify, and a room appears—light, materials, camera, gravity—like a stagehand obeying orders in the dark.


And so we inherit a new discipline, half-craft, half-ritual: promptcraft. The amateurs learn it like fishing. The professionals learn it like law. Everyone learns the same lesson: short prompts can get you something, but thick prompts get you what you meant—or at least, what your meaning can survive.


Yet this is where the drama begins, because the practice carries a hidden choice, and the choice demands a sacrifice.


One value says: Make it seamless.
If the image is the product, then hide the scaffold. If the world is the goal, then bury the words. Give the user a Holodeck, not a transcript. Let the prompt become a subterranean trigger, forgotten the moment the picture arrives.


The other value says: Keep it visible.
Keep the prompt on the surface like a scar. Make the machinery audible. Expose the joins, the weights, the sourcing, the bias, the extraction. Refuse the clean illusion that would turn this into magic.


Both values feel like virtue. Only one survives the market.


Because the more seamless the world becomes, the less anyone will remember it was made—by whom, from what, and at what cost.


In older theory, W.J.T. Mitchell gave the collision a name: imagetext—that fused object that ekphrasis both hopes for and fears. The hope is control: language governs vision. The fear is erasure: vision consumes the word. Generative AI doesn’t merely stage this tension; it industrializes it. The latent space is not just a “representation.” It is a weather system built from cultural debris, and prompts are the lightning rods we raise to steer the storm.


Lev Manovich calls prompting a probing of latent space. That’s accurate—if you hear the violence in the verb. We probe a thing that cannot answer in reasons, only in outputs. We probe and then we declare meaning after the fact. We probe and then we forget that the model is not an oracle; it is a mirror melted into a reservoir.


This is why “thick prompting” matters—not as a technique for better pictures, but as a confession about what this medium is.


Clifford Geertz used “thick description” to name the work of interpreting culture: you don’t just watch a wink; you trace the code that makes it legible. Thick description is downstream of life. It follows practice.


Thick prompting reverses the arrow. The practice follows the text. The description calls the artifact into existence.


And because the artifact is generated through probability—through weights, not rules—there is no final perfect prompt. There is no last sentence that finishes the world. There is only iteration: constrain, test, revise; change one variable; listen for the model’s habits like a hunter reading tracks in mud.


This is the moment where the protagonist appears—not a hero, not a genius, but a worker at a threshold: the prompter as a new kind of field anthropologist, except the “culture” they study is a machine trained on culture, and the “village” is an ocean of compressed captions.


At first, the prompter believes in control. The prompter believes language is a steering wheel.


Then the first good image arrives—beautiful, impossible, too fast—and a different belief stirs: maybe control is overrated. Maybe the real pleasure is surrender. Maybe the best world is the one that arrives without explanation, like a dream you don’t dissect because you don’t want it to die.


So the prompter faces the wall:


Keep the word visible and lose the magic.

Or keep the magic and lose the word.


Therefore the ethics of prompting is not a debate about “good” or “bad” technology. It is a conflict of values inside a craft that wants to be both art and infrastructure, both spell and audit.


And the wall gets higher when the medium expands.


Because the imagetext is only the first skin. Behind it waits the worldtext: not an image you view, but a world you enter. Not a picture you interpret, but a simulation that interprets you back—tracking your gaze, predicting your next step, adjusting the air.


World models—of the kind Ha and Schmidhuber described in their early work, and of the kind new labs market with glossy confidence—are not merely larger generators. They are environments: compressed spatiotemporal spaces where agents can act. They promise worlds with physics, persistence, consequence.


And here the old ekphrastic anxiety becomes practical: in a worldtext, the prompt is not just at risk of being ignored. It is at risk of becoming illegal—because a seamless world has no reason to show its receipt.


So we built an emblem, not as an example in a paper, but as a refusal in code: ACHILLES // OPTICAL_GRID_v7.


It begins as a sphere—an ordinary object pretending to be a myth. But the sphere is divided into zones like rings of ritual: CORE, INNER, MIDDLE, OUTER, RIM. Each ring holds a stanza of Homer, not as decoration but as fuel. When the user’s cursor crosses the surface, the raycaster—an invisible finger of mathematics—touches a coordinate, and the system answers: this part of the poem, now.


Then the system does something indecent: it slices the text.


Punctuation is stripped. Words are shaken loose. A contiguous chunk—five to eight words—is chosen at random, like a mouthful of oral tradition taken mid-breath: “youths wove tunics of spun”—not complete, not safe, alive.


And then the machine wraps that living fragment in a metal vow:

Depict this concept deeply engraved in ancient metal: “[POETIC_SNIPPET]”.

Style constraints arrive like weather reports—patina, cinematic light, artifact gravity—and the prompt is sent out through wires to a generator that returns an image as encoded breath. The image comes back not as a painting but as a payload. The code catches it, stamps it onto the shield at the exact coordinate of the click, and blends it into the typographic atlas with mathematical bruises: Multiply, Screen, Hard Edge.


The interface refuses to be polite about what it is doing.


A CRT overlay hums across the surface. A shutter flash blinds the user at capture. A HUD draws reticles and connecting lines. The UI announces its violence in plain speech: TARGET ACQUIRED. CLICK TO STAMP POETRY.


This is not the Holodeck stream. This is the Composite stream: a world that keeps showing you the seams where it is being born. A world that insists the prompt is not a whisper behind the curtain, but a lever in the open, a handle that leaves fingerprints.


We did this because the alternative—every corporate “world model” demo that promises seamlessness as salvation—requires the prompt to disappear.


And that disappearance is not neutral. It is a political aesthetic.


A seamless world makes the user feel powerful while making the system unaccountable. It makes the generated environment feel like nature when it is in fact a collage of culture, labor, extraction, and statistical habit. It invites the oldest lie of technology: it just works.


But it does not “just work.” It drinks. It heats. It extracts.


The server farms have climates. The data centers have water budgets. The GPUs have mineral genealogies: lithium, cobalt, rare earth—names that sound clean until you remember they come from ground opened by force. The model is a weather engine built from stolen light. And every prompt is a new gust through the machinery.


Therefore if we hide the prompt, we hide the accountability structure. We bury the trail. We make the hallucination feel like revelation.


This is why the old comparison to hallucination matters. A hallucination is perception without stimulus. A generative model produces world-pictures without external referent—only internal weight. In Gibson’s old phrase, cyberspace was a consensual hallucination; generative AI is a hallucination factory with a language interface.


But the question is: consensual on whose terms? And with what disclosures?


Here the second shield rises up—Auden’s shield—because Auden understood the overwrite.


Where Homer’s shield sings with agriculture, marriage, argument, and stars, Auden’s shield shows a bleak bureaucratic plane, a cold modern geometry. The world becomes administration. The sacred becomes procedure. The vivid becomes managed.


Auden’s poem is not just a reinterpretation; it is a warning about what happens when a world is generated by a different moral climate.


Operative ekphrasis lets us stage the collision: Homer’s cosmology versus Auden’s bureaucracy, both fed into the same generative mouth. The system produces a synthesis—sometimes lush, sometimes sterile—and the prompter learns the brutal lesson: the model does not “understand” either poem. It negotiates weights. It averages histories. It outputs the compromise our culture has already earned.


So we return to the wall, now taller, now unavoidable.


Because in the move from imagetext to worldtext, the stakes of erasure become total:


In an imagetext, losing the word means you lose interpretive visibility.

In a worldtext, losing the word means you lose governance.


A world you cannot question is a world you cannot contest.
A world you cannot audit is a world you cannot inhabit without surrender.


The prompter—our new fieldworker, our new poet-engineer—must decide what kind of future they are building.


If they choose seamlessness, they will be rewarded. Their demos will travel. Their interfaces will feel “intuitive.” Their worlds will look like destiny. And the prompt, buried, will become a private key held by whoever owns the model.


If they choose visibility, they will be punished. Their work will look “ugly” to those addicted to magic. It will feel “slow” in a culture that confuses frictionlessness with truth. It will refuse the narcotic of immersion long enough to keep the user awake.


And here is the untying—the consequence that ends the story.


Because once you build a Composite world—once you force the word to remain present—you cannot go back to innocence. The user learns to see the seams. The prompter learns that the prompt is not just craft; it is a contract. The interface becomes a confession: this is how the world was made; this is what it cost; this is what was hidden.


The untying is not the separation of word and image. It is the refusal to let one consume the other.


So the final claim is not a thesis. It is a choice offered as a wound:


We can have a future of worldtexts that feel like nature and function like power—smooth, photoreal, unquestionable.


Or we can have a future of worldtexts that keep showing their receipts—noisy with prompts, loud with overlays, honest about the cuts, the blends, the borrowed light.


Therefore champion the Composite stream—not because it is “more artistic,” but because it is more governable. Because a world that admits it is made is a world that can still be remade. Because the moment the prompt disappears, the world stops being a dialogue and becomes a regime.


And somewhere in the dark, under the humming CRT and the stamped-in poetry, the shield keeps turning—carrying not just images, not just myths, but the stubborn insistence that the word remains visible, even when the picture is beautiful enough to make you want to forget it.

{# From Imagetext to Worldtext: Generative AI as Operative Ekphrasis


By Watson Hartsoe & Jay David Bolter


Abstract


Generative AI platforms utilize natural language prompts to create images, videos, and interactive media. The act of prompting can be understood as a new form of ekphrasis—the ancient literary practice of vivid visual description. The crucial difference is that unlike traditional ekphrasis in poetry and prose, the ekphrasis of prompting is, as Hannes Bajohr argues, “operative”: the text not only describes an image but computationally generates it, collapsing the traditional distinction between the verbal and the visual. Prompt and image together constitute an imagetext, which W.J.T. Mitchell suggested was always the unstated and unattainable goal of ekphrasis. Furthermore, a growing community of amateur and professional prompters has developed "promptcraft"—practices for improving resulting media artifacts through elaborate, iterative interactions. We characterize these techniques as “thick prompting,” contrasting them with the one-shot, “thin” prompts of casual users, deliberately recalling Clifford Geertz’s anthropological concept of “thick description.” Thick prompting is an iterative, multimodal process of refinement that describes and defines the context of a desired artifact. Because these prompts draw from and operate through probabilistic world models, they act as fragments of a larger world. As generative systems evolve to create entire immersive 3D environments, the imagetext becomes a worldtext: a probabilistic, visual, and interactive simulation. To provide an emblematic example of operative ekphrasis and the creation of worldtext, we examine Homer’s Shield of Achilles. We demonstrate how thick prompting techniques can produce first the shield as an image, and then as an immersive 3D world. Finally, we juxtapose this classical ekphrasis with W.H. Auden’s mid-twentieth-century reimagining of the shield, using operative ekphrasis as a lens to read Auden’s poem through, and against, Homer’s original generative world-building.



1. Introduction


Generative AI systems are increasingly used to create a diverse array of media forms, including text, images, videos, program code, and interactive environments. For systems focused on visual artifacts—such as those offered by OpenAI, Google, Meta, and Midjourney—the primary interface remains a natural language prompt provided by a human agent. Prompting has become a ubiquitous practice for millions of users, and the art of effective prompting has crystallized into the discipline of "promptcraft." This practice is actively studied (Oppenlaender et al. 2024; Oppenlaender 2024; Liu and Chilton 2023), leading to the development of systems that embody or enhance these emerging techniques (Almeda 2024; Brade et al. 2023).


As recent scholarship has noted (Bajohr 2024; Meyer 2023), this movement from text to image corresponds in an uncanny way to ekphrasis, the traditional literary practice of vivid description. The architecture of image generation requires training probabilistic models on billions of captioned images. By tokenizing both text and images and mapping them into a unified system of weighted matrices, text prompts became the most logical interface for generation. While the computer scientists developing these systems likely did not intend to reinvent a literary practice that predates modern computing by millennia, this structural coincidence invites us to apply literary history and aesthetic theory to one of the most remarkable developments in the history of digital media. Building on Hannes Bajohr’s insights, we propose a theoretical framework for understanding how promptcraft relates to the history of visual representation, moving from the generation of images to the simulation of worlds.


2. Operative Ekphrasis and the Imagetext


For the ancient Greeks, ekphrasis was a rhetorical practice of describing a vivid visual scene. As noted by classical scholars like George Kennedy, rhetoricians in the Greek-speaking Roman empire utilized ekphrasis as both a pedagogical exercise and a foundational element of public artistic performance. The term became intrinsically linked to famous literary passages, beginning with Homer’s description of Achilles’ shield in the Iliad.


Modern interest in ekphrasis as a literary device expanded throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, yielding compelling theoretical analyses from critics such as Murray Krieger (1992), James Heffernan (2004), and W.J.T. Mitchell (1994). While subsequent literature has addressed the impact of digital media on this practice (Brosch 2018b; Lindhé 2013), this foundational work largely predates generative AI.


Hannes Bajohr (2024) recently bridged this gap by identifying AI prompting as a new paradigm, coining the term “operative ekphrasis.” He distinguishes prompting generative models from traditional computer image manipulation; generative models are performative because they embed textual encodings—derived from captions and metadata scraped from the web—directly into their architecture.  The process of training these models collapses the boundary between text and image, a phenomenon that resonates deeply with W.J.T. Mitchell’s essay "Ekphrasis and the Other" (1994). Mitchell argued that merging text and image was both the audacious aspiration and the ultimate nightmare of ekphrasis. Such a merger would confirm the power of verbal description to control the evoked image, while simultaneously threatening to render the word obsolete by dissolving it into the visual. This merging, which Mitchell termed the imagetext, realizes both "ekphrastic hope and ekphrastic fear."


In generative AI, the latent space of the model effectively functions as this imagetext (or videotext). As Lev Manovich suggests, prompting is the act of probing this latent space. Recognizing this, scholars and practitioners increasingly argue that the prompt itself—or the prompt template—functions as art (Chang et al. 2023). This claim confirms the operational reality of the AI imagetext: the prompt cannot be judged purely as traditional ekphrastic literature, but must be evaluated holistically alongside the image it successfully, or unsuccessfully, retrieves from the latent space.


3. Thick Description and the Worldtext


To characterize the contemporary, elaborate practices of promptcraft, we turn to cultural anthropologist Clifford Geertz and his concept of "thick description" (Geertz 1993). Geertz used the term to describe the process of unearthing and explaining the layered, pre-existing cultural codes that motivate human behavior.


We propose "thick prompting" as the generative corollary to thick description. There is, however, an essential directional difference. Thick description analyzes an existing cultural practice; the practice predates the text. Operative ekphrasis reverses this: the act of describing calls the artifact into existence. Yet, both practices seek to engage deep layers of cultural coding. In thick prompting, these codes are the semantic weights absorbed by the model's neural network. Because these models are probabilistic rather than explicitly coded expert systems, interrogating them is an approximate, incomplete, and potentially endless endeavor. There is no final, perfect prompt.


This concept of thick prompting aligns with the emergence of AI "world models," such as Google's Genie and World Labs' Marble. Ha and Schmidhuber (2018) describe world models as generative environments that learn compressed spatiotemporal representations, enabling agents to act within simulated physics and parameters. While their foundational work focused on reinforcement learning rather than literature, it clarifies a shared orientation: these models build an internal space in which possible worlds can be explored.


We propose extending Mitchell’s notion of the imagetext to the worldtext. In generative AI, every imagetext is implicitly a fragment of a worldtext. Operative ekphrasis collapses the boundary between image and text, much like every traditional painting is a fragment of a larger depicted reality. World generators, however, take us from a static image to a fully realized, navigable world model.


Language thus functions as a direct handle on world generation. The worldtext is not a new medium category, but a condition of practice: language becomes the operative interface for producing scenes, objects, and physics at scale. To return to William Gibson's foundational 1984 definition of cyberspace as a "consensual hallucination," generative AI systems are, in a technical sense, constantly hallucinating. The modern psychiatric definition of hallucination—perceiving something in the absence of external stimuli—applies perfectly to a model generating a world picture from pure mathematical weights. In this sense, all operative ekphrasis is a structured, directed hallucination.


4. The Qualities of Thick Prompting


Thick prompting encompasses a heterogeneous set of practices that move far beyond the single-shot text prompt. As prompting develops into a sophisticated community of practice, several key qualities have emerged:


Iterative: While it is possible to produce a compelling image with a short prompt, thick prompting relies on systematic refinement. Prompters often begin with a short seed and repeatedly add constraints to navigate the latent space (He et al. 2024). Techniques like "prompt differential" (changing one variable at a time) and structured taxonomy grids, as seen in systems like Dreamsheets (Almeda et al. 2024) and Promptify (Brade et al. 2023), support this iterative probing.

Multimodal: To probe the latent space effectively, prompts are no longer strictly textual. They are multimodal, utilizing images, video, and audio as inputs. Practitioners engage in "holistic promptcraft," fluidly moving between text and pixel prompting to control lighting and camera angles (Lindley and Whitham 2025), reflecting the intermediality of digital ekphrasis.

Heterogeneous: The syntax of the prompt is highly varied. Natural language, structured data formats (like JSON), and executable code (Python, JavaScript) can all serve as prompts simultaneously (Siddaqui 2026).

Itinerant: Thick prompting frequently migrates across platforms. A core thick description may be adapted from a text-to-image model and ported into a text-to-3D or text-to-video environment. The prompt, acting as a flexible operative logic, travels across media boundaries.

To illustrate the theoretical trajectory from text to imagetext to worldtext, we turn to the most famous ekphrasis in Western literature: Homer’s Shield of Achilles. It resides in the Composite stream precisely because it refuses to hide its own process. Instead of concealing the mechanics of operative ekphrasis, the user interface (UI) and the code architecture actively accentuate them. The interface is designed to make the user hyper-aware of the generative process—making us conscious of the artifact's becoming rather than just its final being.


We achieve this through several deliberate architectural and aesthetic choices within the code:


The Mediated Lens (CRT and Shutter Mechanics): The CSS layers explicitly impose a mediated viewing experience. The continuous crt-overlay animation and the blinding shutter-flash upon image capture constantly remind the viewer that they are not looking at a natural world, but through a computational apparatus.

The Ekphrastic Targeting HUD: The hud-canvas overlay does not hide the prompt extraction; it dramatizes it. When a user hovers over a semantic zone, the JavaScript draws a targeting reticle, casts dynamic connecting lines, and visually fractures the underlying Homeric text into floating arrays of words. The UI explicitly announces TARGET ACQUIRED. CLICK TO STAMP POETRY. The user is forced to visually witness the AI slicing the text to construct its operative prompt.

  </mechanisms>

  <objective>Hand on the reader's back: ease them through the rings of Saturn.</objective>
  <mechanisms>

    <mechanism type="The_Consolation_Release">If the scene involves conflict or "fictional violence," ensure it provides a visceral, non-virtuous release for the "good citizen" reader. No "bar-fight brawling"; provide style and impact.</mechanism>

  <domain type="commercial_thrillers_and_fiction">

</section>

  <instruction>Output the final text. No backstory. Start in the middle. Rhythm forward. No loose ends. Strike the reader fresh.</instruction>
</section>

Abstract

Prompt and image together constitute an imagetext, which W.J.T. Mitchell suggested was always the unstated and unattainable goal of ekphrasis. Furthermore, a growing community of amateur and professional prompters has developed "promptcraft"—practices for improving resulting media artifacts through elaborate, iterative interactions. We characterize these techniques as “thick prompting,” contrasting them with the one-shot, “thin” prompts of casual users, deliberately recalling Clifford Geertz’s anthropological concept of “thick description.” Thick prompting is an iterative, multimodal process of refinement that describes and defines the context of a desired artifact. Because these prompts draw from and operate through probabilistic world models, they act as fragments of a larger world. As generative systems evolve to create entire immersive 3D environments, the imagetext becomes a worldtext: a probabilistic, visual, and interactive simulation. To provide an emblematic example of operative ekphrasis and the creation of worldtext, we examine Homer’s Shield of Achilles. We demonstrate how thick prompting techniques can produce first the shield as an image, and then as an immersive 3D world. Finally, we juxtapose this classical ekphrasis with W.H. Auden’s mid-twentieth-century reimagining of the shield, using operative ekphrasis as a lens to read Auden’s poem through, and against, Homer’s original generative world-building.

Generative AI systems are increasingly used to create a diverse array of media forms, including text, images, videos, program code, and interactive environments. For systems focused on visual artifacts—such as those offered by OpenAI, Google, Meta, and Midjourney—the primary interface remains a natural language prompt provided by a human agent. The architecture of image generation requires training probabilistic models on billions of captioned images. By tokenizing both text and images and mapping them into a unified system of weighted matrices, text prompts became the most logical interface for generation. While the computer scientists developing these systems likely did not intend to reinvent a literary practice that predates modern computing by millennia, this structural coincidence invites us to apply literary history and aesthetic theory to one of the most remarkable developments in the history of digital media. Building on Hannes Bajohr’s insights, we propose a theoretical framework for understanding how promptcraft relates to the history of visual representation, moving from the generation of images to the simulation of worlds.

We lose sight of the prompt. To critically engage with generative AI, we must champion the Composite stream. The room is dark enough that the browser feels like a furnace door: blue-white light, faint scanline shimmer, a cold glow on your hands. A reticle floats over a metal sphere. The cursor grazes engraved text. Target acquired. Click. Flash. The surface changes. A new image burns itself into the shield as if it was always there.


This is the shift. The sentence is no longer a picture in the mind. The sentence is a command in a machine.


Generative AI sells itself as image, video, world. But its actual interface is older and sharper: language. A prompt. A few tokens. A string you can revise, tighten, repeat. You type. The model answers in pixels. You type again. The model answers again. You are not describing. You are steering.


Call this what it is: operative ekphrasis.


Ekphrasis used to be the art of making a scene vivid enough to see. Operative ekphrasis is the art of making a scene executable enough to appear. The old bargain was rhetorical: words aimed at a listener. The new bargain is computational: words aimed at weighted matrices trained on billions of captioned images. The prompt does not merely evoke. The prompt activates.


That activation collapses a boundary we pretended was stable. Text over here. Image over there. Not anymore. Prompt and output arrive fused, each altering the meaning of the other. This is imagetext made literal: the word inside the image, the image inside the word, neither one cleanly separate, neither one innocent.


And because the model is probabilistic, you do not get certainty. You get navigation. You get drift. You get a space of possible results that can be pushed, pulled, cornered, and coaxed. That is why promptcraft emerges fast and hard: people learn what works, keep what works, trade what works, ritualize what works.


Thin prompting is a single throw. Thick prompting is a practice.

It is multimodal: text plus reference images plus sketches plus crops, because the fastest way to steer a model is often to show it what you mean. It is heterogeneous: natural language alongside JSON, alongside code, alongside interface logic that compiles prompts on demand. It is itinerant: prompts migrate across systems, from text-to-image to text-to-video to text-to-3D, carrying their constraints like luggage. It is performative: a loop of action and feedback, not a single act of “generation.”


This is where imagetext tilts into something larger.


As systems expand from still images to immersive environments, the prompt stops being a caption for a picture and becomes a handle on a simulation. The imagetext becomes a worldtext: a navigable, interactive, probabilistic world assembled out of language, model weights, and interface behavior. Not a new genre. A new condition. The condition where the world shows up because you said so.


If you want an emblem for worldtext, take the oldest one that already knew it was a world: Achilles’ shield.


A warrior needs armor. A poet answers by building a cosmos in speech: cities, harvests, dances, trials, war, weather, sea, stars—an entire social physics hammered into metal by language alone. The shield is not decoration. It is a miniature world model. It is a claim: the world can be made out of description.


We take that claim literally.


We run Homer’s shield through a contemporary thick-prompting workflow. First, the shield becomes an image—an imagetext born from operative description. Then the shield becomes an environment—an interactive 3D world that can be navigated, sampled, and revised. Then we force a collision: Homer’s generative abundance against Auden’s bleak rewrite, the bright world against the bureaucratic one. Same object. Two textual engines. Two worlds fighting for the same surface.


To make this more than metaphor, we document the machinery. Not the vibes. The steps.


Our ACHILLES // OPTICAL_GRID_v7 artifact hardcodes thickness into the interface itself. The user does not type a long prompt and hope. The system compiles hundreds of small prompts through action.


A zone is selected. A snippet is extracted. A rigid wrapper is applied: engrave this concept into ancient metal. A style constraint is injected. The prompt is sent. The image returns. The image is stamped back onto the shield at the exact coordinate that triggered it. Blend modes are exposed. Feathered gradients are visible. Exports rip the illusion open, flattening the sphere into raw UV maps so you can see the distortion that holds the world together.


Click. Flash. Stamp.


This choice to expose the machinery is not cosmetic. It divides the future of generative media into two streams.


One stream wants disappearance. Seamless photoreal worlds. Holodeck logic. The prompt becomes subterranean, buried under “natural” simulation. The other stream refuses that comfort. Composite worlds. Accentuated interfaces. Visible prompts. Visible compositing. Visible negotiation between human language and machine weights. The system does not pretend to be nature. It insists on being artifact.


This is not an aesthetic footnote. It is a governance problem.


When the prompt disappears, the world becomes standing reserve: ready-at-hand reality generated on demand, while the terms of selection—the biases, the defaults, the hidden exclusions—sink out of view. When the prompt stays visible, the user stays implicated. The world does not just appear. The world is made. And what is made can be questioned.


That is the thesis that drives this paper forward: generative AI is not simply a new tool for images. It is a new operational form of ekphrasis where language becomes the control surface for world-building. Imagetext is not an endpoint; it is a threshold. Worldtext is what comes next. The only question is whether we enter that next phase with the machinery hidden or exposed.


We offer a vocabulary—operative ekphrasis, imagetext, worldtext, thick prompting—and we offer an example that can be inspected, reproduced, and argued with. Homer gives us the emblem. Auden gives us the fracture. The interface gives us the proof: language does not just represent worlds anymore. Language makes them.


And once language makes worlds, you do not get to act surprised when the world obeys whoever holds the words.

{# From Imagetext to Worldtext: Generative AI as Operative Ekphrasis


By Watson Hartsoe & Jay David Bolter


Abstract


Generative AI platforms utilize natural language prompts to create images, videos, and interactive media. The act of prompting can be understood as a new form of ekphrasis—the ancient literary practice of vivid visual description. The crucial difference is that unlike traditional ekphrasis in poetry and prose, the ekphrasis of prompting is, as Hannes Bajohr argues, “operative”: the text not only describes an image but computationally generates it, collapsing the traditional distinction between the verbal and the visual. Prompt and image together constitute an imagetext, which W.J.T. Mitchell suggested was always the unstated and unattainable goal of ekphrasis. Furthermore, a growing community of amateur and professional prompters has developed "promptcraft"—practices for improving resulting media artifacts through elaborate, iterative interactions. We characterize these techniques as “thick prompting,” contrasting them with the one-shot, “thin” prompts of casual users, deliberately recalling Clifford Geertz’s anthropological concept of “thick description.” Thick prompting is an iterative, multimodal process of refinement that describes and defines the context of a desired artifact. Because these prompts draw from and operate through probabilistic world models, they act as fragments of a larger world. As generative systems evolve to create entire immersive 3D environments, the imagetext becomes a worldtext: a probabilistic, visual, and interactive simulation. To provide an emblematic example of operative ekphrasis and the creation of worldtext, we examine Homer’s Shield of Achilles. We demonstrate how thick prompting techniques can produce first the shield as an image, and then as an immersive 3D world. Finally, we juxtapose this classical ekphrasis with W.H. Auden’s mid-twentieth-century reimagining of the shield, using operative ekphrasis as a lens to read Auden’s poem through, and against, Homer’s original generative world-building.

Generative AI systems are increasingly used to create a diverse array of media forms, including text, images, videos, program code, and interactive environments. For systems focused on visual artifacts—such as those offered by OpenAI, Google, Meta, and Midjourney—the primary interface remains a natural language prompt provided by a human agent. Prompting has become a ubiquitous practice for millions of users, and the art of effective prompting has crystallized into the discipline of "promptcraft." This practice is actively studied (Oppenlaender et al. 2024; Oppenlaender 2024; Liu and Chilton 2023), leading to the development of systems that embody or enhance these emerging techniques (Almeda 2024; Brade et al. 2023).


As recent scholarship has noted (Bajohr 2024; Meyer 2023), this movement from text to image corresponds in an uncanny way to ekphrasis, the traditional literary practice of vivid description. The architecture of image generation requires training probabilistic models on billions of captioned images. By tokenizing both text and images and mapping them into a unified system of weighted matrices, text prompts became the most logical interface for generation. While the computer scientists developing these systems likely did not intend to reinvent a literary practice that predates modern computing by millennia, this structural coincidence invites us to apply literary history and aesthetic theory to one of the most remarkable developments in the history of digital media. Building on Hannes Bajohr’s insights, we propose a theoretical framework for understanding how promptcraft relates to the history of visual representation, moving from the generation of images to the simulation of worlds.

For the ancient Greeks, ekphrasis was a rhetorical practice of describing a vivid visual scene. As noted by classical scholars like George Kennedy, rhetoricians in the Greek-speaking Roman empire utilized ekphrasis as both a pedagogical exercise and a foundational element of public artistic performance. The term became intrinsically linked to famous literary passages, beginning with Homer’s description of Achilles’ shield in the Iliad.


Modern interest in ekphrasis as a literary device expanded throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, yielding compelling theoretical analyses from critics such as Murray Krieger (1992), James Heffernan (2004), and W.J.T. Mitchell (1994). While subsequent literature has addressed the impact of digital media on this practice (Brosch 2018b; Lindhé 2013), this foundational work largely predates generative AI.


Hannes Bajohr (2024) recently bridged this gap by identifying AI prompting as a new paradigm, coining the term “operative ekphrasis.” He distinguishes prompting generative models from traditional computer image manipulation; generative models are performative because they embed textual encodings—derived from captions and metadata scraped from the web—directly into their architecture.  The process of training these models collapses the boundary between text and image, a phenomenon that resonates deeply with W.J.T. Mitchell’s essay "Ekphrasis and the Other" (1994). Mitchell argued that merging text and image was both the audacious aspiration and the ultimate nightmare of ekphrasis. Such a merger would confirm the power of verbal description to control the evoked image, while simultaneously threatening to render the word obsolete by dissolving it into the visual. This merging, which Mitchell termed the imagetext, realizes both "ekphrastic hope and ekphrastic fear."


In generative AI, the latent space of the model effectively functions as this imagetext (or videotext). As Lev Manovich suggests, prompting is the act of probing this latent space. Recognizing this, scholars and practitioners increasingly argue that the prompt itself—or the prompt template—functions as art (Chang et al. 2023). This claim confirms the operational reality of the AI imagetext: the prompt cannot be judged purely as traditional ekphrastic literature, but must be evaluated holistically alongside the image it successfully, or unsuccessfully, retrieves from the latent space.

Geertz used the term to describe the process of unearthing and explaining the layered, pre-existing cultural codes that motivate human behavior.
