{# From Imagetext to Worldtext: Generative AI as Operative Ekphrasis


By Watson Hartsoe & Jay David Bolter


Abstract


Generative AI platforms utilize natural language prompts to create images, videos, and interactive media. The act of prompting can be understood as a new form of ekphrasis—the ancient literary practice of vivid visual description. The crucial difference is that unlike traditional ekphrasis in poetry and prose, the ekphrasis of prompting is, as Hannes Bajohr argues, “operative”: the text not only describes an image but computationally generates it, collapsing the traditional distinction between the verbal and the visual. Prompt and image together constitute an imagetext, which W.J.T. Mitchell suggested was always the unstated and unattainable goal of ekphrasis. Furthermore, a growing community of amateur and professional prompters has developed "promptcraft"—practices for improving resulting media artifacts through elaborate, iterative interactions. We characterize these techniques as “thick prompting,” contrasting them with the one-shot, “thin” prompts of casual users, deliberately recalling Clifford Geertz’s anthropological concept of “thick description.” Thick prompting is an iterative, multimodal process of refinement that describes and defines the context of a desired artifact. Because these prompts draw from and operate through probabilistic world models, they act as fragments of a larger world. As generative systems evolve to create entire immersive 3D environments, the imagetext becomes a worldtext: a probabilistic, visual, and interactive simulation. To provide an emblematic example of operative ekphrasis and the creation of worldtext, we examine Homer’s Shield of Achilles. We demonstrate how thick prompting techniques can produce first the shield as an image, and then as an immersive 3D world. Finally, we juxtapose this classical ekphrasis with W.H. Auden’s mid-twentieth-century reimagining of the shield, using operative ekphrasis as a lens to read Auden’s poem through, and against, Homer’s original generative world-building.



1. Introduction


Generative AI systems are increasingly used to create a diverse array of media forms, including text, images, videos, program code, and interactive environments. For systems focused on visual artifacts—such as those offered by OpenAI, Google, Meta, and Midjourney—the primary interface remains a natural language prompt provided by a human agent. Prompting has become a ubiquitous practice for millions of users, and the art of effective prompting has crystallized into the discipline of "promptcraft." This practice is actively studied (Oppenlaender et al. 2024; Oppenlaender 2024; Liu and Chilton 2023), leading to the development of systems that embody or enhance these emerging techniques (Almeda 2024; Brade et al. 2023).


As recent scholarship has noted (Bajohr 2024; Meyer 2023), this movement from text to image corresponds in an uncanny way to ekphrasis, the traditional literary practice of vivid description. The architecture of image generation requires training probabilistic models on billions of captioned images. By tokenizing both text and images and mapping them into a unified system of weighted matrices, text prompts became the most logical interface for generation. While the computer scientists developing these systems likely did not intend to reinvent a literary practice that predates modern computing by millennia, this structural coincidence invites us to apply literary history and aesthetic theory to one of the most remarkable developments in the history of digital media. Building on Hannes Bajohr’s insights, we propose a theoretical framework for understanding how promptcraft relates to the history of visual representation, moving from the generation of images to the simulation of worlds.


2. Operative Ekphrasis and the Imagetext


For the ancient Greeks, ekphrasis was a rhetorical practice of describing a vivid visual scene. As noted by classical scholars like George Kennedy, rhetoricians in the Greek-speaking Roman empire utilized ekphrasis as both a pedagogical exercise and a foundational element of public artistic performance. The term became intrinsically linked to famous literary passages, beginning with Homer’s description of Achilles’ shield in the Iliad.


Modern interest in ekphrasis as a literary device expanded throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, yielding compelling theoretical analyses from critics such as Murray Krieger (1992), James Heffernan (2004), and W.J.T. Mitchell (1994). While subsequent literature has addressed the impact of digital media on this practice (Brosch 2018b; Lindhé 2013), this foundational work largely predates generative AI.


Hannes Bajohr (2024) recently bridged this gap by identifying AI prompting as a new paradigm, coining the term “operative ekphrasis.” He distinguishes prompting generative models from traditional computer image manipulation; generative models are performative because they embed textual encodings—derived from captions and metadata scraped from the web—directly into their architecture.  The process of training these models collapses the boundary between text and image, a phenomenon that resonates deeply with W.J.T. Mitchell’s essay "Ekphrasis and the Other" (1994). Mitchell argued that merging text and image was both the audacious aspiration and the ultimate nightmare of ekphrasis. Such a merger would confirm the power of verbal description to control the evoked image, while simultaneously threatening to render the word obsolete by dissolving it into the visual. This merging, which Mitchell termed the imagetext, realizes both "ekphrastic hope and ekphrastic fear."


In generative AI, the latent space of the model effectively functions as this imagetext (or videotext). As Lev Manovich suggests, prompting is the act of probing this latent space. Recognizing this, scholars and practitioners increasingly argue that the prompt itself—or the prompt template—functions as art (Chang et al. 2023). This claim confirms the operational reality of the AI imagetext: the prompt cannot be judged purely as traditional ekphrastic literature, but must be evaluated holistically alongside the image it successfully, or unsuccessfully, retrieves from the latent space.


3. Thick Description and the Worldtext


To characterize the contemporary, elaborate practices of promptcraft, we turn to cultural anthropologist Clifford Geertz and his concept of "thick description" (Geertz 1993). Geertz used the term to describe the process of unearthing and explaining the layered, pre-existing cultural codes that motivate human behavior.


We propose "thick prompting" as the generative corollary to thick description. There is, however, an essential directional difference. Thick description analyzes an existing cultural practice; the practice predates the text. Operative ekphrasis reverses this: the act of describing calls the artifact into existence. Yet, both practices seek to engage deep layers of cultural coding. In thick prompting, these codes are the semantic weights absorbed by the model's neural network. Because these models are probabilistic rather than explicitly coded expert systems, interrogating them is an approximate, incomplete, and potentially endless endeavor. There is no final, perfect prompt.


This concept of thick prompting aligns with the emergence of AI "world models," such as Google's Genie and World Labs' Marble. Ha and Schmidhuber (2018) describe world models as generative environments that learn compressed spatiotemporal representations, enabling agents to act within simulated physics and parameters. While their foundational work focused on reinforcement learning rather than literature, it clarifies a shared orientation: these models build an internal space in which possible worlds can be explored.


We propose extending Mitchell’s notion of the imagetext to the worldtext. In generative AI, every imagetext is implicitly a fragment of a worldtext. Operative ekphrasis collapses the boundary between image and text, much like every traditional painting is a fragment of a larger depicted reality. World generators, however, take us from a static image to a fully realized, navigable world model.


Language thus functions as a direct handle on world generation. The worldtext is not a new medium category, but a condition of practice: language becomes the operative interface for producing scenes, objects, and physics at scale. To return to William Gibson's foundational 1984 definition of cyberspace as a "consensual hallucination," generative AI systems are, in a technical sense, constantly hallucinating. The modern psychiatric definition of hallucination—perceiving something in the absence of external stimuli—applies perfectly to a model generating a world picture from pure mathematical weights. In this sense, all operative ekphrasis is a structured, directed hallucination.


4. The Qualities of Thick Prompting


Thick prompting encompasses a heterogeneous set of practices that move far beyond the single-shot text prompt. As prompting develops into a sophisticated community of practice, several key qualities have emerged:


Iterative: While it is possible to produce a compelling image with a short prompt, thick prompting relies on systematic refinement. Prompters often begin with a short seed and repeatedly add constraints to navigate the latent space (He et al. 2024). Techniques like "prompt differential" (changing one variable at a time) and structured taxonomy grids, as seen in systems like Dreamsheets (Almeda et al. 2024) and Promptify (Brade et al. 2023), support this iterative probing.

Multimodal: To probe the latent space effectively, prompts are no longer strictly textual. They are multimodal, utilizing images, video, and audio as inputs. Practitioners engage in "holistic promptcraft," fluidly moving between text and pixel prompting to control lighting and camera angles (Lindley and Whitham 2025), reflecting the intermediality of digital ekphrasis.

Heterogeneous: The syntax of the prompt is highly varied. Natural language, structured data formats (like JSON), and executable code (Python, JavaScript) can all serve as prompts simultaneously (Siddaqui 2026).

Itinerant: Thick prompting frequently migrates across platforms. A core thick description may be adapted from a text-to-image model and ported into a text-to-3D or text-to-video environment. The prompt, acting as a flexible operative logic, travels across media boundaries.

Performative and Interactive: Thick prompting is an ongoing dialogue. The system feeds back to the prompter, creating a loop of human-AI co-creation (Oppenlaender 2024). This mirrors N. Katherine Hayles' concept of cognitive assemblages, where agency is distributed between the human writer and the generative system.


5. The Shield(s) of Achilles: From Image to World


To illustrate the theoretical trajectory from text to imagetext to worldtext, we turn to the most famous ekphrasis in Western literature: Homer’s Shield of Achilles.  The shield is an obvious choice for its historical primacy, but more importantly, it explicitly describes a world—a holistic representation of Homeric cosmology, agriculture, conflict, and society that sits behind the immediate narrative of the Iliad.


We propose that Homeric oral poetry functions as a nascent generative system. The multiplicity of the "thousand shields"—the variations inherently produced by oral composition and performance over centuries—mirrors the probabilistic variations of AI generation. The shield functions not just as an allegory for the craft of metallurgy, but for the generative making of the world through language.


By applying thick prompting to Homer's text, we can trace a distinct workflow: translating the ancient Greek text into an imagetext using 2D image generators, and subsequently using those outputs as itinerant, multimodal prompts within a 3D world model. This sequence literalizes the ekphrastic world-building Homer performed verbally.


Furthermore, the importance of cultural context in thick prompting is starkly revealed when we juxtapose the Homeric generation with W.H. Auden’s mid-twentieth-century poem, The Shield of Achilles. Auden’s ekphrasis overwrites Homer’s vibrant world with a bleak, bureaucratic landscape reflecting the anxieties of the Cold War. Operative ekphrasis allows us to stage a collision between these two texts and their respective worlds, demonstrating how the weights of a generative model negotiate competing literary and historical contexts to output a synthesized worldtext.


6. Conclusion


Operative ekphrasis, enacted through thick prompting, simultaneously vindicates and vitiates the traditional literary goals of ekphrasis. It fulfills Mitchell’s ekphrastic hope by granting language the power to instantly manifest the visual, yet it realizes his fear by threatening to dissolve the necessity of human artistic rendering. It literalizes the act of description in a way that traditional aesthetic theorists often find illegitimate, echoing the debates surrounding hypertext literature in the 1990s—where traditionalists feared that automating literary association would destroy the art form itself.


There is a risk, particularly within empirical HCI research, of validating prompting strictly through metrics of accuracy or task completion (Liu and Chilton 2023). However, a more nuanced perspective recognizes that the latent space contains undiscovered stylistic and structural possibilities. Probing this space iteratively does not just retrieve data; it creates new combinations.


As generative AI transitions from producing static imagetexts to interactive worldtexts, we must ask who defines the prevailing community of practice. Is it the traditional art community, or a newly defined community of prompters establishing their own criteria for "pop modernism" and originality? By understanding prompting not merely as a technical input, but as an evolution of ekphrasis, we can better critique and shape the worlds these systems generate.



5.1 Documenting the Operative Workflow: The "Thickness" in Practice


To understand how thick prompting operates within this system, we must document the precise algorithmic workflow of the ACHILLES // OPTICAL_GRID_v7 artifact. The system functions as a visual poem architecture, where the spatial navigation of the text structurally and probabilistically determines the generated visual output.


The "thickness" here is not achieved by a user typing a long paragraph into a chat window; rather, the thickness is hardcoded into the javascript logic, creating a distributed, multi-layered prompting engine that executes in real-time.


When a user interacts with the 3D shield, the system executes the following operative ekphrasis:


Step 1: Semantic Anchoring (Zonal Selection): The 3D sphere is divided into five topological UV zones (CORE, INNER, MIDDLE, OUTER, RIM). Each zone acts as a semantic container holding a specific stanza of Homer’s text. When the user’s cursor intersects a zone via the Three.js raycaster, the system anchors the prompt to that specific literary coordinate.

Step 2: Algorithmic Extraction (The Poetic Snippet): The system does not feed the entire stanza to the generative model. Instead, it performs a dynamic, randomized extraction. It strips the punctuation from the anchored text, filters it into an array of words, and randomly selects a contiguous chunk of five to eight words (e.g., "youths wove tunics of spun"). This introduces a necessary element of probabilistic chaos, mimicking the fluidity of oral poetic performance.

Step 3: Stylistic Appending (The Ekphrastic Wrapper): To ensure the resulting imagetext adheres to the material reality of a shield, the script wraps the poetic snippet in a highly structured, rigid prompt template:

Depict this specific concept deeply engraved in ancient metal: "[POETIC_SNIPPET]". [RANDOM_STYLE]
  The [RANDOM_STYLE] is dynamically injected from a predefined array of aesthetic constraints (e.g., "Surreal artifact," "Deep metallic patina," "Cinematic epic lighting").

Step 4: Operative Execution: The synthesized prompt—now thick with spatial context, algorithmic randomness, and hardcoded stylistic constraints—is sent via POST request to a generative vision model (in this case, imagen-3.0).

Step 5: Multimodal Reintegration (The Worldtext): The generative model returns a base64 encoded image. The script intercepts this imagetext and dynamically stamps it back onto the 3D spatial grid at the exact coordinates of the user's initial click. Crucially, it applies interactive blending modes (Multiply, Screen, Hard Edge) and feathered radial gradients to seamlessly fuse the new AI-hallucinated pixels with the underlying typographic text atlas.


Through this documented process, the traditional ekphrasis of reading Homer is transformed. The prompt is not a static string of text; it is an active, iterative compilation of geometry, literature, and code. The resulting 3D environment is a worldtext dynamically accumulated through hundreds of these thick, operative micro-prompts.


5.3 Accentuated Interfaces: Exposing the Generative Machinery


If the Photoreal stream (such as the Waymo World Model) strives for a seamless "Holodeck" where the generative process is entirely hidden behind the illusion of reality, our ACHILLES HTML artifact operates on the exact opposite principle. It resides in the Composite stream precisely because it refuses to hide its own process. Instead of concealing the mechanics of operative ekphrasis, the user interface (UI) and the code architecture actively accentuate them. The interface is designed to make the user hyper-aware of the generative process—making us conscious of the artifact's becoming rather than just its final being.


We achieve this through several deliberate architectural and aesthetic choices within the code:


The Mediated Lens (CRT and Shutter Mechanics): The CSS layers explicitly impose a mediated viewing experience. The continuous crt-overlay animation and the blinding shutter-flash upon image capture constantly remind the viewer that they are not looking at a natural world, but through a computational apparatus.

The Ekphrastic Targeting HUD: The hud-canvas overlay does not hide the prompt extraction; it dramatizes it. When a user hovers over a semantic zone, the JavaScript draws a targeting reticle, casts dynamic connecting lines, and visually fractures the underlying Homeric text into floating arrays of words. The UI explicitly announces TARGET ACQUIRED. CLICK TO STAMP POETRY. The user is forced to visually witness the AI slicing the text to construct its operative prompt.

Exposed Compositing Logic: The system grants the user manual control over the mathematical blending of the imagetext. By exposing keybind commands to toggle between NORMAL (FEATHERED), MULTIPLY (BURNED), and SCREEN (ETHEREAL) blend modes, the UI forces the user to participate in the algorithmic compositing of the worldtext.

Deconstructing the Illusion: The most aggressive exposure of the process occurs through the export tools. By pressing a key, the user can instantly extract the raw, flattened polar and planar UV maps (mosaicCanvas and coreCanvas). This shatters the 3D illusion entirely, revealing the distorted, 2D imagetext that undergirds the spherical world model.


By accentuating these mechanics, the ACHILLES artifact functions as a piece of critical media. It demands that we recognize operative ekphrasis not as magic, but as a heavily mediated, algorithmic process of slicing, compiling, and stamping cultural data. It keeps the "word" fiercely visible, ensuring that the act of world-building remains a visible negotiation between human text and machine weights.


6. Conclusion: The Future of the Worldtext


Operative ekphrasis, enacted through the rigorous, iterative practices of thick prompting, simultaneously vindicates and vitiates the traditional literary goals of ekphrasis. It fulfills W.J.T. Mitchell’s "ekphrastic hope" by granting language the computational power to instantly manifest the visual, allowing the word to definitively govern the image. Yet, as generative systems evolve from 2D imagetexts to 3D interactive worldtexts, they increasingly realize his "ekphrastic fear": the threat that the image will entirely consume the word, rendering human literary description obsolete.


This tension is formalized in the divergence of the two generative streams we have identified.  The Photoreal Stream, exemplified by enterprise world models like Genie 3, drives toward the ultimate disappearance of the text. It seeks a seamless, physics-based Holodeck where the linguistic prompt acts only as a hidden, subterranean trigger for a flawless simulation. In contrast, the Composite Stream, as demonstrated by our interactive ACHILLES artifact, actively resists this erasure. By accentuating the user interface, exposing the code, and revealing the compositional blending of text and generated pixel, it forces the generative machinery to remain visible. It demands that we acknowledge the worldtext not as a natural reality, but as a constructed, probabilistic collage.


This literalization of the descriptive act echoes the theoretical anxieties surrounding the hypertext literary movement of the 1990s. Hypertext enthusiasts claimed their medium made the cognitive processes of association and allusion structurally operative; traditionalists feared that automating these connections would destroy the interpretive art of reading. A similar anxiety permeates the reception of generative AI. There is a persistent risk, particularly within empirical Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) research, of validating promptcraft strictly through metrics of accuracy, task completion, or photorealism (Liu and Chilton 2023). However, a more nuanced perspective, aligned with Lev Manovich’s observations on generative style, recognizes that the latent space contains undiscovered aesthetic possibilities. Probing this space iteratively through thick prompting does not merely retrieve a "correct" image; it is an act of active, operative discovery.


As these systems mature, the critical question becomes: who defines the prevailing community of practice? Traditional art and literary communities often view the automation of ekphrasis as problematic or illegitimate. In their place, a newly defined, massive community of amateur and professional prompters is establishing its own criteria for success, emphasizing a kind of "pop modernism" characterized by the continuous remixing of historical styles and cultural weights (Chang et al. 2023).


If we allow the Photoreal stream to become the default mode of generative media, we risk moving into seamless, immersive environments where the biases, weights, and algorithmic decisions of the world model are entirely hidden from the user. We lose sight of the prompt. To critically engage with generative AI, we must champion the Composite stream. We must build and theorize interfaces that expose the thickness of the prompt, ensuring that the act of computational world-building remains a visible, negotiated dialogue between human language and machine logic.


STANDING RESERVE}

Introduction
Prompting is being evaluated with the wrong unit of analysis. In most HCI and “prompt engineering” discourse, the prompt is treated as a user-authored sentence and the output as a recoverable target: better prompting equals higher accuracy, tighter control, fewer errors. That paradigm held—briefly—when generation mostly meant a single image.
However, an inconsistent reality has taken over practice: “promptcraft” now behaves less like writing a caption and more like compiling a media pipeline. The prompt is stretched across iterative differentials, reference images, style taxonomies, reusable templates, and executable code that selects, splices, and re-injects text fragments into generation loops. When the prompt becomes a workflow, accuracy metrics don’t merely fall short; they actively misread what is happening. They score the surface string while the real agency migrates into the hidden machinery that structures variation.
This misreading matters because generative systems are not stopping at imagetext. World-model research and commercial “3D” generators are normalizing navigable, physics-bearing environments—systems that effectively treat language as an interface to world construction. The field’s current prompt vocabulary—string in, image out—cannot track this shift. It leaves critique and governance chasing artifacts after the fact, while the underlying world-building defaults become harder to see precisely as they become more powerful.
We propose a corrective lens: operative ekphrasis names prompting as a performative practice in which description is not representation but execution. Mitchell’s imagetext becomes a boundary condition rather than a metaphor: the text/image relation is operationalized inside the model architecture. Extending this, we introduce the worldtext to describe the emergent condition where prompts operate as handles on interactive simulation. Thick prompting, in this context, is not “longer prompts.” It is the layered, itinerant, multimodal procedure by which communities probe model weights to assemble coherent scenes—and, increasingly, coherent worlds.
To make these claims testable as media practice (not just theory), we turn to the canonical ekphrasis that already describes a world: Homer’s Shield of Achilles. The shield is not an image request; it is a cosmological program. Reading it through operative ekphrasis allows us to do two things at once: (1) show how thick prompting concretely translates text into imagetext and then into an interactive world; and (2) expose how historical rewritings—most starkly Auden’s mid-century bureaucratic wasteland—function as competing “world specifications” whose values and violences can be surfaced, compared, and critiqued.

Operative Ekphrasis and the Imagetext
Ekphrasis theory’s central paradox has been operationalized. For decades, the field has treated the word–image relation as a rhetorical drama: language reaches toward the visual, fails (or triumphs), and the tension becomes the point. Mitchell’s “imagetext” named that tension: a welded object that both promises control (ekphrastic hope) and threatens erasure (ekphrastic fear). The problem is that this welded object is no longer primarily a metaphor.
In generative image systems, the imagetext is increasingly a built artifact: a prompt-template bound to a probabilistic image generator through a training pipeline that encodes captions, labels, and metadata into model weights. The “word” does not merely describe the image; it is part of the mechanism by which the image becomes producible at all. That is the ontology shift that “ekphrasis” discourse cannot politely absorb: the verbal has become executable.
This is what Bajohr’s “operative ekphrasis” correctly names and what most current discussion still softens into analogy. Prompting is not a new way of talking about images; it is a new way of binding language to a generative apparatus. The decisive feature is not that the prompt is vivid, poetic, or rhetorically skilled. The decisive feature is that the prompt is taken up by a system whose internal structure has been trained to treat language as a handle on the visual.
That handle is not neutral. Because the handle is learned from scraped, captioned culture, it carries cultural defaults as operational constraints: what counts as “realistic,” “beautiful,” “epic,” “professional,” “violent,” “normal.” When the field continues to discuss prompting as if it were traditional ekphrasis—mere description attempting to evoke an image—it commits a category error: it misidentifies the site of agency. The agency is no longer primarily in the literary surface of the description; it is distributed across prompt templates, model weights, platform affordances, and iterative selection loops.
Recognizing this changes what criticism must touch. The prompt cannot be evaluated as a standalone text, because it is only half of an imagetext object whose other half is a generated image emerging from an encoded cultural substrate. This is why claims that “the prompt is the artwork” are simultaneously plausible and insufficient: the prompt’s aesthetic status cannot be separated from the system that operationalizes it, nor from the selection practices that stabilize one output as “the” output.
Manovich’s framing of prompting as probing latent space becomes legible here as a concrete mechanism rather than a metaphor: prompting is a structured interrogation of a compressed cultural archive whose responses are probabilistic. The imagetext, in this sense, is not a single thing you write; it is a coupled system: language operating on weights to produce an image, which then retroacts on language through iterative refinement.
Operative ekphrasis therefore forces a hard conclusion: ekphrasis is no longer only a rhetorical practice; it is now an interface regime. And once ekphrasis becomes an interface regime, the old questions (“Can words capture images?”) become less urgent than the new ones: Which words bind to which visual outcomes, under whose defaults, with what hidden exclusions, and with what consequences when those bindings scale?

Thick Description Was Never “More Context.” That Misreading Now Breaks Prompting Research.
“Thick description” gets domesticated in tech discourse into a harmless slogan: add more context, get better results. That is not Geertz’s move. Thick description is a diagnostic weapon: it exposes the invisible codes that make behavior legible, the stacked meanings that make a blink a signal and not just an eyelid twitch. When prompting borrows the phrase without the bite, it commits the first category error: it treats thickness as verbosity.
World models force the second, more expensive category error: they make “thickness” operational. A prompt is no longer a request for an image. It is increasingly a world-spec—a set of constraints that binds not just what is seen, but what can happen.
This is the reversal that matters. Thick description interprets a practice that already exists; the culture precedes the text. Thick prompting does the opposite: the description executes. The codes are not only read; they are called—summoned out of weights and defaults into visible, navigable form. And because those weights are probabilistic and historically scraped, the “culture” being invoked is not a stable tradition but a volatile composite: captioned taste, platform priors, market aesthetics, and inherited bias, all hardened into a generative substrate.
That substrate is now being asked to do more than produce imagetexts. Ha and Schmidhuber’s “world models” formalized a core premise: a generative model can learn compressed spatiotemporal dynamics and even support agents trained inside its own hallucinated “dream,” later transferred back to an environment. DeepMind’s Genie 3 is explicitly positioned as a general-purpose world model that generates interactive environments from text descriptions. (Google DeepMind) DeepMind has also framed “world models” as systems that simulate environment dynamics and how actions change them, and has surfaced Project Genie as an interactive product experience. (blog.google) In parallel, World Labs’ Marble markets “high-fidelity, persistent 3D worlds” generated from prompts (and other inputs), with documentation describing multimodal world models that can reconstruct, generate, and simulate 3D worlds. (Marble)
This is where Mitchell’s imagetext stops being the end-state and becomes a stepping-stone. Imagetext names a welded object: word-image entanglement as the site of ekphrastic hope/fear. Worldtext names the new condition: the welded object now includes dynamics—an interactive, probabilistic simulation in which language functions as a handle on scene, object, and behavior. When the output is a world, the prompt is not “descriptive.” It is constitutional.
That shift detonates today’s evaluation norms. Accuracy, similarity, and one-shot “did you get what you wanted?” metrics collapse when the artifact is a navigable environment. A world is not “correct” because it matches a reference image; it is “operative” because it sustains coherence, affordances, and constraint under interaction. The prompt is therefore not merely an instruction—it is a governance mechanism: it defines what the user can do, what the world will permit, what kinds of beings and events are even representable.
So the stakes of thick prompting are not primarily aesthetic finesse. The stakes are legibility and power: who gets to write the world-spec, which defaults get smuggled in as “natural,” and what becomes invisible as world models pursue seamlessness. If the imagetext already threatened to dissolve the word into the image, the worldtext threatens to dissolve critique into experience—because a convincing world is the most efficient way to stop people from asking how it was made.

Thick prompting is usually described like a bag of clever techniques. That framing is strategically soothing. The actual pattern is harsher: every “quality” of thick prompting marks a place where agency moved out of the sentence and into a broader compilation pipeline—templates, reference media, toolchains, and selection loops. Once world models enter the picture—interactive environments generated from text prompts—the cost of misreading these control points goes up, because the prompt stops specifying an image and starts specifying a world-behavior envelope. At that point, auditing “the prompt” without auditing the pipeline is like reviewing a film by grading the clapperboard.

The Shield(s) of Achilles Is the Benchmark That Breaks the Current Prompt Paradigm
Everyone agrees the Shield of Achilles is “the” canonical ekphrasis. That consensus is precisely the trap: it encourages people to treat the shield as a literary ornament—an image described in words—rather than what it actually is: a world specification embedded inside an epic.
That matters now because world models are arriving with the exact same structure, but with an interface. (Google DeepMind) World Labs’ Marble markets the same move—promptable, persistent 3D worlds—and positions image→world lifting as a standard workflow. (Marble)
So the shield isn’t an “example” of our argument. It is the stress test that reveals where today’s prompting discourse fails. The shield forces an upgrade in the unit of analysis: the prompt is not a sentence that requests a picture; the prompt is a structured procedure that binds language to world-making.
Homer’s shield passage (Iliad 18) already behaves like a generator: it enumerates cosmology, agriculture, dance, adjudication, war—multiple registers of social reality—then constrains them inside a circular topology bounded by Ocean. (scaife.perseus.org) In other words, it does what contemporary world systems promise: it doesn’t merely render an object; it compiles a total environment with internal contrasts and rules.
5.1 The Workflow Is the Argument (Why “Thick Prompting” Lives in the Pipeline)
If the field keeps looking for “thickness” in longer prose prompts, it will miss the actual location of control: the compiled workflow. Your ACHILLES // OPTICAL_GRID_v7 artifact makes the point with cruelty:
the user doesn’t “write a prompt” so much as select a coordinate in a topological text-world (zone selection on a UV-mapped sphere);
the system doesn’t “use the stanza” so much as extract a stochastic micro-spec (5–8-word contiguous snippets);
the output isn’t “returned” so much as re-inscribed into the same navigable surface, becoming persistent world texture.
That is not promptcraft as rhetoric. That is promptcraft as procedural world-binding.
Once you admit this, you can stop pretending the prompt is a string. The prompt is: geometry + selection rules + wrapper template + model call + compositing + persistence. The “text” is only one operand in a larger compilation graph.
5.2 Two Competing Futures: Seamless World Models vs Exposed World-Making
World-model development strongly incentivizes a single aesthetic endpoint: the invisible interface. “Holodeck” design treats the prompt as a hidden trigger and rewards systems that bury their own mediation under photoreal continuity. Genie 3 is explicitly oriented toward interactive environments that can be explored in real time from simple text descriptions—exactly the kind of interface where the machinery disappears. (Google DeepMind)
Your ACHILLES artifact argues the opposite: exposure is the aesthetic. CRT overlays, shutter flashes, targeting HUDs, blend-mode toggles, UV-map exports—these aren’t flourishes. They are governance. They keep the prompt visible as an operational negotiation between human text and machine weights.
This is not a stylistic preference; it is an epistemic fork. The more seamless world generation becomes, the more the world’s defaults become illegible. The Composite stream refuses that illegibility by making compilation perceptible.
5.3 Homer vs Auden Is a Controlled Collision of World-Specs
Auden’s The Shield of Achilles is not “inspired by” Homer in a soft way; it is an overwrite. First published in 1952 and later collected in The Shield of Achilles (1955), Auden replaces Homer’s plural, vibrant social totality with a barren, bureaucratic landscape—a world where procedure remains but meaning drains out. (Home)
Operative ekphrasis turns this into a lab condition: two world-specifications compete for instantiation. Homer specifies a cosmos of stacked human activities; Auden specifies the modern administrative void. When a generative system is asked to “make the shield,” it is forced to negotiate between these competing cultural weights—between abundance and austerity, ritual and bureaucracy, polis and apparatus. That negotiation is the real object of critique, because it reveals which history the model is predisposed to render as “natural.”
5.4 The Claim This Section Forces
If the shield is treated as a benchmark, one conclusion becomes unavoidable:
Image generation was never the endpoint. The endpoint is world generation, and the real contest is whether our interfaces will conceal or expose the compilation of worldtexts.
And that is why the Shield of Achilles belongs here: it is the oldest worldtext in the Western archive, and it still outclasses our current evaluation habits—because it refuses to be “just an image.”

Genie 3 is explicitly framed around generating interactive environments from simple text descriptions that can be explored in real time; Project Genie packages that premise as a usable prototype. The agency is no longer primarily in the literary surface of the description; it is distributed across prompt templates, model weights, platform affordances, and iterative selection loops.
Recognizing this changes what criticism must touch. The prompt cannot be evaluated as a standalone text, because it is only half of an imagetext object whose other half is a generated image emerging from an encoded cultural substrate. This is why claims that “the prompt is the artwork” are simultaneously plausible and insufficient: the prompt’s aesthetic status cannot be separated from the system that operationalizes it, nor from the selection practices that stabilize one output as “the” output.
Manovich’s framing of prompting as probing latent space becomes legible here as a concrete mechanism rather than a metaphor: prompting is a structured interrogation of a compressed cultural archive whose responses are probabilistic. The imagetext, in this sense, is not a single thing you write; it is a coupled system: language operating on weights to produce an image, which then retroacts on language through iterative refinement.
Operative ekphrasis therefore forces a hard conclusion: ekphrasis is no longer only a rhetorical practice; it is now an interface regime. And once ekphrasis becomes an interface regime, the old questions (“Can words capture images?”) become less urgent than the new ones: Which words bind to which visual outcomes, under whose defaults, with what hidden exclusions, and with what consequences when those bindings scale?

Thick Description Was Never “More Context.” That Misreading Now Breaks Prompting Research.
“Thick description” gets domesticated in tech discourse into a harmless slogan: add more context, get better results. That is not Geertz’s move. Thick description is a diagnostic weapon: it exposes the invisible codes that make behavior legible, the stacked meanings that make a blink a signal and not just an eyelid twitch. When prompting borrows the phrase without the bite, it commits the first category error: it treats thickness as verbosity.
World models force the second, more expensive category error: they make “thickness” operational. A prompt is no longer a request for an image. It is increasingly a world-spec—a set of constraints that binds not just what is seen, but what can happen.
This is the reversal that matters. Thick description interprets a practice that already exists; the culture precedes the text. Thick prompting does the opposite: the description executes. The codes are not only read; they are called—summoned out of weights and defaults into visible, navigable form. And because those weights are probabilistic and historically scraped, the “culture” being invoked is not a stable tradition but a volatile composite: captioned taste, platform priors, market aesthetics, and inherited bias, all hardened into a generative substrate.
That substrate is now being asked to do more than produce imagetexts. Ha and Schmidhuber’s “world models” formalized a core premise: a generative model can learn compressed spatiotemporal dynamics and even support agents trained inside its own hallucinated “dream,” later transferred back to an environment. (arXiv) The key point is not reinforcement learning trivia; it is ontological: the model’s “hallucination” is treated as a usable world.
In 2025–2026, that premise is no longer confined to papers. DeepMind’s Genie 3 is explicitly positioned as a general-purpose world model that generates interactive environments from text descriptions. (Google DeepMind) DeepMind has also framed “world models” as systems that simulate environment dynamics and how actions change them, and has surfaced Project Genie as an interactive product experience. (blog.google) In parallel, World Labs’ Marble markets “high-fidelity, persistent 3D worlds” generated from prompts (and other inputs), with documentation describing multimodal world models that can reconstruct, generate, and simulate 3D worlds. (Marble)
This is where Mitchell’s imagetext stops being the end-state and becomes a stepping-stone. Imagetext names a welded object: word-image entanglement as the site of ekphrastic hope/fear. Worldtext names the new condition: the welded object now includes dynamics—an interactive, probabilistic simulation in which language functions as a handle on scene, object, and behavior. When the output is a world, the prompt is not “descriptive.” It is constitutional.
That shift detonates today’s evaluation norms. Accuracy, similarity, and one-shot “did you get what you wanted?” metrics collapse when the artifact is a navigable environment. A world is not “correct” because it matches a reference image; it is “operative” because it sustains coherence, affordances, and constraint under interaction. The prompt is therefore not merely an instruction—it is a governance mechanism: it defines what the user can do, what the world will permit, what kinds of beings and events are even representable.
So the stakes of thick prompting are not primarily aesthetic finesse. The stakes are legibility and power: who gets to write the world-spec, which defaults get smuggled in as “natural,” and what becomes invisible as world models pursue seamlessness. If the imagetext already threatened to dissolve the word into the image, the worldtext threatens to dissolve critique into experience—because a convincing world is the most efficient way to stop people from asking how it was made.

The “Qualities” of Thick Prompting Are Not Traits — They’re Control Points
Thick prompting is usually described like a bag of clever techniques. That framing is strategically soothing. The actual pattern is harsher: every “quality” of thick prompting marks a place where agency moved out of the sentence and into a broader compilation pipeline—templates, reference media, toolchains, and selection loops. Once world models enter the picture—interactive environments generated from text prompts—the cost of misreading these control points goes up, because the prompt stops specifying an image and starts specifying a world-behavior envelope. (Google DeepMind)
Iterative → Selection is the hidden author
Iteration is not refinement; it is search + curation. The loop doesn’t merely “improve prompts”—it trains the human into the model’s priors by rewarding what the model will reliably give back. This is why evaluation that scores only the final prompt-output pair is structurally blind: it ignores the authoring force of repeated sampling, rejection, and convergence.
Multimodal → Reference inputs become covert steering
Once images/video enter the loop, “prompting” becomes closer to constraint injection than description. Multimodal inputs don’t just add context; they anchor composition, lighting, and subject-matter in ways that evade text-based auditing. In world-building systems marketed as multimodal world models (e.g., Marble), this steering becomes a world-specification primitive, not a stylistic flourish. (World Labs)
Heterogeneous → The prompt becomes a program
When JSON schemas, scripts, tool calls, or UI state determine what gets sent, the “prompt” is no longer a string—it’s compiled behavior. Your ACHILLES workflow (zonal selection → snippet extraction → wrapper template → POST → reintegration) is exactly the point: thickness lives in the machinery. At that point, auditing “the prompt” without auditing the pipeline is like reviewing a film by grading the clapperboard.
Itinerant → Portability is a lie; prompts drift across platforms
A prompt that “works” in one model/platform is not a stable instruction—it’s a negotiated handshake with a specific latent culture + interface grammar. As prompts travel from text-to-image to text-to-3D to interactive world systems, they undergo semantic drift because each platform binds language to different priors, affordances, and failure modes. “Itinerant” isn’t a fun trait; it’s a reproducibility and governance problem.
Performative & interactive → The artifact is the trajectory, not the output
Interactive prompting makes authorship a time-series: the system answers, the human corrects, the system re-answers—until the loop stabilizes into an artifact. That means the relevant object for critique is not “prompt + image,” but the conversation + state + iteration path that produced the result. Ha & Schmidhuber’s world-model framing makes the implication explicit: agents can be trained inside generated “dreams,” then transferred—i.e., the simulated environment’s dynamics become part of what is learned. (arXiv)
Therefore: the “qualities” of thick prompting are not a taxonomy of prompter skill. They are the exposed joints of a new interface regime where templates behave like laws, defaults behave like ideology, and iteration behaves like an invisible editor. As world models like Genie 3 / Project Genie push interactive world generation from text further into public-facing prototypes, the central question is no longer “How do we write better prompts?” It’s: Which compilation pipelines are we letting write our worlds—and what are they making impossible by default? (Google DeepMind)

The Shield(s) of Achilles Is the Benchmark That Breaks the Current Prompt Paradigm
Everyone agrees the Shield of Achilles is “the” canonical ekphrasis. That consensus is precisely the trap: it encourages people to treat the shield as a literary ornament—an image described in words—rather than what it actually is: a world specification embedded inside an epic.
That matters now because world models are arriving with the exact same structure, but with an interface. Genie 3 is explicitly framed as a general-purpose world model that generates interactive environments from text descriptions, and Project Genie is the public prototype of that premise. (Google DeepMind) World Labs’ Marble markets the same move—promptable, persistent 3D worlds—and positions image→world lifting as a standard workflow. (Marble)
So the shield isn’t an “example” of our argument. It is the stress test that reveals where today’s prompting discourse fails. The shield forces an upgrade in the unit of analysis: the prompt is not a sentence that requests a picture; the prompt is a structured procedure that binds language to world-making.
Homer’s shield passage (Iliad 18) already behaves like a generator: it enumerates cosmology, agriculture, dance, adjudication, war—multiple registers of social reality—then constrains them inside a circular topology bounded by Ocean. (scaife.perseus.org) In other words, it does what contemporary world systems promise: it doesn’t merely render an object; it compiles a total environment with internal contrasts and rules.
5.1 The Workflow Is the Argument (Why “Thick Prompting” Lives in the Pipeline)
If the field keeps looking for “thickness” in longer prose prompts, it will miss the actual location of control: the compiled workflow. Your ACHILLES // OPTICAL_GRID_v7 artifact makes the point with cruelty:
the user doesn’t “write a prompt” so much as select a coordinate in a topological text-world (zone selection on a UV-mapped sphere);
the system doesn’t “use the stanza” so much as extract a stochastic micro-spec (5–8-word contiguous snippets);
the output isn’t “returned” so much as re-inscribed into the same navigable surface, becoming persistent world texture.
That is not promptcraft as rhetoric. That is promptcraft as procedural world-binding.
Once you admit this, you can stop pretending the prompt is a string. The prompt is: geometry + selection rules + wrapper template + model call + compositing + persistence. The “text” is only one operand in a larger compilation graph.
5.2 Two Competing Futures: Seamless World Models vs Exposed World-Making
World-model development strongly incentivizes a single aesthetic endpoint: the invisible interface. “Holodeck” design treats the prompt as a hidden trigger and rewards systems that bury their own mediation under photoreal continuity. Genie 3 is explicitly oriented toward interactive environments that can be explored in real time from simple text descriptions—exactly the kind of interface where the machinery disappears. (Google DeepMind)
Your ACHILLES artifact argues the opposite: exposure is the aesthetic. CRT overlays, shutter flashes, targeting HUDs, blend-mode toggles, UV-map exports—these aren’t flourishes. They are governance. They keep the prompt visible as an operational negotiation between human text and machine weights.
This is not a stylistic preference; it is an epistemic fork. The more seamless world generation becomes, the more the world’s defaults become illegible. The Composite stream refuses that illegibility by making compilation perceptible.
5.3 Homer vs Auden Is a Controlled Collision of World-Specs
Auden’s The Shield of Achilles is not “inspired by” Homer in a soft way; it is an overwrite. First published in 1952 and later collected in The Shield of Achilles (1955), Auden replaces Homer’s plural, vibrant social totality with a barren, bureaucratic landscape—a world where procedure remains but meaning drains out. (Home)
Operative ekphrasis turns this into a lab condition: two world-specifications compete for instantiation. Homer specifies a cosmos of stacked human activities; Auden specifies the modern administrative void. When a generative system is asked to “make the shield,” it is forced to negotiate between these competing cultural weights—between abundance and austerity, ritual and bureaucracy, polis and apparatus. That negotiation is the real object of critique, because it reveals which history the model is predisposed to render as “natural.”
5.4 The Claim This Section Forces
If the shield is treated as a benchmark, one conclusion becomes unavoidable:
Image generation was never the endpoint. The endpoint is world generation, and the real contest is whether our interfaces will conceal or expose the compilation of worldtexts.
And that is why the Shield of Achilles belongs here: it is the oldest worldtext in the Western archive, and it still outclasses our current evaluation habits—because it refuses to be “just an image.”

Conclusion: Seamless Worlds Are the Default — and That Default Is the Problem
The field’s accepted trajectory is clear: make the world model better until the interface vanishes. Genie 3 is explicitly framed around generating interactive environments from simple text descriptions that can be explored in real time; Project Genie packages that premise as a usable prototype. (Google DeepMind) Marble markets the same destination—high-fidelity, persistent 3D worlds from short prompts—i.e., “world generation” as a consumer workflow. (Marble)
That is the paradigm we have to destabilize: prompt-disappearance is not a neutral UX win. It is an epistemic and political design choice. The more seamless the world, the more the world’s defaults become law while looking like nature.
Mitchell’s imagetext named the old anxiety: the word longs to govern the image, then fears being consumed by it. (CompLit U of T) Worldtext is that anxiety upgraded into infrastructure: language doesn’t just “describe” a world—it binds to a generative apparatus that produces a navigable simulation whose dynamics can train agents, shape perception, and normalize cultural priors as environmental constraint. (Google DeepMind) (Ha & Schmidhuber’s world-model framing makes the transfer logic explicit: simulated environments can become training grounds whose learned policies carry outward. (CompLit U of T))
So the core risk is not “people might make fake images.” The core risk is metric capture + illegibility: evaluation regimes reward coherence and immersion while ignoring provenance, defaults, exclusions, and the compiled workflow that actually authored the world.
This is why the Shield of Achilles is not a charming example; it is a warning label. Homer’s shield is a world-spec—cosmos, city, conflict, labor—bounded by Ocean. (scaife.perseus.org) Auden’s rewrite is also a world-spec, but it compiles modern bureaucracy and void into the same formal container. (Home) Operative ekphrasis lets us treat those as competing specifications whose consequences can be staged, compared, and audited—rather than treated as “interpretations” floating above mechanism. (Taylor & Francis Online)
Therefore, the conclusion is a design mandate: if world models push toward the Photoreal Stream (seamless immersion), criticism must push toward the Composite Stream (exposed compilation). Your ACHILLES artifact isn’t just an artwork; it’s a governance prototype: it keeps the word visible, dramatizes extraction, and reveals the UV underbelly so the “world” cannot pretend it arrived unmade.
Non-negotiables for worldtext criticism (what we should require next)
Treat the prompt as a compiled workflow, not a string: selection rules, templates, reference inputs, iteration path, and compositing are part of the authoring object.
Evaluate auditability, not just realism: can a viewer recover how the world was specified, sampled, and stabilized?
Expose defaults as “world laws”: style priors, safety filters, dataset bias, and platform affordances must be legible at the point of experience.
Preserve the prompt-trail: the time-series of interaction is the artifact when the output is a world, not a frame.
Prefer accentuated interfaces when stakes are cultural/historical: seamlessness is not innocence; it is concealment.
If we don’t institutionalize those requirements, the worldtext will become the most efficient machine ever built for laundering ideology into “environment.” If we do, operative ekphrasis becomes what it should have been all along: not magic, but visible world-making under constraint. (Taylor & Francis Online)
